## 2026-07-28

`sources/mom/TICVAI_Discry_Wrkshp_Day_1_Jul_28_2026.docx` · 3,620 words

### Minutes of Meeting

- TICVAI Technical Discovery Workshop – Architecture & Infrastructure

Date: 28 July 2026Meeting Type: Technical discovery and architecture workshopPrimary Objective: To review the proposed TICVAI architecture, infrastructure approach, deployment model, technology stack, offline operations, scalability, database strategy, multilingual support, and the documentation required for the next stages of discovery.

### Participants

- TICVAI Team

- Softlabs Team

### 1. POS Design Reference and Functional Walkthrough

- Qossai began by demonstrating an earlier point-of-sale application prototype that had been developed as part of a previous engagement which was later discontinued.

- The prototype was shared as an initial design and functional reference rather than as a solution to be copied directly.

- The demonstrated POS functionality included:

- product and ticket browsing;

- filtering by event type, pricing and other criteria;

- ticket selection and cart creation;

- upselling of related products or experiences;

- cash and other checkout methods;

- seat-selection workflows;

- calendar, capacity and time-slot visibility;

- AI assistant functionality;

- operational notifications and alerts;

- membership details and loyalty points;

- discounts and promotional benefits;

- customer association with transactions;

- notes against individual tickets;

- shift management and shift closing;

- multiple active carts;

- holding and resuming carts;

- cart and transaction history;

- order search;

- refund processing;

- global platform search;

- configurable dashboard widgets;

- transaction and refund statistics;

- a proposed “Magic Bar” for quickly accessing frequently used functions;

- a “Build Your Experience” workflow to help cashiers sell bundled experiences without searching through hundreds of ticket types.

- Makrand confirmed that this would be useful as a baseline for the UI/UX team to understand the client’s preferred operational style and visual direction.

Qossai clarified that the intention is not to reproduce the same interface. Softlabs is expected to evaluate it, improve the user experience and recommend a more efficient and scalable design.

- Softlabs agreed to:

- review the temporary prototype link;

- capture the relevant screens and workflows for internal reference;

- involve the design team;

- propose improvements to usability, layout and functionality.

- Qossai agreed to share the application link and access details after the meeting.

### 2. Workshop Format and Expectations

- The client requested that future workshops be supported by focused presentations prepared by Softlabs for each subject area.

- Each presentation should ideally explain:

- the proposed solution;

- the recommended technology;

- the implementation approach;

- alternative approaches where relevant;

- the rationale for the recommendation;

- key dependencies;

- risks and limitations;

- required client inputs.

Chinmay acknowledged that this workshop had initially been approached as an input-gathering session, but agreed that future sessions would be presented through curated topic-wise presentations rather than by navigating directly through the proposal.

- The client also requested formal architecture documentation, including:

- High-Level Design, or HLD;

- Low-Level Design, or LLD;

- system-component diagrams;

- service-to-service communication;

- module interactions;

- end-to-end information flow;

- cloud-resource requirements;

- deployment architecture.

- These documents are not required immediately for the next meeting, but must be prepared progressively as the architecture is refined.

### 3. Overall Architecture Philosophy

- Softlabs presented the proposed architectural philosophy as:

- API-first;

- cloud-agnostic;

- domain-driven;

- modular;

- microservices-oriented;

- independently scalable;

- capable of cloud and on-premise deployment.

- The core principle is to ensure that interfaces, modules, external integrations and hardware adapters remain loosely coupled.

- This would allow future changes such as:

- switching cloud providers;

- changing an integration partner;

- replacing a hardware vendor;

- introducing new APIs;

- scaling a specific module;

- deploying to a customer-owned environment;

- without having to redesign the entire platform.

- The proposed initial approach is to define the APIs and data contracts first, followed by development of the interfaces and integrated applications.

### 4. Cloud Infrastructure: Managed Services vs Virtual Machines

- Qossai raised an important question on whether the solution should use:

- virtual machines hosted on Azure or AWS; or

- managed cloud services such as Azure SQL, web applications and equivalent AWS services.

- The client’s view was that managed services may be:

- more cost-effective;

- easier to deploy;

- easier to maintain;

- faster to scale;

- better suited for enterprise customers.

- Softlabs explained that the final decision should be based on:

- expected usage volume;

- concurrent traffic;

- deployment complexity;

- operating cost;

- maintenance effort;

- geographical data-residency requirements;

- scalability;

- client-specific infrastructure requirements.

- The teams agreed that managed cloud services should be given serious preference, subject to a technical and commercial comparison.

- Softlabs will eventually provide a comparative infrastructure recommendation covering Azure and AWS.

### 5. Data Residency

- The client confirmed that cloud-managed services can still comply with UAE data-residency requirements, provided the resources are deployed in an approved UAE cloud region.

- A relevant example was shared where a government-related client required all data to remain within the UAE.

- The agreed principle is:

- data must remain in the client-approved geographical region;

- enterprise or government customer data must not be copied into TICVAI’s own central environment;

- any backup, high-availability or disaster-recovery architecture must remain within the customer’s approved infrastructure arrangement.

### 6. Two Deployment and Commercial Models

- The client clarified two distinct deployment models.

- 6.1 TICVAI-hosted SaaS model for smaller customers

- Smaller customers would subscribe online through TICVAI’s platform.

- The proposed flow would be:

- Customer selects the required modules.

- Customer completes online payment.

- Customer enters venue and business details.

- The platform automatically provisions the customer environment.

- The customer configures products, tickets, users and venue information.

- The customer begins using the system.

The client prefers that each customer receive an isolated database or logically independent data store rather than mixing all customer data in one shared database.

- 6.2 Dedicated enterprise deployment

- Larger enterprise or government customers may require:

- their own Azure or AWS subscription;

- their own database;

- dedicated infrastructure;

- on-premise deployment;

- direct contract with the cloud provider;

- client-controlled high availability and disaster recovery.

- In such cases, Softlabs/TICVAI would deploy the product into the customer’s environment.

- No customer data would be replicated back to the TICVAI-hosted environment.

### 7. Cloud Resource Documentation

- The client requested a structured infrastructure document for major cloud providers, particularly Azure and AWS.

- The future document should specify:

- minimum viable infrastructure for a small customer;

- infrastructure for medium and large deployments;

- managed services required;

- database services;

- storage services;

- networking components;

- expected CPU and memory;

- auto-scaling approach;

- redundancy requirements;

- high-availability options;

- disaster-recovery options;

- expected deployment differences between Azure and AWS.

- The client clarified that this is a later-stage deliverable and does not need to be completed immediately.

### 8. Thin and Thick Applications

- Softlabs explained the proposed division between thin and thick applications.

- Thin applications

- These would primarily include:

- browser-based admin portals;

- customer-facing web storefronts;

- reporting dashboards;

- web-based management interfaces.

- The server would execute the primary business logic.

- Thick or offline-capable applications

- These would include:

- point-of-sale applications;

- handheld ticket-validation applications;

- mobile operational applications;

- selected customer-facing mobile functions.

- These applications must continue supporting critical operations during temporary internet outages.

### 9. Technology Stack

- The following technology direction was discussed.

- Web front end

- React

- Mobile applications

- React Native preferred

- Flutter considered but not preferred

- The client agreed that React Native appeared appropriate due to:

- cross-platform support;

- performance;

- design flexibility;

- ecosystem maturity;

- available integrations;

- Softlabs’ practical experience.

- Backend

- .NET for enterprise business services

- Python for AI and machine-learning components

- Node.js only where justified for real-time or specialised use cases

- Data and messaging

- PostgreSQL as the initial principal database

- Apache Kafka as the messaging backbone

- Redis for sessions, tokens and high-speed access

- Elasticsearch for enhanced search

- SQLite or a similar embedded database for mobile/offline storage

- Docker and Kubernetes for containerisation where applicable

- Grafana and OpenTelemetry for monitoring and observability

- The selected stack remains subject to refinement during discovery.

### 10. MongoDB and Approved Technology Constraints

The client advised that MongoDB had historically not been approved by the relevant Dubai digital authority, referred to in the discussion as “DESC” or a similar authority.

- MongoDB must therefore not be treated as automatically approved.

- Allam agreed to verify:

- whether MongoDB is now approved;

- which NoSQL alternatives are approved;

- whether Cosmos DB remains an approved option;

- which infrastructure and security technologies are officially permissible.

- Softlabs clarified that the restriction appears to be specifically related to MongoDB rather than all NoSQL databases.

- PostgreSQL remains the preferred starting point because it can support:

- conventional relational data;

- JSON data;

- selected vector-search requirements;

- multiple operational use cases.

- Dedicated vector databases can be introduced later if performance requirements justify them.

### 11. Microservices and Domain Boundaries

- Softlabs presented an initial model containing 12 domain-oriented service groups.

- Each service group is expected to:

- remain independently deployable;

- own its data schema;

- scale independently;

- avoid unnecessary coupling;

- prevent failure in one domain from affecting others.

- Examples include:

- ticketing;

- sales and commerce;

- finance;

- operations;

- marketing;

- access control;

- customer engagement;

- platform administration.

- Qossai asked how functions such as the following would be classified:

- CRM;

- wallet;

- loyalty;

- reporting;

- inventory.

- The initial view was that they could be assigned under the most appropriate domain, such as:

- loyalty and wallet under ticketing or customer engagement;

- reporting under finance or a dedicated analytics layer;

- inventory under commerce or operations.

- The final service boundaries will be determined through the detailed HLD and LLD exercise.

### 12. Hybrid and On-Premise Deployment

- The client reconfirmed that the platform must support:

- public cloud;

- client-specific private cloud;

- hybrid environments;

- on-premise installations.

- All selected components should therefore be capable of running without mandatory dependence on a single proprietary cloud service.

- The principal challenge for on-premise deployments will be:

- fixed hardware limitations;

- horizontal scaling;

- update management;

- deployment of new releases;

- customer connectivity restrictions.

- Possible update approaches include:

- secure remote deployment;

- customer-exposed deployment endpoints;

- offline deployment packages;

- onsite installation where required.

- The final mechanism may differ by client.

### 13. Environment Strategy

- The proposed delivery environment structure includes:

- Development

- For:

- active development;

- unit testing;

- integration testing;

- internal quality assurance.

- Pre-production

- For:

- user acceptance testing;

- performance testing;

- security validation;

- pilot readiness.

- Production

- For:

- live operations;

- end-user transactions;

- customer deployment.

- Softlabs confirmed that an internal development environment would be created from the beginning.

The client requested access to functional modules as soon as they become mature enough for review, rather than waiting for the full solution or pre-production release.

- Softlabs agreed to provide access progressively, module by module, enabling early feedback.

### 14. High Availability and Disaster Recovery

- The discussion clarified the distinction between:

- keeping a copy of customer data in TICVAI’s environment; and

- maintaining high availability or disaster recovery within the customer’s environment.

- The agreed position is:

- customer databases will not be copied into TICVAI’s central environment;

- high availability may be offered as an optional infrastructure configuration;

- disaster recovery should be supported;

- disaster recovery should preferably be in a separate region;

- the customer may directly decide and fund its HA/DR configuration through its cloud agreement.

For example, if the production environment is hosted in the UAE, the DR environment may be hosted in another approved regional location such as Bahrain, subject to regulatory approval.

### 15. Offline POS and Access-Control Operations

- Offline operations were one of the most detailed areas discussed.

- The client made it clear that offline support must be available in:

- POS applications;

- handheld ticket-validation applications;

- access-control applications;

- other critical operational applications.

- 15.1 General admission tickets

- POS must continue selling general admission tickets during an internet outage.

- General admission tickets are easier to support offline because they may not involve:

- fixed seats;

- time-slot inventory;

- capacity-controlled allocations.

- Similarly, access-control applications must continue scanning and validating tickets during a connectivity failure.

- 15.2 Local validation database

- The client strongly preferred a secure local database on the handheld device.

- During an outage:

- the device would validate tickets against the local database;

- scans would be stored locally;

- the information would synchronise when connectivity returns.

The client did not prefer an approach based only on identifying whether the QR code format belongs to TICVAI because that could increase fraud risk.

- 15.3 Seat and time-slot bookings

- The client highlighted a serious risk with offline selling of:

- assigned seats;

- time slots;

- limited-capacity products.

- If POS, website, B2B and kiosks lose synchronisation, multiple channels may sell the same seat or consume the same capacity.

- Softlabs acknowledged that unrestricted offline selling for allocated inventory would create an unacceptable overbooking risk.

### 16. Proposed Offline Inventory Pooling

- Qossai suggested a potential solution using channel-specific inventory pools.

- For example, remaining seats or capacity could be divided among:

- B2C;

- B2B;

- POS;

- kiosks;

- mobile channels.

- During normal online operation, inventory could be managed flexibly.

- During an outage, each channel would sell only from its reserved allocation.

- This would reduce the risk of multiple offline channels selling the same inventory.

- The same concept could apply to:

- seat blocks;

- zones;

- time-slot capacity;

- general capacity pools.

- The teams considered this a promising approach but agreed that Softlabs should analyse it further.

- The design should also consider:

- unused inventory in one pool;

- reallocation during normal operations;

- local network coordination among POS terminals;

- reconciliation when connectivity returns;

- exception handling;

- operational controls.

- No final design was approved during the meeting.

### 17. QR Codes and Offline Ticket Validation

- The solution must support:

- secure QR-code generation;

- changing or dynamic QR codes where required;

- cryptographic validation;

- offline recognition of legitimate tickets;

- local storage of validation keys or ticket data;

- synchronisation after reconnection.

- The target discussed for ticket validation was below approximately 500 milliseconds.

- Bluetooth Low Energy and venue-presence validation had also been considered earlier and remain subject to further technical review.

### 18. Performance and Scalability

- The preliminary targets discussed included:

- ticket validation under 500 milliseconds;

- web-page loading under approximately 3 seconds;

- mobile-application loading under approximately 2 seconds;

- initial API throughput of approximately 200–1,000 requests per second;

- support for at least 5,000–15,000 concurrent or active guests in the initial architecture;

- the ability to scale significantly beyond those initial numbers.

- Qossai clarified that event traffic can be highly unpredictable.

- A major event may attract:

- tens of thousands of simultaneous visitors;

- heavy browsing without purchase;

- sudden traffic spikes;

- high seat-map read activity;

- multiple simultaneous sales channels.

An example was discussed in which approximately 50,000 users could visit a website at the same time when tickets for a major performer are released.

### 19. Auto-scaling and Virtual Waiting Room

- Both parties agreed that the solution should support two complementary mechanisms.

- Auto-scaling

- The infrastructure should automatically increase or reduce resources based on:

- traffic;

- API load;

- active sessions;

- transaction volume;

- database demand.

- Virtual waiting room or queue management

- The platform should also support a configurable waiting-room facility where only a controlled number of customers may enter the booking flow at once.

- Possible features include:

- branded waiting-room page;

- customer’s venue logo;

- estimated waiting time;

- controlled admission intervals;

- configurable maximum active users;

- progress indicators;

- back-office controls.

- The queue-management requirement must work independently for each customer and venue.

### 20. Tenant Isolation During Traffic Spikes

- The client highlighted that a major event for one tenant must not degrade performance for another tenant using the same TICVAI-hosted infrastructure.

- For example:

- an arena may experience extremely high demand;

- a museum may have light daily traffic;

- both may be hosted within the broader TICVAI platform.

- The architecture must ensure that:

- one tenant’s traffic does not consume all shared resources;

- databases and services remain isolated;

- auto-scaling can occur at the required tenant or service level;

- queue management can be configured independently;

- high-demand tenants can be separated into dedicated pools where required.

- Softlabs agreed to study this in more detail as part of the storage, caching and infrastructure design.

### 21. Read-Heavy and Write-Heavy Patterns

- Dinesh explained that large ticketing platforms often experience a very high read-to-write ratio.

- Many visitors may:

- browse events;

- inspect seat maps;

- compare prices;

- check schedules;

- leave without purchasing.

- This becomes particularly important for assigned-seating events.

- The architecture should therefore consider:

- caching;

- read replicas;

- optimised queries;

- specialised high-traffic data pools;

- horizontal scaling;

- efficient indexing;

- separating frequently accessed information.

- The client confirmed that this concern is most relevant for high-demand seating events and less important for small admission-only venues.

### 22. Small-Customer Database Provisioning

- The client’s preferred model for smaller self-service subscribers is:

- each subscriber receives an automatically created database;

- the database remains logically and operationally separate;

- tenant data is not mixed;

- configuration begins immediately after online subscription.

- Softlabs noted that smaller isolated databases may provide:

- better tenant separation;

- faster indexing;

- easier customer migration;

- improved security;

- simpler backup and restoration.

- However, the final approach remains open for internal technical analysis.

- The team will compare:

- separate database per tenant;

- shared database with isolated schemas;

- hybrid model based on customer size.

### 23. Database Optimisation and Archiving

- The client requested support for long-term data archiving.

An example was discussed where a customer may operate the system for more than five years but keep only the most recent three years in the live database.

- Possible approach:

- Define a configurable retention period.

- Run an automated background archival service.

- Move older transactions to an archive database.

- Remove the archived records from the active database.

- Allow reports and historical searches to retrieve archived information when required.

- Softlabs confirmed that this can be designed into the HLD and LLD.

- The final design should support:

- customer-specific retention policies;

- manual or automated archival;

- continued access to historical data;

- minimal effect on production performance.

### 24. Reporting Database and Read Replica

- The client raised the concern that running a two- or three-year report against the live transactional database could affect ticket sales and core operations.

- Softlabs agreed that reporting should not place heavy load on the primary operational database.

- The proposed direction includes:

- read replicas;

- reporting database;

- replicated analytical data;

- separate reporting queries;

- archival data integration.

- This architecture will allow users to run large reports without degrading live transaction performance.

### 25. Storage of Images and Content

- It was clarified that image files should not be stored directly in PostgreSQL.

- The database would contain:

- image URLs;

- file metadata;

- references.

- The image files themselves would be stored in:

- S3;

- Azure Blob Storage;

- equivalent object or block storage.

- Other CMS and transactional data may remain in PostgreSQL.

### 26. Web Application Firewall and Approved Security Components

- The client requested confirmation that the platform would include a Web Application Firewall.

- Softlabs confirmed that a WAF would form part of the architecture.

- However, the client explained that the relevant Dubai authority may approve only selected firewall technologies.

- Allam agreed to verify and share:

- approved WAF products;

- permitted security services;

- technology-compliance documentation;

- any authority-issued approved-component list.

- Softlabs will select the firewall after reviewing the permitted options.

### 27. Internationalisation and Arabic Support

- Arabic must be treated as a core platform requirement and not as a later localisation activity.

- The platform must support Arabic RTL across:

- web applications;

- mobile applications;

- POS;

- reports;

- emails;

- WhatsApp messages;

- SMS;

- notifications;

- tickets and receipts;

- administrative interfaces.

- The initial language priority is:

- English

- Arabic

- Russian

- Chinese

- Other languages such as Spanish at a later stage

- The design and database must be capable of supporting additional languages without major redevelopment.

### 28. Items Deferred to the Next Workshop

- The multi-tenancy strategy was intentionally deferred because both teams agreed it requires a separate and detailed discussion.

- The next session is expected to cover:

- multi-tenancy;

- infrastructure;

- API gateway;

- tenant isolation;

- tenant provisioning;

- shared versus dedicated services;

- database strategy;

- platform-management considerations.

- Chinmay will prepare a focused presentation for the next workshop rather than reviewing the proposal directly.

### 29. Decisions and Agreements

- The following broad agreements were reached:

- The POS prototype will be treated as a reference, not copied directly.

- Softlabs will recommend UI/UX improvements.

- Future workshops will use focused presentations.

- HLD and LLD documents will be prepared progressively.

- The platform will follow an API-first, cloud-agnostic and domain-driven architecture.

- Managed cloud services will be evaluated against virtual machines.

- Both Azure and AWS deployment models will be documented.

- Customer data will not be copied into TICVAI’s central environment.

- React will be used for the web platform.

- React Native is the preferred mobile framework.

- .NET and Python are the preferred backend technologies.

- PostgreSQL will be the initial primary database.

- MongoDB approval must be revalidated.

- Cloud, hybrid and on-premise deployments must be supported.

- Development, pre-production and production environments will be maintained.

- The client will receive access to usable development modules progressively.

- Offline support is mandatory for critical POS and access-control functions.

- General admission should continue during outages.

- Uncontrolled offline selling of allocated seats and capacity is not acceptable.

- Channel-based inventory pools will be evaluated.

- Auto-scaling and virtual waiting rooms are required.

- One tenant’s traffic must not degrade another tenant.

- Reporting should use replicas or a separate reporting database.

- Archival must be designed into the database architecture.

- Arabic must be supported across all customer communication channels.

- Multi-tenancy will be discussed in the next workshop.

### 30. Action Items

- Softlabs Team

- Review and preserve the POS prototype for UI/UX reference.

- Share the prototype with the design team.

- Propose an enhanced POS user experience.

- Prepare focused presentation material for future workshops.

- Prepare the High-Level Architecture document.

- Prepare the Low-Level Architecture document.

- Develop system and data-flow diagrams.

- Define Azure and AWS deployment options.

- Prepare minimum infrastructure requirements for different customer sizes.

- Define auto-scaling and queue-management architecture.

- Analyse tenant-isolation strategies.

- Evaluate separate database per tenant, schema isolation and hybrid approaches.

- Design the offline POS and handheld-validation architecture.

- Evaluate the channel-based offline inventory-pooling model.

- Design reporting read replicas or a reporting database.

- Include archival in the database design.

- Define cloud, hybrid and on-premise update strategies.

- Finalise the proposed technology stack after compliance validation.

- Prepare the next presentation on multi-tenancy, platform infrastructure and API gateway.

- Share any required client inputs at least one day before each workshop.

- Update the workshop tracker and completion status.

- Share the meeting transcript and MOM.

- TICVAI Team

- Share the POS prototype link and access credentials.

- Confirm the current MongoDB approval status.

- Share the approved alternative NoSQL technologies, if applicable.

- Share the approved WAF and security-component list.

- Share any relevant Dubai authority technology-compliance documents.

- Provide expected user volumes and transaction estimates for different customer categories.

- Provide anticipated peak traffic for major events.

- Clarify preferred infrastructure expectations for small, medium and enterprise customers.

- Review Softlabs’ forthcoming HLD and LLD documents.

- Provide any required information before the next architecture workshop.

### 31. Next Meeting

- The next workshop is planned for the same morning time slot, approximately 10:30 AM IST, Thursday, July 29th 2026.

- The proposed subject for the next workshop is:

- Multi-Tenancy Strategy, Platform Infrastructure and API Gateway

- The client requested that Softlabs communicate the next workshop agenda and any information required from the TICVAI team at least one day in advance.

### Minutes of Meeting

- TICVAI Kickoff — Technical Discovery & Architecture Workshop

- Date 30 July 2026 Project TICVAI

- --- --- --- ---

- Meeting Type Technical Discovery & Architecture Workshop Prepared by Chinmay Parab

### Primary Objective

- To review the proposed TICVAI platform architecture, multi-tenancy model, governance approach, deployment strategy, versioning process, API structure, and base project setup.

### Participants

- - TICVAI

- - Softlabs Team

- A genda

- - Review the proposed multi-tenant architecture

- - Discuss governance and tenant hierarchy

- - Review API structure and project setup

- - Discuss deployment and software release strategy

- - Define software versioning approach

- - Plan the next technical workshop

### 1. Overview of Architecture Presentation

Chinmay Parab opened the session, noting that the presentation had been prepared to cover both the current discussion topics and the topics originally planned for the following session. The presentation addressed:

- - Multi-tenancy architecture

- - Governance model

- - API structure

- - Base project setup

- The objective was to provide a broader architectural view before proceeding with implementation-specific discussions.

### 2. Proposed Multi-Tenant Hierarchy

- The Softlabs team presented the proposed hierarchical structure for the platform:

- Tenant └─ Organization / Brand └─ Region └─ Branch └─ Venue └─ Department

- ---

- The purpose of this hierarchy is to provide:

- - Clear tenant separation

- - Better deployment management

- - Scalability for multiple organizations

- - Support for clients operating across several locations

- - Department-level isolation and access control

- The hierarchy was designed so that each client could manage multiple organizations, geographical regions, branches, venues, and departments within a single tenant.

### 3. Feedback on Organizational Structure

- Chinmay requested feedback on the proposed hierarchy, specifically asking whether:

- - Additional hierarchy levels should be introduced

- - Existing levels should be merged

- - The current structure adequately supports future scalability

- Allam noted that TICVAI had already prepared a more detailed organizational hierarchy, and that:

- - The document would be shared after the meeting

- - The structure would be explained in detail

- - Both structures could then be compared before making a final architectural decision

- Outcome: The existing proposal remains under review until the TICVAI structure is evaluated.

### 4. Deployment Workflow Discussion

- Discussion shifted toward software deployment and release management. Allam proposed a structured deployment workflow centered on a staging environment:

- Development ↓ Staging Environment ↓ Customer Notification ↓ Customer Testing ↓ Customer Approval ↓ Production Deployment

- ---

- Under this process:

- - New releases are first deployed to staging

- - Customers receive notifications whenever a new version becomes available, including:

- - New features

- - Bug fixes

- - Release notes

- - Customers validate functionality in staging

- - The release is promoted to production only after customer approval

- Benefits Discussed

- - Reduced production risk

- - Better customer confidence

- - Opportunity for user acceptance testing

- - Controlled production rollouts

### 5. Standardizing Deployment

- Chinmay discussed simplifying deployments by reducing operational friction. Topics included:

- - Standardizing deployment processes

- - Standardizing database migrations

- - Automating repetitive deployment activities

- - Making production releases more seamless

- Standardization was noted to significantly improve maintainability and reduce deployment complexity.

### 6. Global Versioning Strategy

- A significant portion of the discussion focused on version management.

- Minor Releases

- Qossai suggested that minor releases should:

- - Notify customers when available

- - Remain optional

- - Allow customers to postpone installation if new functionality is not immediately required

- Examples: small enhancements, minor bug fixes, and UI improvements.

- Major Releases

- Major platform releases would follow a different process, including:

- - Advance notification to customers

- - A defined support lifecycle

- - End-of-support announcements for older versions

- - Mandatory migration to the latest supported version

- Example discussed:

- Version 3 ↓ End of Support Notice ↓ Mandatory Upgrade ↓ Version 4

- ---

### 7. Benefits of a Unified Platform Version

- Qossai explained why maintaining a single supported version is beneficial. Supporting multiple production versions creates challenges including:

- - Increased maintenance effort

- - More difficult debugging

- - Longer support cycles

- - Higher development overhead

- - Complex feature management

- Maintaining a single supported version instead enables:

- - Faster bug resolution

- - Easier customer support

- - Simplified testing

- - Consistent deployments

- - Lower maintenance costs

- The Softlabs team agreed that this approach aligns with long-term platform maintainability.

### Decisions Made

- Multi-Tenant Architecture

- - Retain the proposed tenant hierarchy for review

- - Compare it with the detailed TICVAI organizational structure before finalizing

- Deployment Strategy

- The team agreed on a staged deployment model where:

- - Releases are first deployed to staging

- - Customers validate changes

- - Production rollout occurs only after customer approval

- Version Management

- - Minor releases remain optional

- - Major releases become mandatory after the defined support period

- - Long-term objective: maintain one primary supported production version

- Standardization

- Deployment processes and database migration strategies should be standardized wherever possible to minimize release complexity.

### Action Items

- Share detailed organizational hierarchy TICVAI Team Pending

- Review and compare hierarchy models Softlabs & TICVAI Pending

- Finalize multi-tenant architecture Both Teams Pending

- Define standardized deployment workflow Softlabs Team In Progress

- Document software versioning policy Softlabs Team Pending

- Standardize database migration process Softlabs Team In Progress

- Next Meeting

- Date: Friday, 31 July 2026

- Time: 10:30 AM

- Planned Topics

- - API structures

- - Base project setup

- - Remaining architecture discussions

- - Additional technical topics to be circulated before the meeting

- Closing Remarks

The meeting concluded with agreement on the overall architectural direction for the TICVAI platform. Both teams aligned on the need for a scalable multi-tenant architecture, a standardized deployment process, and a simplified version management strategy that minimizes operational overhead while ensuring a consistent customer experience.

- Chinmay confirmed that the Minutes of Meeting and the agenda for the next session would be circulated via email before the following day's workshop.

`sources/mom/TICVAI_MoM_31Jul2026__1_.docx` · 4,586 words · **held as Markdown, no Word original**

### Minutes of Meeting

- TICVAI Technical Discovery Workshop — Security, Non-Functional Requirements & UI/UX Planning

- Date 31 July 2026 Project TICVAI

- --- --- --- ---

- Meeting Type Technical Discovery Workshop — Security, NFRs & UI/UX Planning Prepared by Chitrangi Mestry

- Duration Approx. 1 hour 7 minutes Session Part of ongoing series

### Primary Objective

To finalize outstanding security and non-functional requirements — including scalability, availability, disaster recovery, offline architecture, payments, and localization — and to align on the plan for the upcoming dedicated UI/UX session.

### Participants

- - TICVAI Team

- - Softlabs Team

### Agenda

- - Session scope adjustment & UI/UX session scheduling

- - Reference UI flow & application vision alignment

- - Recap of security features

- - Non-functional requirements: scalability & availability

- - Consistency, replication & disaster recovery

- - Cost planning & cloud provider evaluation

- - Ticket validation & offline architecture

- - Point-of-sale data sync strategy

- - Capacity estimates & case studies

- - Compliance & data protection

- - Offline functionality scope

- - Payments & regional preferences

- - Internationalization & localization

- - Observability & dashboards

- - Monday UI/UX session planning

- - Email communication protocol

### 1. Session Scope Adjustment & UI/UX Scheduling

Chinmay Parab opened by noting that multi-tenancy had already been covered in a previous session and would not need to be revisited, making today's session comparatively shorter. He proposed holding a dedicated UI/UX session on Monday. Qossai agreed, and Chinmay clarified that wireframe development should start in parallel as the sessions progress, rather than waiting for the UI/UX session to begin — both agreed to keep Monday for the dedicated UI/UX walkthrough while wireframing starts in the background.

### 2. Reference UI Flow & Application Vision

Aishwarya More, Softlabs' designer, joined and asked whether the new platform's UI flow would follow the same structure as a reference system Qossai had shared from a prior project, or whether changes were expected. Qossai clarified that the shared link was only a starting point/baseline, not something to copy directly — the intent is to enhance it, and he asked for Softlabs' design experience and suggestions on what could be improved for the user. He explained the reference was originally a point-of-sale system for cashier-led ticket sales, built roughly four to five months earlier with AI assistance, and that a similar approach might also serve TICVAI's B2B customers.

Aishwarya confirmed her question was specifically about navigation/flow consistency rather than visual design. Qossai responded that the flow is largely similar but varies by ticket type — the team has admission tickets, time-slot tickets, and seat-assignment tickets, each with a distinct flow. For example, the admission flow goes straight to a quantity selector, while the seat-assignment flow requires selecting the day, then the time, then the seat. He proposed walking through this in more detail during Monday's session. Chinmay added that Sahil is also expected to join from Monday, and noted that Nilesh had confirmed the shared reference and platform structures would serve as the team's baseline — isolating each platform's UI and starting wireframes early would give a strong boost to the discovery phase and speed up front-end development later.

### 3. Recap of Security Features

Chinmay confirmed that most security features had already been covered in a previous session, including JWT-based authentication as part of the multi-tenancy design, a policy-based SSO system, RBAC (role-based access control) permissions, and a seven-year audit trail requirement. With this confirmed, the discussion moved on to non-functional requirements.

### 4. Non-Functional Requirements: Scalability & Availability

Chinmay outlined the non-functional requirement areas: scalability, availability, ticket validation latency, web page load time, mobile app load time, peak concurrent users, and peak API throughput — noting most of these had already been discussed in detail previously, so this would be a shorter pass focused on availability.

Qossai stressed the importance of availability, sharing a real example from a previous project: a ticketing platform his team installed for a theatre in Bahrain went down when approximately 30,000 people tried to purchase tickets simultaneously for a concert by a very popular regional singer. The outage took several days to resolve and ultimately cost the team the client relationship. He emphasized that TICVAI's infrastructure, auto-scaling, and overall resilience need to be strong enough to avoid a similar failure.

Allam reinforced the reputational risk, noting that an outage during a high-profile event could spread rapidly on social media and damage the brand. Chinmay acknowledged the point and confirmed the team is treating this as a benchmark to design around. He noted Softlabs is bringing in outside expertise for this specific concern — a consultant referred to as "Geo," who has over 15 years of deployment experience at Reliance Jio, one of the largest telecom/ISP networks in the world, with combined concurrent-user scale exceeding major US providers.

Chinmay also noted that Softlabs' own past experience has generally been at an enterprise scale of around 2,000–3,000 concurrent users, and that the company's CTO, Dinesh Jadhav, has broader experience across multiple large-scale projects. Qossai added context: only a small fraction of TICVAI's clients (attractions, museums, exhibitions) will see this kind of extreme traffic — it mainly applies to live events such as concerts or football matches — but that segment still needs to be handled well, since it's disproportionately high-risk.

- Allam proposed building a queue management capability directly into the system rather than relying on a third-party tool, so that traffic entering the site can be throttled from the back office itself.

- Chinmay confirmed platforms like Terraform are already used to monitor server load, and that dashboards will also need to respect the tenancy model — so a venue manager can view traffic specific to their own venue.

### 5. Consistency, Replication & Disaster Recovery

Dinesh Jadhav, joining partway through, asked whether high availability should take priority over strict consistency. A confirmed availability is the priority, and described the intended queue mechanism in more detail: guests are placed in a queue to preserve their connection, informed of an estimated wait time, and let through in controlled batches (e.g., 200–300 guests per minute) as load allows; completed transactions must reliably trigger email confirmations and ticket delivery, and payments must be processed correctly.

Dinesh raised the need for heavy replication to support both scaling and disaster recovery (DR) across regions. Allam clarified DR would be an optional, tenant-selectable module rather than a default for all clients, since it carries additional cost — some tenants may be comfortable keeping data within a single region (e.g., UAE only) without DR. Dinesh noted that even without DR, read replicas would likely be needed to support scalable architecture, implying eventual consistency rather than strict consistency, alongside liveliness checks/observability so a standby system can take over if a component fails.

Allam confirmed the high-availability model: if one SQL instance or web service goes down, another takes over; DR (in a separate region, replicating the full stack including SQL) is a distinct, separately configured capability. Dinesh shared that in his prior experience at BookMyShow, caching was distributed via Redis clusters deployed across regions to support performance, and suggested a similar approach here — Allam agreed this should be implemented. The team aligned on a target uptime of 99.99%, and agreed that performance/load testing (deliberately pushing traffic to observe system behavior) should be built into the implementation plan.

Dinesh flagged that, since this is being built from scratch and is a new scale of project for the team, cost needs to be considered carefully alongside scalability — the team will need firm estimations of expected users to correctly size components such as replica counts and load balancing, particularly for the higher-cost components.

### 6. Cost Planning & Cloud Provider Evaluation

Allam proposed that the team first complete the HLD/LLD design to identify every required component, since different cloud providers offer different equivalent services — a plan should then be prepared separately for both AWS and Azure so cost and fit can be compared once the design is in place.

Qossai asked for Softlabs' advice on AWS vs. Azure, noting TICVAI would look to negotiate favorable pricing with whichever provider is selected. Dinesh gave an initial view: AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud generally offer comparable or equivalent services, so provider choice mainly comes down to resource availability and cost for the specific services required — noting AWS resources tend to be very readily available — but confirmed a final recommendation should wait until the HLD/LLD and component list are complete, in case a specific required service is only available on one platform. Allam agreed, reiterating that provider comparison (including which region/scenario each performs best in) should follow the design work, not precede it.

- Separately, Qossai clarified TICVAI's two deployment approaches for context:

- Approach 1 — Shared multi-tenant server: Smaller clients (e.g., individual museums/exhibitions) connect to TICVAI/Softlabs' own shared server infrastructure. This server needs to be built for long-term scalability — starting with perhaps five or six clients but designed to reach 100–200+ over a few years.

- Approach 2 — Dedicated client-hosted server: Larger clients (e.g., large venues or stadiums) host on their own Azure/AWS server, built to a minimum specification that TICVAI/Softlabs provides.

To illustrate the scale difference, Qossai gave two contrasting examples: a stadium such as Real Madrid's (~60,000 seats) could sell out within a few hours of tickets going live for a major event, generating extremely high concurrent load, whereas a client like a water park or museum might see a maximum of around 2,000 visitors per day — a much lower and steadier load (roughly five people per minute). The system therefore needs a plan that can fit both extremes without over- or under-provisioning either type of client, which points to an auto-scaling architecture rather than a fixed one. Dinesh summarized this back as an auto-scaling architecture requirement, which Qossai confirmed.

Dinesh flagged that auto-scaling has direct cost implications on cloud billing, and the team should be comfortable with and aware of these costs as usage scales. Qossai confirmed TICVAI already has some experience with this on Azure — currently, scaling for known high-traffic events (e.g., an upcoming concert) is done manually: resources are scaled up ahead of the event and back down once it concludes. For the new platform, the goal is to automate this process rather than rely on manual intervention. Allam proposed that once Dinesh has the HLD/LLD ready (prepared per cloud provider), the teams hold a dedicated follow-up session to work through both deployment scenarios in detail.

### 7. Ticket Validation & Offline Architecture

Chinmay walked through the team's current thinking on ticket validation, noting the architecture has largely been settled: validation must work completely offline, and should optionally integrate local BLE (Bluetooth) verification — requiring Bluetooth to be enabled on the validating device — as a way of confirming the staff member is physically present at the entry gate while scanning. This BLE requirement would be configurable, since not all venues will need it.

- - The QR code on a ticket regenerates every 15–30 seconds (configurable), secured through two-way key encryption generated at ticket-creation time.

- - The point-of-sale/scanning device validates and confirms the key offline, storing the result in a local SQLite database in case of lost connectivity.

- Once connectivity returns, the device syncs stored records to the central servers in batches, in the sequential order the events actually occurred, tagged with both the original recorded time and the sync time.

- Because this typically runs on a capable, multi-core thick client, the sync process is planned to run on an isolated thread/process separate from scanning, validation, and cryptography — so syncing does not add latency to gate entry.

- Chinmay invited further input on additional functionality for these devices; no further additions were raised at this point.

### 8. Point-of-Sale Data Sync Strategy

Allam raised a related question: whether point-of-sale product configuration, pricing, and rules should be stored locally (SQLite) for performance, rather than fetched from the server on every transaction. His suggestion was that configuration should sync to the local device in real time whenever it changes, so that a sale checks the local copy first (for speed) while the resulting transaction is sent to the server in real time. Qossai noted he wasn't certain which approach is better from a performance standpoint, since many competitive ticketing solutions today don't rely on a local database and still perform well — Softlabs' advice was requested on this point.

Qossai also asked whether a cashier without a dedicated POS device (e.g., using a tablet) could access the system via a browser URL rather than installing the app. Chinmay confirmed the core application is React Native and requires installation, but a lightweight web version could be built as an alternative — with the tradeoff that the web version would not support offline functionality, which requires the installed "thick" client with its own local ledger/database that later syncs to the server.

Qossai shared a cautionary example: a previous client site with poor internet connectivity ran an online-first architecture without a local database, which caused tickets to intermittently fail to reach the server. Allam acknowledged that some sites do rely on 4G SIM connections with weaker connectivity, though Qossai noted such cases are relatively rare compared to the overall client base, and suggested giving clients the choice between approaches. Chinmay agreed a comparative case study was warranted and committed to including a pros/cons comparison of online-first vs. offline-first architecture — particularly for POS — alongside the HLD/LLD diagrams he is preparing. He also proposed a middle-ground approach: default to an online, real-time product catalogue, but fall back to the last-synced catalogue automatically if connectivity is lost, so browsing performance stays fast without fully sacrificing offline resilience.

Allam separately confirmed the platform must be device-agnostic — able to run on both Android and iOS (and by extension, web) — so that sales can continue on any available device even where full offline capability isn't required.

### 9. Capacity Estimates & Case Studies

Chinmay shared initial target figures for launch: approximately 15,000 peak concurrent customer users, 300 peak concurrent staff users, 1,000 API requests per second, and support for 70+ different venue locations. He acknowledged these are ambitious starting numbers and proposed refining them with more granular client-tier segmentation (e.g., small / mid-tier / large clients) rather than a simple two-way split, including cost ceilings for horizontal scaling and base requirements per tier — to be delivered as a follow-up case study once TICVAI shares more specific numbers.

### 10. Compliance & Data Protection

Allam confirmed he had already shared two documents relating to data-protection ('DES') compliance; Chinmay acknowledged he had not yet reviewed them and committed to doing so. Allam noted he is also sourcing additional supporting documentation on his end. On PCI DSS specifically, Allam advised that TICVAI should be able to obtain relevant certification support from their payment provider, and offered to assist further if needed.

On card data handling, Allam was clear that full card numbers must never be stored — only a masked representation (e.g., last four digits) should be retained, and it must be encrypted, sufficient only to let a user identify which card was used for reference purposes.

### 11. Offline Functionality Scope

Chinmay confirmed the offline requirement applies to POS terminals, handheld/ticket-validation devices (turnstiles, scanners), and staff and customer mobile apps — all of which will maintain a local SQLite database and sync to the server in sequential order (with both recorded and synced timestamps) once connectivity returns.

Allam added one refinement: the system should detect the loss of connectivity automatically and switch to offline mode on its own, without requiring manual intervention from the cashier — and should automatically restore online mode and sync all pending transactions once connectivity returns. Chinmay agreed, adding that the offline state should also be clearly visible in the UI (e.g., a visible mode indicator or greyed-out unavailable functionality), with the exact visual treatment to be worked out during Monday's UI/UX session. Qossai added that the POS should also raise an alert when a venue goes offline.

- Capacity-based products

Allam raised a specific edge case: products with a managed capacity (e.g., seat-assigned tickets) rely on inventory that is tracked centrally across all sales channels, so they cannot be reliably sold while offline. He proposed that any attempt to sell a capacity-based product while offline should be blocked with a clear notification, rather than allowed through or silently failing — since allowing it risks overlap/double-selling once the device reconnects. Non-capacity products remain sellable offline without this restriction.

- Food & beverage vs. retail inventory

Allam distinguished food & beverage (F&B) products from retail: F&B stock depletion is typically calculated at day's end based on recipe/ingredient usage rather than in real time, so F&B items can continue to be sold while offline. Retail items, by contrast, need real-time inventory tracking since stock is finite and centrally maintained across store and warehouse — without real-time depletion, overselling becomes a risk.

- Kitchen display system (KDS)

Chinmay described the intended model as closer to a café than a fast-food chain — a single POS handling both order-taking and payment, without a separate kitchen-facing system feeding live orders. Allam clarified TICVAI does not need Softlabs to build a full kitchen display system, only an integration point to send order information to an existing KDS for display. Qossai confirmed this integration requirement is already listed in the requirement matrix; Chinmay agreed to double-check and revisit it later, noting that full offline support for such an integration would be non-trivial since orders need to reach the kitchen system in real time.

### 12. Payments & Regional Preferences

Chinmay confirmed that, as previously agreed, only cash payments are supported while offline, since card payment processing requires connectivity. On regional payment habits, Allam noted that in this market, customers primarily use Apple Pay or Google Pay via stored cards on their phone wallets and tap to pay, rather than scanning a QR code as is more common in India via UPI. Chinmay confirmed UPI-style QR payments could be considered as a later addition rather than part of the initial scope.

### 13. Internationalization & Localization

Chinmay confirmed the platform needs to support English and Arabic at minimum, with Russian, Spanish, and Mandarin also discussed as likely additional languages. He raised the question of translation quality assurance — whether Softlabs would provide native-language validation, or whether TICVAI's own team would review translated content.

Allam proposed an AI-assisted workflow: source text is entered in English, machine-translated into the target language, and then reviewed/validated by the tenant's own team via the back office/CMS before publishing — noting that translation is typically owned by the tenant since they understand their own brand voice and marketing style best. This should apply consistently everywhere text appears: the website, the point-of-sale interface (e.g., Arabic-only product names/menus for certain regions), and the mobile app.

Qossai added that the broader goal is to make the system genuinely multi-language and easy to extend — allowing a new language to be added as a configuration change rather than a development effort. He described a prior project where a translation spreadsheet (with columns per language) was distributed to native speakers for review, then fed back through an AI translation pass — a similar table-driven, low-effort workflow for adding new languages is desired here.

### 14. Observability & Dashboards

Chinmay closed the core technical discussion by reiterating the need for dashboards and observability, including tenant-level visibility for venue managers, which will directly support scaling decisions. He noted this will be finalized as part of the HLD/LLD work, including a recommended observability platform, and invited TICVAI to share any platform preferences at that stage.

### 15. Monday UI/UX Session Planning

Chinmay confirmed that Monday's session would primarily be a presentation from TICVAI's side, since Softlabs wants to understand TICVAI's product vision directly. He committed to sharing the full list of application pages/screens that same day, structured by device, tenant, and sub-screen, so the TICVAI team could start reviewing UI component requirements in advance.

Qossai clarified the application landscape for context: there is a POS/tablet-facing application that will carry TICVAI's own branding and UI direction, and separate B2C and B2B mobile applications that are white-label by design. For the white-label apps, Qossai proposed showing examples from prior B2C/B2B implementations his team has delivered, to establish a similar flow — the key point for Monday is understanding which elements are customizable per client (e.g., header, footer, colour scheme, calendar) rather than redesigning the flow itself, with the same logic applying to the mobile application.

Qossai reiterated that TICVAI does not have hands-on UI/UX design experience and is relying on Softlabs' advice on which elements to adjust. He again highlighted that the product involves three to four distinct flows — for example, the admission ticket flow versus the seat assignment flow (which requires selecting a time before a seat) — and confirmed TICVAI would walk Softlabs through their vision and intended experience for each flow on Monday.

Chinmay reconfirmed Aishwarya (Softlabs' designer) would be part of Monday's session, and that he would send a follow-up email to Qossai outlining specifically what additional information Softlabs needs from TICVAI ahead of that session.

### 16. Email Communication Protocol

Allam raised a process concern: emails from Chinmay had been arriving under the same recurring subject line, making it difficult for the TICVAI team to locate the content of a specific email later. He asked that future emails use a clear, distinct subject line per topic, with separate threads for separate matters, so the team can follow up on and close out specific items more easily.

Chinmay agreed this made sense, noting he had previously been instructed by Makrand to keep all communication within a single thread — but confirmed that going forward he would create separate, clearly subject-lined threads for topic-specific items, such as UI/UX-related or architecture-related matters.

Allam reinforced the reasoning: distinct, clearly labelled threads would let the team follow up on and close a specific email once resolved, rather than having to search and drill back through a long, mixed thread — something that had been difficult for them so far. Chinmay reconfirmed he would use a separate subject line per topic as requested, thanked the group, and closed the session, noting he was looking forward to involving Makrand going forward.

### Decisions Made

- Session Planning

- - Multi-tenancy will not be revisited, as it was already covered in a previous session

- - A dedicated UI/UX walkthrough is scheduled for Monday, 3 August 2026, to be led primarily by TICVAI's side

- - Wireframe development will begin in parallel with ongoing sessions, rather than waiting for the UI/UX session

- Architecture & Scalability

- The platform will use an auto-scaling architecture capable of serving both very high-traffic clients (e.g., stadiums, concerts) and low, steady-traffic clients (e.g., museums, water parks)

- - Two deployment approaches are confirmed: a shared multi-tenant server for smaller clients, and dedicated client-hosted servers (to a minimum spec) for large clients

- - Built-in queue management will be developed in-house rather than sourced from a third party

- - Target uptime is 99.99%; load/performance testing will be included in the implementation plan

- Cloud provider selection (AWS vs. Azure, potentially GCP) will be finalized only after HLD/LLD component planning is complete, with a plan prepared for each major provider

- Data, Consistency & Disaster Recovery

- - High availability takes priority over strict consistency; eventual consistency (via read replicas) is acceptable

- - Disaster recovery will be an optional, tenant-selectable module rather than a default, due to cost

- - Distributed Redis caching will be implemented, based on prior team experience at BookMyShow

- - Card data will never be stored in full — only a masked/last-four-digit representation, encrypted, per PCI DSS guidance

- Offline & Point-of-Sale

- Ticket validation will work fully offline, with optional BLE-based proximity verification, QR codes refreshing every 15–30 seconds, two-way encryption, and local SQLite storage synced to the server once online

- - Data sync will run on an isolated thread/process, separate from scanning and validation, to avoid added latency

- - Offline/online mode switching will be automatic, with a clearly visible indicator in the UI (exact treatment to be defined in the UI/UX session)

- - Capacity-based products (e.g., seat-assigned tickets) cannot be sold while offline; non-capacity products can

- - F&B items can be sold while offline (stock isn't depleted in real time); retail items require real-time inventory tracking

- - A full kitchen display system will not be built — only an integration point to an existing KDS

- The platform must be device-agnostic (Android, iOS, and web), and a lightweight web-accessible version will be considered for devices without the installed app — with the caveat that offline support requires the installed thick client

- Payments & Localization

- - Only cash payments are supported offline; card payments require connectivity

- - Apple Pay / Google Pay (tap-to-pay) are the primary regional digital payment methods; UPI/QR-style payments may be added later

- - The platform will support English, Arabic, Russian, Spanish, and Mandarin, with translations AI-assisted and validated by the tenant's own team

- - New languages should be addable via configuration, without requiring development effort

- Process

- - Chinmay will share the application page/screen list with TICVAI ahead of Monday's session

- - Going forward, all emails will use clear, topic-specific subject lines with separate threads per topic — a change from the previous single-thread approach

### Action Items

- Action Item Owner Status

- --- --- ---

- Prepare HLD & LLD architecture diagrams, covering both client-hosted and Softlabs-hosted deployment scenarios Chinmay Parab In Progress

- Prepare a case study comparing online-first vs. offline-first POS architecture (pros/cons, incl. scanner & POS data-sync approach) Chinmay Parab Pending

- Prepare a client-tiered case study (small/medium/large) with scaling ceilings and cost implications Chinmay Parab Pending

- Review compliance documentation shared by Softlabs (DES compliance, PCI DSS) Chinmay Parab Pending

- Double-check requirement matrix for kitchen display system (KDS) integration scope Chinmay Parab Pending

- Share the full list of application pages/screens (structured by device, tenant, and sub-screens) with TICVAI Chinmay Parab Pending

- Send follow-up email detailing information required from TICVAI for the UI/UX session Chinmay Parab Pending

- Prepare HLD & LLD design documentation for each major cloud provider (AWS, Azure) Dinesh Jadhav Pending

- Hold a dedicated follow-up session once HLD/LLD are ready to finalize cloud provider approach per deployment scenario Softlabs & TICVAI Pending

- Source and share any additional compliance documentation Allam Allam In Progress

- Provide expected user/traffic numbers segmented by client tier TICVAI Team Pending

- Provide input on cloud provider preference (AWS/Azure) ahead of the design review TICVAI Team Pending

- Prepare and present TICVAI's UI/UX vision, including B2C/B2B examples and flow walkthroughs (admission ticket, seat assignment, etc.) TICVAI Team Pending

- Use clear, topic-specific subject lines and separate threads for future email communication Both Teams Ongoing

- Next Meeting

- Date: Monday, 3 August 2026

- Time: To be confirmed

- Planned Topics

- - UI/UX walkthrough, led primarily by the TICVAI team

- - TICVAI's vision for application flows (admission ticket, seat assignment, and related flows)

- - B2C/B2B white-label examples and customizable UI elements (header, footer, colour, calendar, etc.)

- - Review of the application page/screen list shared by Softlabs

- - Wireframe review

- Closing Remarks

This session moved through the remaining security and non-functional requirements — availability, scalability, disaster recovery, offline architecture, payments, and localization — building on prior sessions and closing out most open items in these areas. Both teams aligned on an auto-scaling, tenant-aware architecture with optional disaster recovery, a fully offline-capable validation and POS model, and a configuration-driven approach to multi-language support. The session concluded with agreement to shift focus to a dedicated UI/UX walkthrough on Monday, led by TICVAI, alongside parallel wireframe development, and to adopt clearer, topic-specific email communication going forward.
