## 2026-08-03

`sources/mom/TICVAI_UIUX_MoM_03Aug2026.docx` · 3,180 words

### Minutes of Meeting

- TICVAI UI/UX Discovery Workshop — Point of Sale, F&B, Web & Mobile

### Date

- 3 August 2026

### Project

- TICVAI

### Meeting Type

- UI/UX Discovery Workshop — POS, F&B, Web & Mobile

### Prepared by

- Chitrangi Mestry

### Primary Objective

To walk through TICVAI's vision for the point-of-sale (cashier) interface, food & beverage module, and B2C/B2B web and mobile applications, and to align on the UI/UX approach, reference material, and next steps for wireframing.

### Participants

- TICVAI Team

- Softlabs Team

### Agenda

- Session framing and scope for the day

- Point-of-sale (cashier) UI walkthrough

- UX design approach discussion (hot functions vs. search-driven UI)

- Food & beverage module walkthrough

- Table management & dining service models

- B2C/B2B website walkthrough (multi-site, white-label configuration)

- AI-assisted website generation

- Ticket flow variations by product type

- Website structure, localization & authentication

- Reference material & design research

- Mobile application strategy

- Wireframing approach & next steps

- Email communication & scheduling

### 1. Session Framing

Qossai noted he had received Chinmay's document but needed more time to review it fully. He proposed that today's session instead focus on addressing the questions Chinmay had submitted in advance, and on walking through the food & beverage and point-of-sale ticket-selling flows. Chinmay confirmed he had spent the weekend reviewing various UI reference platforms but had no additional material specifically prepared for today's session.

### 2. Point-of-Sale (Cashier) UI Walkthrough

Qossai shared his screen to walk through a point-of-sale interface his team had previously built. He was clear this was intended as a design reference and starting point only, not something to copy directly — the goal is to enhance and redesign it enough that it doesn't look like a copy, while retaining the strong underlying UX ideas. He highlighted several elements of the design:

A prominent search ("magic banner") letting the cashier reach functionality — such as refunds or resending a ticket — via search, rather than through static menus or sidebars

- A right-hand panel surfacing events, tour guides, and packages, with filtering across exhibitions, tours, and films

- Header metrics showing tickets sold and revenue for the current shift

- The ability to hold multiple in-progress carts ("cards"), plus a transaction history view supporting delete, expire, and merge actions

An embedded AI assistant the cashier can query directly — for example, to find today's promo code, process a refund, or switch between light/night themes

- A notification system surfacing both ticket-related alerts (cancellations, capacity nearing or at its limit) and system alerts (printer offline, POS offline)

A slide-in "drawer" pattern for ticket details, replacing full-page navigation — selecting a ticket opens a drawer showing inclusions and rules/restrictions, followed by date/time selection and, where relevant, seat selection, including configurable seating rules (e.g., requiring a group's seats to stay together)

- Add-to-cart with upsell add-ons, including an AI-generated upsell prompt (e.g., suggesting the cashier add two more items to unlock a bundle discount)

Membership integration: searching a customer by mobile number or name to link a sale to their membership, viewing wallet balance, loyalty points, linked family members, and an RFID/barcode reference, with the ability to top up a member's wallet directly

- Shift-level settings: light/dark mode, currency selection (affecting displayed pricing based on the cashier's location), language selection, screen brightness, and manual online/offline toggling

- End-of-shift reconciliation: the cashier enters cash on hand and reviews a shift summary before confirming it for reporting and audit

### 3. UX Design Approach Discussion

Allam proposed a hybrid pattern: alongside the search-driven approach, provide a set of always-visible "hot function" buttons for high-frequency actions (e.g., refund, check transaction, print last receipt), rather than requiring the cashier to search for everything. He asked for Softlabs' recommendation on the best-practice approach. Qossai agreed a combination of both might be ideal and deferred to Softlabs' UX judgment on the right balance.

Chinmay compared the demoed interface to a separate AI-generated reference PDF shared previously, noting the demoed version felt cleaner and better spaced, while the PDF felt more cluttered with smaller touch targets — a meaningful concern for touchscreen/tablet use, where adequate spacing helps prevent mis-taps. Qossai agreed the PDF was the older, dated design, and confirmed the demoed interface should be treated as the primary direction, with the PDF only as secondary reference. Allam added that whichever approach is chosen needs to work consistently across all cashier device types — POS terminals, tablets, iPads, and kiosks.

Aishwarya More sought clarification on scope, asking whether the earlier-shared reference link was for the customer-facing (B2C) side while today's demo was the cashier/admin-facing POS. Allam and Qossai clarified that both the current demo and the earlier link were cashier-facing POS interfaces — not a back-office configuration panel — and that the previously shared PDF was AI-generated inspiration material for color and theming only, not a literal design to follow.

### 4. Food & Beverage Module Walkthrough

Qossai walked through a simplified F&B flow: from the menu, the cashier selects a category (e.g., drink or meal), then item-level options (e.g., sauce, size), adds to cart, and proceeds to payment — again noting the final design should follow the primary POS reference rather than this specific screen. For table service, a "new order" flow shows a seat/table layout; once a table is selected, the associated menu is assigned to that table for ordering.

### 5. Table Management & Dining Service Models

Allam noted the demoed table layout was dated and recommended a more graphical, visual table-map style — for example, visually distinct two-seat vs. four-seat tables — where the cashier selects a table and then enters the number of covers. He distinguished two common service models the platform needs to support:

- Quick-service: the guest orders and pays at the counter before food is served

Fine dining: a table is opened, items are added over the course of the visit, and the bill/invoice is only printed and paid at the end

Chinmay asked for clarification on the purpose of per-seat/per-table tracking, noting that in India a single combined bill is typical without itemized splitting. Allam explained the functionality exists to support flexible bill-splitting for a table — by amount, by number of covers, or by category (e.g., one guest paying for food and another for drinks) — which Chinmay confirmed made sense once explained.

Qossai added that within a venue/park, the F&B module would be accessed from the same top-level navigation area as other experiences (tours, guides), and that table-management functionality would only surface for venues with an associated restaurant configuration, per the requirement matrix.

### 6. B2C/B2B Website Walkthrough (Multi-Site, White-Label)

Qossai demonstrated several live client websites — including a general example, a museum-style site, and a science-centre example — to illustrate the platform's white-label, multi-site configuration model:

Each site shares the same underlying platform/template but is configured independently — header, footer, logo, colors, fonts, and hero banner are all client-editable from the backend

- Ticket listings are data-driven: creating a new ticket automatically surfaces it on the relevant site based on category configuration

- Some clients operate multiple branded sites from the same underlying setup (e.g., two brands sharing a footer but with distinct headers and hero banners)

- A "powered by [platform]" footer credit is fixed and not client-editable

- One example site included a live integration with a government satisfaction-survey ("happiness meter") service

- All sites are fully mobile-responsive — for example, the desktop calendar view collapses into a mobile-optimized layout

- Qossai stressed the goal of giving clients as much design flexibility as possible within this configurable structure.

### 7. AI-Assisted Website Generation

Qossai showcased a personal example — a website for his own football academy — built entirely using AI website-generation tools within about one day, supporting three languages (Arabic, Russian, English). He strongly advocated for incorporating AI-assisted design/generation directly into the platform's website-building capability, keeping site design (header, footer, color, font, layout) separate from content (tickets and their data), with tickets automatically flowing into the site's structure once published.

He noted a second, larger client website shown earlier had also been built almost entirely by an AI design tool integrated with Microsoft's AI services, with human review layered on top to catch and correct small errors — a process that took only four to five days end-to-end.

### 8. Ticket Flow Variations by Product Type

Allam shared a further demo website containing multiple live ticket types (event tickets, open-dated tickets, time-slot tickets) to illustrate flow variation. Qossai and Allam described the different navigation patterns required per ticket type:

- Admission tickets: no date/time selection — goes straight to quantity/cart

- Dated tickets: date selection only

- Timed tickets: date, then time

- Seated tickets: date, then time, then seat selection

Some clients (e.g., certain museums with a small number of standard configurations, such as 5–6 floors) prefer to start by asking for the number of guests first, which narrows the calendar to only dates/times with sufficient availability

Allam summarized this as two broad selection patterns: (a) choose the event, then date, then time, see availability, then select the product; or (b) choose the product, enter a quantity, choose a date, and see only the time slots with sufficient remaining capacity. Chinmay flagged that this range of variations will need deeper UI exploration, since a meaningful number of customization scenarios are likely to be required.

### 9. Website Structure, Localization & Authentication

Allam clarified the platform's customization boundaries: banner, header, footer, and background color are all CMS-configurable per client, but the overall site structure and navigation flow remain fixed — the flow automatically adapts based on the underlying product's configuration (e.g., dated vs. non-dated vs. seated vs. membership products each surface the appropriate fields automatically).

Additional platform capabilities demonstrated included a multi-language toggle switching the entire site's content; checkout support for guest checkout, registered-account checkout, and single sign-on (e.g., Okta, Azure AD, and a ticketing-specific SSO); and a distinction between "ticket holder" (per-ticket detail capture, where required) and "reservation owner"/buyer (the single point of contact whose details are captured once per booking and who receives the tickets by email).

Qossai demonstrated a UAE Pass integration as a live example: a customer logs in via mobile number, approves a push notification, and confirms with biometric verification, after which their verified personal details are pulled automatically into the booking and a linked backend account is created. Chinmay noted this is conceptually similar to Aadhaar-based KYC autofill flows used on many Indian government and consumer platforms.

### 10. Reference Material & Design Research

Qossai proposed that a similar interaction pattern used in the POS drawer (e.g., a right-to-left slide-in panel) could also suit the B2C cart/checkout experience, and asked Softlabs to research current market best practices for ticket-booking UX (web and mobile) to help guide the design, rather than simply reusing the demoed references as-is. He shared several reference links (including a PDF and three example client websites) in the meeting chat for the team's review, noting some file-attachment issues in the call platform meant a couple of items would be sent via email instead. Allam specifically recommended the team review the "Viva Ticket" website as a reference containing many of the flow variations discussed.

### 11. Design Alignment & Team Input

Aishwarya confirmed that, having gone through the walkthrough, her outstanding UI questions had largely been addressed and she would review the shared reference material further.

Sahil Karangutkar, joining partway through, shared design-trend observations from his own research — noting a broader shift toward modern, minimalistic, spacious, cross-device designs that still convey a sense of place (e.g., a venue or park) — and asked for confirmation on process: whether Softlabs should propose two to three enhanced visual concepts drawing on the shown references, for TICVAI to react to and steer, rather than directly replicating what was shown.

Qossai confirmed this was exactly the intent — the demoed material was for concept understanding only, and Softlabs, as the design partner, should research the market and propose the strongest modern UI/UX direction, leveraging AI-assisted design tooling where useful, similar to how his own example sites had been produced.

Chinmay proposed that Sahil collate the design references/inspiration he had gathered over the previous week and share them with Qossai and Allam for feedback, organized separately for the customer-facing mobile app, the customer-facing website, and the back-office/admin pages. Sahil and Qossai agreed to exchange reference material both ways.

### 12. Mobile Application Strategy

Qossai noted the team's existing mobile applications are dated and not ideal references, but mentioned having seen an interesting pattern elsewhere using product video rather than static images for tickets, which he would try to share separately if he could locate it.

On Chinmay's earlier email question about whether access-control and employee functionality should be combined into one mobile app or kept separate, Qossai expressed a clear preference for two separate applications:

- A dedicated access-control app, installed on handheld devices or fixed terminals, scoped purely to entry validation/scanning

A separate employee app covering broader staff functionality (approvals, alerts/messages, and other matrix-defined features), which may include a basic ticket-validity lookup for support purposes, but not full scanning

Qossai's reasoning was that access control needs to remain narrowly scoped and reliable, and that in some cases the two capabilities may even be licensed or sold separately. Chinmay agreed this isolation made sense. Qossai noted further access-control screen details (e.g., customer photo, ticket information, validity status) would be covered in a future workshop.

### 13. Wireframing Approach & Next Steps

Chinmay proposed that, since Softlabs already has a full list of required screens (maintained in a tracking spreadsheet), the team begin wireframing the screens where requirements are already clear, sharing them with TICVAI for feedback as they go — expecting that seeing tangible designs will likely surface further ideas and refinements from TICVAI's side. Qossai agreed this iterative approach was the right one, expecting some follow-up changes as wireframes are reviewed, and confirmed today's discussion had addressed two of the three questions Chinmay had submitted in advance, with the remaining item largely covered as well.

### 14. Email Communication & Scheduling

Chinmay proposed splitting ongoing email communication into two separate threads going forward: one for shared reference material/data, and a separate one for kickoff meeting and workshop minutes — consistent with the topic-specific threading approach agreed in the previous session. He confirmed the link/chain for reference material that Qossai had requested previously.

On scheduling, Chinmay proposed the next session for the following day, offering Wednesday as an alternative. Qossai confirmed TICVAI was flexible on either date and asked Chinmay to confirm based on his team's availability and send a calendar invite.

Separately, Allam proposed that a33 into a shared tracker, with a separate, recurring weekly meeting set up specifically to review it and confirm task ownership. Chinmay agreed and confirmed he would set this up. The call closed with thanks all around.

### Decisions Made

- Point of Sale

Qossai's demoed cashier interface is confirmed as the primary reference/baseline, to be enhanced by Softlabs rather than copied directly; the previously shared PDF remains secondary color/theme inspiration only

- Softlabs will explore a hybrid of quick-access "hot function" buttons and search-driven functionality, and recommend the best approach

- The slide-in "drawer" interaction pattern (for date/time and seat selection) is retained in place of full-page navigation

- Membership management, the embedded AI assistant, and shift-management features (as demoed) are confirmed directions for the POS, to be refined by Softlabs

- The design must work consistently across all cashier device types: POS terminals, tablets, iPads, and kiosks

- Food & Beverage

The core F&B flow (menu → item options → cart → payment) and table management are confirmed as required; final visuals will be redesigned by Softlabs with a more modern, graphical table-map style

- Table/seat-level structure is required to support flexible bill-splitting (by amount, covers, or category)

- The platform must support both quick-service and fine-dining service models

- Website & B2C/B2B

Multi-site, white-label configuration is confirmed: header, footer, color, font, and hero banner are client-editable; the "powered by" footer credit is fixed; site structure stays fixed but adapts automatically based on product configuration

- AI-assisted website generation will be explored as part of the platform's website-building capability

- Ticket flow must support multiple navigation patterns depending on product type (admission, dated, timed, seated), requiring further UI exploration for customization scenarios

- Checkout will support guest, registered, and SSO-based login (including a UAE Pass-style integration), with a clear separation between "ticket holder" and "reservation owner"/buyer

- Softlabs will research current market best practices for ticket-booking UX rather than replicate the shown references as-is

- Mobile Applications

- Access control and employee functionality will be built as two separate mobile applications, not combined

- Access-control screen details will be discussed in a future workshop

- Process

- Wireframing will begin immediately on screens with clear requirements, shared iteratively with TICVAI for feedback

- Sahil will collate and share design references, organized by mobile app, website, and admin/back-office pages

- Email communication will be split into separate threads for reference material vs. meeting minutes/workshops

- The next session will be tomorrow or Wednesday, to be confirmed based on Softlabs' availability

- A shared open-items tracker and a recurring weekly review meeting will be set up

### Action Items

- Action Item

- Owner

- Status

- Collate design references/inspiration and share with TICVAI, organized by mobile app, website, and admin/back-office pages

- Softlabs (Sahil & Aishwarya)

- Pending

- Begin wireframing screens with clear requirements and share iteratively with TICVAI for feedback

- Softlabs Design Team

- In Progress

- Recommend a UX approach combining quick-access "hot function" buttons with search-driven POS functionality

- Softlabs Design Team

- Pending

- Set up separate email threads for reference material vs. meeting minutes/workshops

- Chinmay Parab

- Pending

- Confirm team availability and send calendar invite for the next session (tomorrow or Wednesday)

- Chinmay Parab

- Pending

- Create and populate a shared open-items tracker (HLD/LLD progress, pending TICVAI requests, etc.)

- Chinmay Parab

- Pending

- Propose a time for a recurring weekly tracker-review meeting

- Chinmay Parab

- Pending

- Share the referenced PDF and additional example website links via email (Teams attachment issue)

- Qossai

- Pending

- Qossai

- Pending

- Pending

- Confirm availability for the proposed weekly review meeting

- Pending

- Next Meeting

- Date: Tomorrow (Tuesday, 4 August 2026) or Wednesday, 5 August 2026 — to be confirmed

- Time: To be confirmed

- Planned Topics

- Continued UI/UX discussion and review of any wireframes completed in the interim

- Access-control screen details (customer photo, ticket information, validity status)

- Review of design references shared by both teams

- Closing Remarks

This session was a deep, screen-shared walkthrough of TICVAI's vision for the point-of-sale, food & beverage, and B2C/B2B web and mobile experiences. Both teams aligned on treating the demoed POS and website examples as directional references rather than literal designs to copy, with Softlabs taking the lead on researching best-practice UX and proposing enhanced concepts — including possible use of AI-assisted design tooling. Key structural decisions were confirmed around white-label site configuration, ticket-flow variations by product type, authentication options, and a two-app split for access control vs. employee mobile functionality. The session closed with an agreement to begin wireframing immediately on clear-requirement screens, split email communication by topic, and set up a shared tracker with a recurring weekly review meeting.

## 2026-08-05

`sources/mom/TICVAI_Kickoff_MoM_2026-08-05.docx` · 1,465 words

### Minutes of Meeting

- TICVAI Kick-off Meeting — Ticketing Code & Venue Operations

### Date

- 5 August 2026

### Project

- TICVAI

### Meeting Type

- Kick-off Workshop — Ticketing Code & Venue Operations

### Prepared by

- Chitrangi Mestry

### Primary Objective

To walk through the ticketing code and venue operations in detail — the system architecture, ticket/product classification, B2B distribution models, QR code and entitlement architecture, offline selling rules, seat mapping, and event/resource management for the TICVAI ticketing platform.

### Participants

- TICVAI Team

- Softlabs Team

### 1. Session Framing

Chinmay proposed that Qossai's team lead a review workshop of the topics covered so far, so that content originates from Qossai's side rather than being framed entirely by Chinmay's team's understanding. Qossai agreed and suggested demonstrating the back-end configuration of another ticketing solution to help the team understand backend concepts more concretely. Allam requested that Chinmay's team review the functionality requirement matrix before each workshop so that clarifications can be discussed live.

### 2. B2B Ticket Distribution Models

- Allam outlined three B2B integration models for partners (OTAs/agencies):

Option 1 — API Consumption: partner consumes the platform's API for products, prices, and availability, and sells on their own platform. Bookings flow into TICVAI; the platform earns commission per ticket sold. Partner profiles store pricing, discounts, and product access, with settlement via credit limit, advance payment, or card (e.g., Stripe).

Option 2 — B2B Portal: partner uses a TICVAI-developed B2B platform (structured like B2C, but with login credentials), with pre-configured pricing/products and the same commission tracking.

Option 3 — Bulk QR Code Generation: for partners without technical capability, the platform generates a bulk batch of tickets (e.g., 5,000) with a validity window, delivered as QR codes (e.g., CSV) for the partner to import and resell.

- All three options follow the same downstream processes for pricing, commission calculation, and reporting.

- Certified integrations (e.g., BookMyShow, Platinum List, Ticketmaster) will be surfaced via a marketplace module that clients can activate after purchasing the core solution.

### 3. Infrastructure & Server Architecture

Chinmay flagged that server infrastructure must scale for high-volume, API-driven bulk sales (e.g., large concerts routed through partner APIs). Allam confirmed dedicated, segregated resources are needed per channel — on-site operations, B2C, B2B, and OTA/API traffic — so load on one channel does not degrade the others.

### 4. Ticket Catalogue & Product Types

- The team reviewed and refined the ticket/product classification:

- Admission, Admission + Dated, Admission + Dated + Timed, and Admission + Dated + Timed + Seated as the core progression.

Event/Resource — a flexible category for any bookable experience; can be dated, timed, seated or non-seated, and may or may not require a resource. Agreed to merge "event," "seated," and "resource" into this single category.

- Regular, group (shared or individual QR codes, partial check-in tracking), family (bundled adult/child pricing), and package tickets (combining multiple products into one).

Membership / Season Pass — non-dated, defined by start/end date rather than quantity; requires customer profile capture and supports renew, upgrade, cancel, and extend workflows.

- Gift Voucher — value-based or product-based, redeemable online or in-venue.

Identity (purchaser data) and entitlement (access rights) will be stored as separate entities, since binding identity directly to the ticket would complicate vouchers and group/multi-person bookings.

### 5. Multi-venue / Multi-tenant Ticketing

Allam demonstrated an example (Ferrari World / Miral Experiences) with single-park tickets, multi-park combo tickets, and tiered annual passes with configurable blackout dates. The system must support a single QR code granting conditional access across multiple attractions, tracking usage per attraction.

### 6. Entitlement, QR Codes & Encryption Architecture

Chinmay proposed a private-key-on-server / public-key-on-turnstile signing model so turnstiles can validate offline. Discussion clarified that a ticket is fundamentally a virtual entitlement (an ID in the system), not a physical object, and can be linked to any medium — QR code, NFC/RFID wristband, bank card, or email — with multiple media per ticket or multiple ticket components per medium both supported. Access rights are granted at venue and zone/event level rather than via one universal key, and add-on purchases after entry can either issue a new QR code or extend the existing wristband/QR code ("entitlement add-on").

### 7. Sales Channels, Pricing & Cart

- Channels: web store, mobile app, kiosk, and walk-up/POS.

- Pricing is configurable per channel via a centralized "price matrix"; each channel pulls its price automatically once published.

- A single cart/order must support mixed purchases (e.g., family tickets plus gift vouchers) with unified checkout and identity capture.

### 8. Offline Selling Rules

- Inventory is pre-allocated across offline-capable nodes (e.g., 100 tickets per node) to prevent overselling; unused quota is reallocated once nodes reconnect and sync.

- For seated/zoned venues, Qossai proposed network-based zoning — POS terminals sharing a network share real-time seat state; disconnected networks require their own offline zone.

- Offline mode triggers automatically on connectivity loss; whether zoning is automatic or client-enabled should be configurable per venue.

### 9. Seat Mapping & Venue Builder

- A one-time, canvas-based venue/seat-map builder is required per venue.

- Qossai proposed AI-assisted layout generation from AutoCAD/DXF (best) or PDF exports (fallback, via OCR), targeting ~90–95% automation with client-led correction of the remainder.

Dinesh raised concerns about client self-service risk (drawing on BookMyShow experience); Qossai clarified this is a licensed self-service product, distinct from BookMyShow's managed B2C model, so AI-assisted client-led configuration remains the core vision.

- Allam shared a sample format: PDF seating diagram paired with an Excel manifest of section/row/seat numbers.

### 10. Event & Resource Management

- Confirmed an "event" is not a distinct entity — it is simply another product category, seated/non-seated, dated/timed, with or without an associated resource.

Each product is configured with venue/zone-level access permissions (e.g., Zone 1 = main entrance, Zone 2 = auditorium), each potentially covered by its own access-control hardware.

- For large multi-attraction venues, each internal experience is its own product with its own capacity, time slots, and access model (scheduled/paid, first-come-first-served/free, or pay-on-the-spot).

A venue reconfigured for a special event (e.g., a stadium hosting a concert) is treated the same as standard operations at the system level — no structural distinction is needed.

### 11. Queue Management

Queue management will be scoped once the high-level architecture is finalized, with Dinesh's team owning this area; no further discussion was needed at this stage.

### 12. Hardware & Third-Party Integrations

- Turnstile SDK/API documentation requested now, ahead of a thick-client integration approach; printer/POS integrations assumed to use a universal SDK.

- Qossai to confirm and share hardware specification documents; procurement timing (rental vs. Mumbai-based local sourcing) to be revisited at ~80% development completion.

- Banking/payment gateway (e.g., DCT) documentation can follow during the discovery phase.

- WhatsApp/SMS integration to be discussed in a dedicated follow-up session.

### 13. Mobile / POS App Design References

Qossai shared reference apps (Al Qadiya/Six Flags Saudi Arabia, and "The District" by Zomato), citing their use of video over static images as a design inspiration. Aishwarya confirmed she is building mockups for the food-ordering/counter app using these and the previously shared POS PDF as references, to be shared once complete.

### Action Items

- Action Item

- Owner

- Status

- Document the finalized ticket classification (product types, incl. Membership, Event/Resource) as a diagram and circulate for confirmation

- Chinmay Parab

- In Progress

- Test AI-based seat-layout generation using available sample layouts (screenshots/PDFs) as a worst-case baseline

- Chinmay Parab

- Pending

- Locate and share the AutoCAD/PDF seating drawing from the Bahrain project (also to be shared with 3D vendor "3DDV")

- Allam

- Pending

- Prepare and schedule a demo session on multi-tenant configuration and event/access management

- Allam

- Pending

- Confirm and share turnstile and other hardware SDK/specification documents

- Qossai / Allam

- Pending

- Share the previously created weekly open-items tracker

- Chinmay Parab

- Pending

- Complete and share mock-ups for the food ordering / POS counter app

- Aishwarya More

- In Progress

- Share banking (DCT) and communications (WhatsApp/SMS) integration documentation ahead of a dedicated session

- Qossai

- Pending

- Next Meeting

- Date: Tomorrow or Friday (7 August 2026) — to be confirmed via WhatsApp

- Time: To be confirmed

- Planned Topics

- Demonstration of multi-tenant configuration and event/access management

- Review of the finalized ticket classification diagram

- Follow-up on hardware documentation and AI seat-layout testing

- Closing Remarks

This session provided a deep, screen-shared walkthrough of TICVAI's ticketing architecture — covering ticket classification, B2B distribution models, entitlement and QR code design, offline selling rules, seat mapping, and event/resource management. Both teams aligned on treating events strictly as a product category, on identity/entitlement separation, and on an AI-assisted, client-led approach to seat-map building. Next steps include a solution demo session, hardware and integration documentation, and setting up a recurring weekly tracker-review meeting.

## 2026-08-07

`sources/mom/TICVAI_BackendDeepDive_MoM_07Aug2026.docx` · 4,393 words

### Minutes of Meeting

- TICVAI Reference System Deep-Dive — Backend Configuration & Ticketing Logic

### Date

- 7 August 2026

### Project

- TICVAI

### Meeting Type

- Reference System Deep-Dive — Backend Configuration & Ticketing Logic

### Prepared by

- Chitrangi Mestry

### Primary Objective

To walk through the backend configuration and functional logic of an existing, mature ticketing platform — covering system/tenant setup, product and pricing configuration, events and time slots, entitlements, promotions, resource management, point-of-sale operation, reporting, and access control — as a functional reference for TICVAI's own platform, and to align on next steps for UI/UX design.

### Participants

- TICVAI Team

- Softlabs Team

### Agenda

- Session framing and reference system context

- System organization: tenant and site setup

- Operating areas, workstations and permissions hierarchy

- Roles and user management

- Base parameters: devices and payment methods

- Data mask: flexible custom data capture

- Task scheduler: automated system jobs

- Legacy POS layout designer and system logging

- Statistical groups and website content integration

- Tax configuration

- Accounts management (B2B and B2C)

- Products configuration: metric sheets, pricing and components

- Tenant/B2B onboarding and self-registration flow

- Events, integrations and performances (time slots)

- Capacity splitting via envelopes

- Entitlement components: re-entry, expiration and sale restrictions

- Promotions and dynamic offers

- Resource management

- Maintenance tools

- Live point-of-sale transaction walkthrough

- Dashboards and reporting

- Report and document template design

- Tiered ticketing and access control deep dive

- Next workshop planning

### 1. Session Framing

Allam shared his screen to demonstrate two types of ticketing configuration, starting with a multi-site system in which multiple venues are configured within a single database. He was explicit that the purpose was to help the team understand how a mature ticketing platform is configured conceptually — not to replicate the exact structure. Chinmay confirmed this framing and followed along with questions throughout.

### 2. System Organization: Tenant & Site Setup

Allam began with system organization, where the base tenant is configured. Each tenant onboarded to the platform receives a unique system ID and a tenant/system code, which is associated with every transaction. The system-level configuration also defines the operating calendar — either a standard midnight-to-midnight transaction day, or an alternative (e.g., 6am to 6am) — with licensing applied at the system level.

Within a tenant, individual sites (venues) are configured, each with a unique ID — the demo included several example sites (an adventure park, an in-flight experience, a diving operator, and desert/palm-based excursion brands). Within each site, "operating areas" represent departments (e.g., B2B, B2C, OTAs, on-site/point-of-sale, management, finance). Permissions and rights can be configured at multiple levels — site, operating area, workstation, role, or individual user — with settings applied at the site level (e.g., password complexity policy, UI rights, configuration rights) cascading globally to all users and workstations under that site.

### 3. Operating Areas, Workstations & Permissions Hierarchy

Each operating area belongs to a site and has its own set of point-of-sale workstations (terminals) associated with it; sales reporting can be scoped to a specific operating area, showing all transactions from its associated workstations. Each workstation configuration records its connected devices — receipt printer, barcode scanner, ticket printer — so that a cashier logging into a given workstation automatically has access to the correct hardware. Every workstation also has its own activity log and rights configuration.

### 4. Roles & User Management

Roles (e.g., cashier, supervisor, manager, administrator) are fully configurable, each with its own set of privileges. A single user can be assigned multiple roles and switch between them at login (e.g., logging in as a cashier vs. a supervisor) to validate what access each role provides. Allam noted one gap in the reference system worth addressing in TICVAI's platform: a "roles comparison" view, letting an admin directly compare two roles side-by-side (e.g., confirming a cashier role excludes refund/void permissions that a supervisor role includes) to make permission management easier and less error-prone.

### 5. Base Parameters: Devices & Payment Methods

Base parameters cover system-wide configuration, starting with devices — printers, access-control devices, and scanners are each configured with an appropriate driver (e.g., specific printer brands), then assigned to individual workstations.

Payment methods (cash, card, PayPal, bank transfer, etc.) are configured similarly. Card payment methods are associated with a payment driver for the relevant terminal/provider (e.g., a named payment device integration). A "virtual credit card" option also exists for standalone card terminals not directly integrated with the system — in this case, the cashier manually enters the authorization code returned by the physical terminal, preserving reporting accuracy even without a live integration.

Chinmay asked whether the driver-based integration approach would be standard for TICVAI. Allam confirmed that Stripe and Network International integrations had already been agreed as part of the current scope, and that additional payment driver integrations can be added over time as needed — whatever isn't already integrated would need to be built.

### 6. Data Mask: Flexible Custom Data Capture

Allam introduced "data mask" as one of the most important features in the reference system — a flexible mechanism for capturing custom information anywhere in the platform. Data can be captured at the account level (for any customer type — B2B, B2C, etc.), the event level, as extended ticket information, or per product ("metric cell" level, i.e., tied to a specific ticket/product).

Fields can be standard (e.g., first name, email address) or fully custom, with configurable field types (text, dropdown, radio button, true/false), multi-language labels, and validation rules (min/max length, required/optional). Reusable "mask tables" support shared dropdown value sets (e.g., a full country list) that can be linked to any relevant field. Custom fields were shown supporting venue-specific requirements — for example, a checkbox confirming a guest is not pregnant, required before a specific product can be purchased, or a weight-range field for a specific activity.

Chinmay asked whether TICVAI would need to define all data-capture fields themselves, or whether Softlabs would provide standard fields. Allam confirmed standard fields (names, countries, currencies, etc.) would be provided out of the box, while venue- or product-specific custom fields would be configured through this same data-mask mechanism as needed, without requiring new development for each new field.

### 7. Task Scheduler: Automated System Jobs

- The task scheduler manages recurring automated jobs, including:

Purge job: automatically checks reservations left in an incomplete ("reserved but unpaid") state for longer than a configurable threshold (e.g., 20–30 minutes) and releases the held capacity back into inventory

Release capacity job: similarly releases inventory held in an abandoned cart (added but never checked out) after a period of inactivity, so it becomes available to other customers

- Data export job: exports reports or ERP-format files to a shared location on a schedule

- Revenue recognition job: runs overnight to move ticket revenue from a "deferred" to a "redeemed" status based on which tickets were actually scanned/used

### 8. Legacy POS Layout Designer & System Logging

Allam briefly showed "sales board management," a drag-and-drop point-of-sale button/layout designer allowing products and system functions (e.g., ticket list, reservation list, transaction list, media lookup) to be placed as buttons with customizable fonts and colors. He was explicit that this specific interface is old and not intended as a design reference — it was shown only to illustrate the underlying functional concept.

History log management captures a full audit trail of system activity — logins, shift start/end times, and every change made (old value vs. new value) across every screen and transaction. Logging can be enabled or disabled, and historical logs can be archived. A related "task status" feature allows internal, in-system task assignment and follow-up between staff (e.g., a cashier flagging something for a supervisor) without relying on email or messaging apps. A built-in help menu provides step-by-step tutorials with screenshots for common tasks (e.g., how to sell a ticket at the POS).

### 9. Statistical Groups & Website Content Integration

Statistical groups are used to categorize and display products on the tenant-facing website — for example, a diving operator's site groups its offerings into categories such as scuba diving, free diving, and snorkelling, each showing selectable packages. Allam demonstrated live: selecting a package on the tenant website (which is managed by the tenant) leads through to checkout on the TICVAI-managed booking platform. Package details shown on the website — title, description, terms, age limits, and images — are all pulled from data-mask fields configured in the backend and sync automatically to the live site when updated.

### 10. Tax Configuration

Tax packages define one or more applicable taxes per product, which can be marked inclusive or exclusive of the listed price, with configurable rounding rules. Allam flagged an important capability that should be included in TICVAI's platform: the ability to calculate tax on tax (compound tax) — for example, applying a second tax rate on top of a price that already includes a first tax, rather than calculating both taxes independently from the base price.

### 11. Accounts Management (B2B and B2C)

Accounts are organized into categories — broadly B2B (main accounts and agent/child accounts) and B2C (guest checkout and registered checkout). A sample B2B account showed key fields on its financial tab: credit limit, credit days, and a linked, account-specific price list, meaning a given B2B partner can be assigned different pricing than the general public. Accounts can be structured as a main account with one or more linked child accounts, and every account shows its full linked sales/transaction history. A B2C customer profile example similarly showed a purchase and transaction history tied to that individual.

### 12. Products Configuration: Metric Sheets, Pricing & Components

Product configuration ("stores") is organized per site. Products are defined in a "metric sheet" — the core product/ticket configuration table — categorized both by product type (e.g., scuba diving, free diving) and by sales channel (B2C, point of sale/on-site, OTA, etc.), since the same underlying product may need separate channel-specific setup.

An individual product record includes pricing (fixed price, tax inclusive/exclusive), a linked print template (the PDF ticket layout), a system-generated product/matrix code, a toggle for whether reservation details must be captured at time of sale, and "entitlements" — what the ticket actually grants, including whether it can be upgraded, whether it allows loading value onto a stored-value card, its linked event (if any), re-entry rules, and its linked performance/time-slot structure.

Multiple price lists can be defined per sales channel (e.g., box office/on-site, B2C, OTA) so the same product can carry different prices depending on where it's sold, and pricing can vary seasonally (a winter/summer pricing example was shown). The platform's "components" and "attributes" model is central to flexible product creation: a component (e.g., "ticket type") can have multiple attributes (e.g., adult, youth, senior, infant, child), each priced independently — adding a new attribute automatically generates a new sellable product variant without additional setup. Sales permissions (who is authorized to sell a given product) can be restricted by site, operating area, workstation, or role.

### 13. Tenant/B2B Onboarding & Self-Registration Flow

At Chinmay's request, Allam demonstrated the tenant/B2B onboarding process. A new B2B partner account can be created directly from the backend, or through a self-registration flow on the tenant's own website: a "become a partner" link leads to a registration form (built via data mask) capturing company type, name, address, Emirates/state, and required documents such as a trade license and VAT/TRN certificate.

Submitting the form creates a pending account record and automatically emails the tenant's operations/business team. The team reviews and validates the submitted documents — for example, rejecting an expired trade license with a message prompting resubmission — and negotiates commercial terms (pricing, commission) before approving the account. Approval automatically generates login credentials (with a temporary password) which are emailed to the registrant; on first login, the user is required to set their own password.

### 14. Events, Integrations & Performances (Time Slots)

Dinesh Jadhav, joining partway through, raised a clarifying question on event/product relationships: whether every product necessarily needs an associated event. Allam confirmed this is not the case — an event is only needed where date, time, and capacity control are required; a simple open-dated product (e.g., general park admission valid for a set period) does not need one.

Events also carry an "integration type" setting — for example, an event can be linked to a third-party availability/ticketing platform, so that at time of sale the system checks live availability on that external platform and issues the corresponding QR code from it, rather than managing capacity independently.

"Performances" are the system's term for time slots. Creating performances involves selecting a date range (specific weekdays or all days), a fixed start and end time, a slot duration (e.g., 30 or 60 minutes), "minutes on screen" (how long past its start time a slot remains sellable at the POS — e.g., a 10:00am slot sellable until 10:10am), and separate access-control timing ("time opening"/"time limit") governing how early or late a ticket holder may physically enter relative to their booked time (e.g., entry allowed from 9:30am for a 10:00am slot, with a cutoff at 10:20am). An on-sale date range controls when the performance itself becomes purchasable. Performances can be bulk-created across a date range, capacity can be edited individually or via multi-select bulk edit, and individual performances can be suspended, resumed, or cancelled (e.g., suspending due to weather risk, later resuming once resolved).

### 15. Capacity Splitting via Envelopes

"Envelopes" allow a performance's total capacity to be split across sales channels — for example, of 100 total spaces for a scheduled show, 30 could be reserved for B2C, 40 for B2B, and 30 for on-site sale — so that availability shown to each channel reflects only its allocated share, configured once and applied automatically across all performances it's linked to.

### 16. Entitlement Components: Re-entry, Expiration & Sale Restrictions

Entitlement components define what a ticket actually grants and how it behaves. "Components" (such as an event or an upgrade) can carry configurable "attributes" — for example, re-entry can be set as not allowed, allowed once per day, or unlimited. Expiration rules offer many configurable options (end of week, end of month, end of year, a variable expiration date, based on first use, or based on the specific performance date/time). Sale restrictions allow minimum/maximum sellable quantity rules per customer (e.g., a promotional bundle requiring a minimum purchase of two), and group-ticket handling can be configured by fixed price or fixed quantity. A single ticket can also be linked to multiple events/entitlements simultaneously (e.g., one ticket granting access to several different experiences).

### 17. Promotions & Dynamic Offers

Coupons can be generated either as a single, shared promo code (e.g., for social media distribution) or as a batch of unique, single-use alphanumeric codes distributed individually to customers, with configurable reuse rules.

"Dynamic offers" apply automatic, rule-based discounts without requiring a code — for example, a "bring your guest" buy-2-get-1-free structure, buy-3-get-2-at-50%-off, or a fixed-amount discount for a minimum quantity. Multiple rules can be layered onto a single offer, each scoped to specific products via the metric sheet, and the discounted item is automatically added to the cart with its price adjusted (e.g., to zero) once the qualifying condition is met.

### 18. Resource Management

Resource management is an optional module for tracking bookable resources tied to a product or package — for example, a desert excursion package that requires both a vehicle and a driver. A resource "template" defines the required resource types for a given product; individual resources (specific vehicles, named drivers) are listed and can be scheduled with an availability calendar/roster (marking specific dates as unavailable). Once resources are linked to an event, the system checks both resource availability and remaining capacity at the time of sale — whether sold via POS or online — before allowing the booking to proceed.

### 19. Maintenance Tools

Maintenance tools include account activation/deactivation, and a duplicate-detection and profile-merge feature — flagged as heavily used in this region, since common name spelling variations (e.g., different transliterations of the same name) frequently create multiple profiles for the same customer. The merge tool consolidates two profiles into one, carrying over the combined transaction history. A user-log deletion tool is also available for clearing historical logs.

### 20. Live Point-of-Sale Transaction Walkthrough

Allam performed a full, live ticket sale to illustrate the end-to-end POS flow: selecting a performance/time slot (showing real-time remaining capacity), adding a product, and being prompted to attach a reservation account — either searching for an existing customer or creating a new one, with mandatory vs. optional fields driven entirely by the data-mask configuration (e.g., a required weight range, date of birth). He added an add-on product, proceeded to checkout, and — because the configuration required per-ticket detail capture — entered individual "ticket owner" information for each ticket (distinct from the overall "reservation owner"/buyer), noting this can enforce rules such as a minimum age per ticket holder. Payment was completed in cash, generating a printed ticket and a booking reference/reservation code.

Looking up the resulting reservation showed full transaction detail — items purchased, customer information, payment method, applicable taxes, and an optional post-purchase survey — along with the ability to reprint the receipt or regenerate the ticket PDF. The sample PDF ticket included a live QR code, a unique ticket number/barcode ("media identifier"), customizable branding/layout, terms and conditions, and the associated guest name. Allam clarified the distinction between a "ticket ID" (unique to each individual ticket) and a "media code" (which can be shared across multiple tickets scanned together as a single group under one QR code).

### 21. Dashboards & Reporting

Built-in dashboards include a Sales Summary (scoped to the logged-in cashier, showing transactions, payment totals, any voids/refunds, and a time-based chart of activity) and an Admission Summary (an access-control view showing real-time headcount of guests who have entered a venue based on ticket scans).

The platform includes an extensive report library, filterable by site, operating area, sales channel, workstation, or user. Example reports demonstrated included a Sales Report (payment-method breakdown, totals, voids, deposits, and itemized ticket sales) and a Payment Summary report (per-cashier payment breakdown, e.g. credit card totals).

### 22. Report & Document Template Design

Report templates can be custom-built by advanced users with SQL/scripting knowledge, and exported in PDF or Excel format. Ticket and receipt document layouts are designed via a drag-and-drop template builder, placing dynamic variables (e.g., guest name, ticket number, QR code) onto a background image/layout — demonstrated using an existing venue's ticket template.

### 23. Reference System Access & Documentation

Chinmay asked whether Softlabs' backend team could get direct hands-on access to the reference system themselves, noting that even as an older system, an understanding of its backend schema and database structure could meaningfully reduce TICVAI's own schema design effort (estimating perhaps 60% of it could be informed this way). Allam confirmed direct system access would not be possible. Qossai offered an alternative: sharing the full system manual/documentation, which covers backend configuration in detail and should serve a similar purpose — to be shared via WhatsApp or a shared folder, expected later that day or the next, once Qossai was back at his home setup.

Allam reiterated his overall framing: functionally, the reference system is extremely rich — almost anything needed for ticketing already exists in some form — but its technology and UI/UX are dated, which is the core gap TICVAI's platform is meant to address.

### 24. Tiered Ticketing & Access Control Deep Dive

To illustrate the access-control/entitlement model in a concrete example, Allam walked through a second reference site (a safari/tour-style venue) offering tiered Bronze, Silver, and Gold packages, each priced by adult/child/infant:

Bronze: a single-entry admission event (no re-entry at the main gate) plus unlimited re-entry to certain included attractions during the visit (e.g., an aviary, a themed area, and a show)

- Silver: includes everything in Bronze, plus access to additional areas (e.g., a dedicated "silver terminal" and a guided safari/truck tour)

- Gold: full access to all areas via a dedicated gold entrance and gold terminal

Each tier's allowed access points are defined by the client filling in a matrix template indicating exactly which gates/attractions that ticket tier may scan into. In the system, this is configured as a chain: Locations (the venue) contain Admission Profiles (e.g., "Bronze," mapped to the specific gates it may use, such as main entrance and exit/retail shop); each Gate has associated Access Points (handheld scanners); and explicit deny rules can be configured to actively block a ticket type at a gate it isn't entitled to use — for example, a Gold ticket is explicitly denied at the Silver/Bronze entrance, ensuring strict tier separation is enforced by the system even if physically attempted.

### 25. Next Workshop Planning

Chinmay proposed returning to UI/UX topics for the next workshop, tentatively Monday, covering the client-facing mobile app and staff/employee mobile app together, alongside the tenant website and TICVAI's own website. Qossai asked for clarification on direction — whether Softlabs should present concepts, or TICVAI would present their vision as before. Chinmay confirmed the same format as the previous UI/UX session: Softlabs should bring whatever application or site examples they have prepared for review. He noted the tenant-facing application is expected to require comparatively little UI/UX discussion, while the client-facing mobile app and staff/employee mobile app will need more design input. Qossai confirmed his understanding of the scope: the client mobile application and the employee/venue mobile application.

### 26. Q&A: Performance Suspend/Resume

Tanmay Dukhande asked whether a suspended performance can be resumed. Allam confirmed yes — suspension is a status/state change, not a deletion, so a performance can be resumed at any time before its original start time (for example, suspending due to anticipated bad weather and later resuming once the risk has passed). Chinmay noted this confirms the platform should manage performance availability via a disable-able state rather than deleting and recreating records.

### Decisions Made

- Reference & Approach

The demonstrated system is treated as a functional reference only — rich in ticketing functionality, but its UI/UX will not be replicated; TICVAI's platform will modernize the experience while covering equivalent functional depth

Direct hands-on access to the reference system will not be provided; the full system manual will be shared instead to support backend schema and design work

- Core Platform Structure

Multi-tenant, multi-site structure with system/tenant IDs, configurable operating calendar, and a permissions/rights hierarchy spanning site, operating area, workstation, role, and user levels is confirmed as the model to build toward

A flexible "data mask"-style custom field system (supporting text, dropdown, radio, boolean fields, multi-language labels, and reusable value lists) is required, with standard fields provided out of the box and custom fields configurable per venue/product without new development

- A roles-comparison view (to directly compare permissions between two roles) is confirmed as a desirable addition not present in the reference system

- Products, Pricing & Events

- Products will use a flexible components/attributes model, allowing new ticket-type variants (e.g., new age categories) to be added via configuration rather than development

- Multiple, channel-specific and seasonal price lists per product are required

- Events are only required for products needing date/time/capacity control; simple open-dated products do not need an associated event

Performances (time slots) require separate configuration for POS sale-window timing ("minutes on screen") and access-control entry windows ("time opening/limit"), plus bulk creation, capacity editing, and a suspend/resume (not delete) state model

- Capacity must be splitable by sales channel via an envelope-style mechanism

- Tax configuration must support compound tax (tax-on-tax) calculation, in addition to standard inclusive/exclusive handling

- Entitlements, Promotions & Resources

Entitlement rules must support configurable re-entry limits, a wide range of expiration rule types, minimum/maximum sale-quantity restrictions, group-ticket handling, and linking a single ticket to multiple events

- Both single/shared promo codes and bulk-generated unique codes are required, alongside automatic, rule-based dynamic offers (e.g., buy-2-get-1-free) that don't require code entry

- An optional resource-management module (for bookable assets like vehicles and staff, with scheduling/rostering) is confirmed as a desirable capability

- Operations, POS & Access Control

- Duplicate-account detection and profile-merge functionality is required, given its high relevance in this region

The POS flow will follow the demonstrated logical structure (performance/slot selection → customer/reservation lookup or creation → cart → per-ticket detail capture where required → payment → ticket/receipt generation), reimagined with modern UI/UX

- Tickets require a documented distinction between a unique ticket ID and a shareable media/QR code

Tiered ticket access control (e.g., Bronze/Silver/Gold) will be modelled via location → admission profile → gate → access point, with explicit deny rules to enforce tier separation

- Built-in dashboards (cashier-level sales summary, venue-level admission summary) and a filterable report library (with custom report/document template design) are confirmed as required capabilities

- Process

The next workshop will return to UI/UX, covering the client-facing mobile app and staff/employee mobile app, alongside a lighter-touch look at the tenant and TICVAI websites

- Softlabs will bring prepared application/site concepts to that session, following the same format as the previous UI/UX workshop

### Action Items

- Action Item

- Owner

- Status

- Share the full reference system manual/documentation (backend configuration guide) via WhatsApp or shared folder

- Qossai

- Pending

- Share the open-items task/tracker sheet along with today's MoM

- Chinmay Parab

- Pending

- Use the reference manual and today's walkthrough to inform backend schema and database design

- Softlabs Backend Team

- Pending

- Prepare mobile application concepts (client-facing and staff/employee apps) for Monday's UI/UX session

- Softlabs Design Team

- Pending

- Prepare tenant website / TICVAI website material for Monday's UI/UX session (expected to be light-touch)

- Softlabs Design Team

- Pending

- Confirm scope and agenda for Monday's UI/UX workshop

- Chinmay Parab

- Pending

- Offer further deep-dive demos on specific reference-system areas on request in future sessions

- Qossai

- Ongoing

- Incorporate compound/tax-on-tax calculation capability into tax engine requirements

- Softlabs Backend Team

- Pending

- Incorporate profile duplicate-detection and merge functionality into requirements (high regional relevance)

- Softlabs Backend Team

- Pending

- Next Meeting

- Date: Monday (date to be confirmed)

- Time: To be confirmed

- Planned Topics

- Client-facing mobile application UI/UX

- Staff/employee mobile application UI/UX

- Tenant website and TICVAI website (lighter-touch discussion)

- Closing Remarks

This was an unusually deep, functionality-focused session: Allam walked the team through nearly every major configuration area of a mature, 20+ year old ticketing platform — tenant/site setup, permissions, custom data capture, products and pricing, events and time slots, entitlements, promotions, resource management, a live point-of-sale transaction, reporting, and a detailed access-control example. Both teams were aligned throughout that this system serves as a functional reference to learn from, not a design to copy — TICVAI's own platform will aim to deliver equivalent depth with a modern, AI-friendly, and easy-to-configure experience. Chinmay found the walkthrough especially valuable for understanding entitlement structures and product customization ahead of the team's own schema design work. The session closed with agreement to return to UI/UX topics next, focused on the client and staff mobile applications.
