## 2026-08-10

`sources/mom/TICVAI_Kickoff_MoM_2026-08-10.docx` · 3,303 words

### Minutes of Meeting

- TICVAI Technical Discovery Workshop — B2C App, Employee App and Layout builder App

### Date

- 10-August-2026

### Project

- TICVAI

### Meeting Type

- Technical Discovery Workshop — B2B, B2C and Employee app

### Prepared by

- Chitrangi Mestry

### Primary Objective

Softlabs Group to demonstrate the proposed UI/UX design and functionality for the TICVAI Guest (B2C) mobile application and the Staff/Employee mobile application, for review and feedback.

### Agenda

- Walkthrough of the B2C Guest Mobile App — design, configuration/back-office builder, and end-to-end booking journey

- Walkthrough of the Employee (Staff Operations) Mobile App — roles, task/work order management, inventory, approvals, and ticket scanning

- Discussion of open questions on AI concierge, multi-currency, third-party integrations, database/tenancy architecture, and app ownership

- Alignment on next steps: action item tracker, and scheduling of the next deep-dive session

### 4. Detailed Discussion

- 4.1 B2C Guest Mobile App — Configuration & Builder Module

- Allam walked through the mobile app back-office “builder” module that lets a tenant white-label and configure the guest app without code changes.

Branding & theming: Client logo upload (multiple formats), selectable colour themes, app icon, and custom font upload. A live preview is available before publishing changes.

Font & layout guardrails (open question raised): Chinmay flagged that unrestricted custom fonts/sizes could break layouts (e.g., cursive/bold fonts overflowing banner or description components). Agreed that size/format restrictions and pixel limits (e.g., banner image ≤ 1024px) are needed, with validation on upload and an explanatory note shown to the tenant admin.

- Layout builder: Header, footer, logo, bottom navigation icons, and colours are all configurable from the builder.

- Banner & promotion management: Configurable banner sizing; promotion/block activation via toggle.

- Custom content pages: Museum/venue-specific pages (e.g., “Plan Your Visit”, Accessibility) with accessibility-guideline compliance to be followed.

FAQs and Policies: Configurable FAQ section; Terms & Conditions, Privacy Policy, Cookie Policy (accept/deny prompt), and a fully configurable, tiered Refund Policy (e.g., no refund <24h, 50% between 24–48h, 100% refund >48h) driven by back-office rules per business.

Module & page enablement: Ticketing & Booking, Membership, Events, Attractions, Virtual Queue, F&B, Retail, and Parking modules can be enabled/disabled per tenant based on licence. Tenant-specific add-ons (Lost & Found, AI Concierge Chat, multi-language support, integrations) are similarly toggleable and will appear automatically as new integrations are built.

- Review & Publish: Final step in the builder flow before the configuration goes live.

- 4.2 AI Concierge Chat — Open Item

Chinmay raised that the AI concierge was originally scoped to use a third-party LLM API with PII scrubbing/masking of sensitive data. Qossai indicated the AI approach is not yet fully clear on the client side and requested a dedicated AI workshop to align on the technical approach before committing to a token/billing model.

Chinmay noted token utilisation cost would likely need to be billed separately from a fixed subscription fee, to avoid cost exposure if a tenant's usage exceeds planned limits.

Decision: Deferred — a separate AI workshop to be scheduled to walk through the mechanism and jointly decide the best approach (aligns with the platform's Tier 1/Tier 2/Tier 3 AI framework already documented separately).

- 4.3 B2C Guest App — End-to-End Booking Journey

- Home page: Logo, banner, and category tabs (Tickets, What's On, Plan Your Visit, Map).

Explore & purchase flow: Categories (Attractions, Exhibitions, Events, Dining, Shops, Experiences) → attraction/admission ticket selection (driven by back-office configuration) → date/time slot selection → add-ons (configurable per ticket type or generic) → review & pay → confirmation.

Confirmation & delivery: “Add to Wallet” (Apple Wallet / Google Wallet based on device), and tickets can additionally be sent via WhatsApp, SMS, or email depending on the guest's chosen delivery method.

Guest profile & wallet: Gift vouchers and a stored-value “money card”/wallet; “My Tickets” (all purchased tickets) and “My Reservations” (bookings, each containing one or more tickets) with reservation details and date-modification capability.

Ticket transfer: Tickets can be transferred to another person via email/SMS with an optional message; supports keeping ownership while renaming the ticket holder, or fully transferring both.

- Membership: Membership ID, validity, entitlements (free entry, F&B offers, etc.), linked members (view), membership card, and renewal/history.

- Calendar integration & wishlist: Add bookings to Apple/Google/Outlook calendar with reminders; wishlist for F&B and retail items to purchase later on-site.

- 4.4 Venue Map, Queueing, F&B, Retail & Parking

Venue map: Customisable park/venue map showing attractions, dining, retail, and restrooms. Qossai proposed defining image/format guidance for tenants uploading maps to avoid errors, and referenced the Kidzania app's interactive 3D-style map as a benchmark for a better experience.

Live wait times / virtual queue: Displays estimated wait time per ride/attraction (e.g., “41 minutes”). Confirmed this typically depends on a third-party camera/sensor system at the venue; TAIS/TICVAI will build the underlying functionality and expose a standard API for the client's chosen third-party system to feed queue data into.

Food & Beverage: Browse restaurants/outlets and order; pickup-location option shown automatically per outlet, with delivery as an additional option (delivery requires the guest's location) when the venue uses the platform's own F&B module — a distinct, separate integration path exists if a venue uses a third-party F&B solution.

- Retail: Similar model to F&B — pickup location or delivery.

Parking: Two supported models: (1) fully platform-native — guest purchases parking, receives a QR code scanned by a handheld device at the gate; (2) integrated with a third-party parking/ANPR system — guest enters their plate number, which is whitelisted so the barrier opens automatically on arrival. Both flows are to be supported in the app.

- 4.5 Third-Party Integration Approach

- Chinmay asked whether all B2B/third-party integrations (parking, queue timing, etc.) would follow one standard pattern.

Agreed approach: Standardise on exposing the platform's own APIs for third parties to consume wherever possible (this is the preferred default). Where a third-party provider insists the platform must instead push data into their API, that will be handled as an additional bespoke integration, assessed for effort case by case.

- 4.6 AI Functions, Lost & Found, Reviews, Loyalty

- AI concierge: Guests can ask natural-language questions (ticketing, F&B, retail, venue info, timings) and receive answers grounded in the venue's configured data.

- Lost & Found: Guests can log lost items; back-office staff can match and mark items as found for guest collection, with full tracking.

- Post-visit review/feedback (survey), Loyalty & Rewards, Offers & Promotions, Profile, and Help & Support are also part of the app.

- 4.7 Account Creation, Localisation & Multi-Currency

Sign-up: Simple registration via phone number or email, each verified with an OTP (sent via WhatsApp or SMS/email as configured), followed by minimal profile capture (first/last name).

- Language: Full multi-language support (Arabic and others such as Chinese), consistent with the platform's i18n/RTL architecture already agreed.

Multi-currency display vs settlement — key discussion: Two options were discussed: (a) a display-only “approximate” conversion using a back-office-configured rate, useful only so the guest understands roughly what they will pay while the transaction still settles in the local/base currency; and (b) full Dynamic Currency Conversion (DCC) via the payment gateway itself, where the guest genuinely pays and is charged in their own currency at the gateway level, while the booking/back-office record is always kept in the venue's configured base currency.

Real-time FX rate (raised by Reshma): Exchange rates fluctuate constantly and should not be hardcoded as static master data; a live/real-time FX rate source (API) is needed.

Client rate-setting behaviour (Qossai): In practice, most regional clients (~90%) prefer to set the conversion rate manually in the back office and apply a margin (e.g., quoting 3.80 when the market rate is 3.68) as an additional revenue source, rather than integrating a live exchange-rate API (e.g., XE). Both a manual-with-margin option and a third-party live-rate integration option should be supported.

POS parity: The same foreign-currency display/charge logic should apply at the Point of Sale, with all transactions recorded in the base currency for accounting, plus a dedicated report showing total foreign-currency collections by currency.

- 4.8 Checkout Extras — Delivery, Waiting Room, Upsell/Cross-Sell, Seating, Resources

- Ticket delivery method: WhatsApp, SMS, email, or Apple Wallet, selectable at checkout/confirmation; tickets can also be emailed to a third party.

Branded virtual waiting room: Activates automatically above a configurable concurrent-buyer threshold (example discussed: 500 concurrent buyers) during high-demand on-sales; shows a wait time and is branded consistently with the tenant's mobile app theme.

- Maintenance page: Customisable holding page shown to guests during planned platform maintenance/upgrades.

Upsell & cross-sell: System-driven prompts — e.g., upsell a yearly membership on top of a general admission purchase, or cross-sell a family ticket bundle when two adult + two child tickets are added to the cart, each with associated discounts/benefits.

- Seating & resource booking: Seated events use the previously agreed seat-map flow; resource bookings (e.g., cabana rental) decrement a capacity-based inventory on booking.

- 4.9 “Plan Your Adventure” (Itinerary Planner)

A guided itinerary-planning feature (benchmarked against Skidata's equivalent) letting a guest plan their visit day (which rides/attractions, in what order) ahead of time, tied to their ticket purchase and saved as a personal visit profile.

Group sharing (raised by Chinmay): Requested the ability to share an itinerary with a group — e.g., via an in-app QR code a friend can scan to receive/join the itinerary, or an invite-to-join mechanism. Agreed as a valuable addition (Qossai confirmed interest); to be incorporated into the design.

Dynamic QR code: Ticket QR codes are temporary/non-scannable until the guest is on-site (validated by location/system state), then activate and continuously refresh to prevent misuse — previously agreed approach, reconfirmed.

- 4.10 Bundle Packages

Packages combine multiple components (ticket + meal + retail, or ticket + event ticket, etc.) within a single attraction, sold at a discount to encourage cross-module spend — distinct from an itinerary spanning multiple attractions.

- Reshma's clarification/question: Whether this differs from a Klook-style multi-attraction custom package. Confirmed it is a within-attraction package, not a cross-attraction one.

Pre-defined vs dynamically built packages: Both approaches were discussed — offering curated pre-built packages for direct purchase, and/or allowing guests to dynamically build their own bundle by adding items to the cart, with the system automatically detecting eligible combinations and applying an automatic discount (e.g., 5–10%). Softlabs to consider how to incorporate the dynamic-bundling approach.

Design inspiration: Qossai suggested reviewing product presentation on apps such as Talabat/similar platforms (using product video rather than static images) and referenced a previously shared benchmark app (“222”) for further UI/UX inspiration.

- 4.11 Queue Wait-Time Accuracy (Follow-up)

Reshma followed up on how ride wait-time accuracy would actually be achieved. Confirmed two standard integration options: consuming a third-party queue-management/ticketing API, or consuming camera/people-counting sensor data installed on-ride. Agreed approach: TICVAI exposes a standard API for queue/wait-time data that any third-party system can push into; direct integration with a specific vendor's system would be treated as additional bespoke work.

- 4.12 B2C App — Customisation, Ownership & Architecture (Q&A)

Customisation scope (Pradnya): Confirmed the guest app's structure/layout is fixed; tenants can customise graphics, colours, fonts, and enabled tabs/modules, and the checkout flow adapts automatically to the product type configured (seated, timed-slot, date-only, etc.) — no ability to add entirely new custom components.

App store ownership (Pradnya): Open question — Qossai's view is the tenant should own the published app (their own Apple/Google developer account, since they bear the cost and account terms), but with the platform's branding embedded (e.g., “built by Ticvai”). Softlabs to advise on the recommended approach and process, including a simple flow for the tenant to enter their developer credentials and as automated a submission/approval process as possible.

Data architecture per tenant (Pradnya): Confirmed each tenant gets its own dedicated database (e.g., a “Dubai Museum” database), with all of that tenant's sales channels (B2C web, B2C mobile, B2B, kiosk, tablet) connecting into the same single database so a guest's login/session is consistent across channels. Two deployment models exist: (1) shared TICVAI-hosted infrastructure with an isolated database per tenant, or (2) a fully separate, client-hosted database (e.g., on the client's own Azure/AWS) when the client wants full physical separation.

Reshma's supporting rationale: Separate databases per tenant avoid any risk of configuration or data mixing between customers and keep each tenant's settings, rates, and views fully independent.

### 5. Employee (Staff Operations) App — Walkthrough

- 5.1 Login, Roles & Dashboard

- Login: Username/password or SSO.

Role selection (changed during discussion): Original design showed a manual role-selection screen after login; Qossai proposed this should instead be fully automatic based on the user's back-office role configuration, taking the employee directly to their role-specific home screen. agreed this makes more sense and will be adopted.

Role-based dashboard: Shows task counts, work orders, and inspections relevant to the logged-in employee's access; the entire navigation set (approvals, inventory, etc.) is filtered by the employee's assigned role/permissions.

- 5.2 Core Navigation & Modules

- Work Orders, Task & Assets, Inventory/Safety/Inspections, Attendance, Approvals/Requests (store requisitions, leave requests, etc.), Incidents, Communications, and Venue Map.

- Notifications: Categorised by type — some requiring action, some purely informational.

- Search: Search across tasks and incidents.

- Create: Quick-create for maintenance requests, IT support, cleaning/safety/security requests, store requests, purchase requests, and leave requests.

- Employee ID/profile and preferences.

- 5.3 Task, Work Order & Asset Management

- Task logging: Maintenance/operations staff log tasks (e.g., “fix water leak”, “fire extinguisher inspection”) with priority and scheduled date/time.

- Work order lifecycle: Created → assigned → in progress → review → closed, with a timer tracking resolution duration.

Photo vs barcode capture (raised by Chinmay): Asked whether faulty assets without a barcode (e.g., a broken pipe or valve) could instead be logged with a photo rather than a barcode scan. Confirmed: yes — photo capture is the primary/preferred method for this use case, since many maintenance items (pipes, lighting, etc.) have no barcode to scan.

- 5.4 Inventory & Procurement

- Item lookup: Search by name or barcode scan to view stock levels and availability across stores/warehouses.

- Inventory count & goods receipt: Both manageable directly from the employee app.

Procurement workflow: Requisition raised in the app → department-head approval → purchasing creates a Purchase Order (comparing vendor quotations for best price) → PO sent to vendor → goods received → items issued to the requesting department.

Low-stock / par-level automation: Minimum stock thresholds (e.g., 100 units) automatically trigger a draft requisition when breached, for review and confirmation before it proceeds through the purchasing workflow.

- 5.5 Multi-Stage Approval Workflow

A generic, configurable multi-step approval engine applies broadly — not only to inventory/procurement, but also to actions such as price changes and new product creation.

Example flow (pricing change) walked through by Qossai: IT/Operations initiates → Operations Manager approves → Finance approves → CEO approves → returns to IT for publishing to the relevant sales channels.

Approval actions: Approve, Reject, Return, or Request More Information, with an AI-generated approval summary shown alongside the request and a visible workflow trail of who has approved at each stage.

- Confirmed audience: Applicable to venue-level managers and supervisors, with the specific approval chain/assignees configurable per workflow type.

- 5.6 Roster, Leave & Break Management, Resources

- Roster/shift schedule: View shift timings, upcoming shifts, and clock in/out of a shift.

- Leave requests: Submitted through the app so resourcing/coverage is visible in advance.

- Break management: Staff log break windows so a replacement can be scheduled (e.g., to avoid leaving a ticket counter unstaffed).

Guest assistance / resources: Team supervisors, announcements, and quick access to venue information (e.g., opening hours) so staff can answer guest queries directly from the app.

Attraction status & Lost and Found: Live ride/attraction status visibility, and staff can log found items directly, which then surface for guest claim via the Lost & Found desk/workflow.

- 5.7 Ticket Scanning / Access Control App

Dedicated scanning app: A separate, dedicated iOS/Android app for ticket validation, intended for devices used solely as scanners (e.g., mounted at turnstiles/gates), so those devices show only scanning functionality rather than the full employee app.

Embedded scanning: The same ticket-validation capability is also available inside the main Employee App, so staff do not need to switch apps if using a general-purpose device for occasional scanning.

Offline requirement (raised by Chinmay — important): Scanning must work as a native/installable app capability (not a web app), so that ticket validation continues to function fully offline (e.g., if turnstile network connectivity drops or a device has no data connection), storing scans locally and syncing to the server once connectivity is restored.Allam confirmed this is the intended offline-first approach, consistent with the platform's offline architecture.

- 5.8 Additional Employee App Areas (Noted, Not Demoed in Detail)

- Training & Knowledge Base, Employee Recognition, and further AI-assisted functionality within the employee app.

### 6. Key Decisions & Agreements

Font and image upload restrictions (size/pixel limits) will be enforced in the mobile app builder to protect layout integrity, with guidance notes shown to tenant admins.

- A dedicated AI workshop will be scheduled to align on the AI concierge's technical approach and commercial/token-billing model before finalising the design.

Standardise third-party integrations on TICVAI exposing its own APIs for partners to consume as the default pattern; vendor-mandated inbound-push integrations will be scoped as additional bespoke work case by case.

Support both a manual (admin-set, margin-inclusive) and a live third-party FX-rate option for multi-currency display, in addition to full Dynamic Currency Conversion at the payment gateway; all transactions settle and are recorded in the venue's base currency, with a separate foreign-currency collections report.

- Add group-sharing capability (QR code / invite-to-join) to the “Plan Your Adventure” itinerary planner.

- Employee app role screen will be removed in favour of fully automatic, back-office-driven role routing immediately after login.

- Asset/incident logging in the employee app will prioritise photo capture over barcode scanning for items without barcodes (pipes, valves, lighting, etc.).

Ticket scanning/access-control functionality must be a native, installable capability with full offline operation and sync-on-reconnect — not a web-based feature — available both as a dedicated scanner app and embedded within the general employee app.

Each tenant will have its own isolated database; all of a tenant's sales channels (web, mobile, B2B, kiosk, tablet) connect to that single tenant database. A separate, client-hosted database option remains available for tenants requiring full physical separation.

### 7. Open Items / Questions for Follow-Up

App store ownership model: whether the tenant or TICVAI owns the published Apple/Google Play app listing, and how TICVAI branding is embedded regardless of ownership — Softlabs to advise on recommended approach and a simplified credential/submission flow for tenants.

- Detailed design/build of dynamically bundled packages (auto-discounting on qualifying cart combinations) to be worked through.

- Confirm final venue-map guidance/format standard for tenants (referencing Kidzania-style interactive map as a UX benchmark).

- AI concierge technical mechanism and cost/billing model — pending dedicated AI workshop.

## 2026-08-12

`sources/mom/TICVAI_Kickoff_MoM_12Aug2026.docx` · 4,957 words

### Minutes of Meeting

- TICVAI Kick-off Meeting — POS Session & Role Management, Guest App Publishing, Finance & Ledger Deep-Dive

### Date

- 12 August 2026

### Project

- TICVAI

### Meeting Type

- Kick-off Meeting — POS Session Management, Guest App Publishing & Finance/Ledger Deep-Dive

### Prepared by

- Chitrangi Mestry

### Primary Objective

To clarify POS session, break, and role-permission handling across workstations and roaming ("flying pause") terminals; align on a publishing approach for client-branded guest applications; and walk through the finance and ledger architecture — the dual-ledger data model, VAT/tax logic, revenue recognition, refund processing, settlement/reconciliation, and financial reporting — as a functional and technical reference for TICVAI's platform, alongside planning next steps for infrastructure compliance review and the following UI/UX-focused workshops.

### Participants

- TICVAI Team

- Softlabs Team

### Agenda

- POS session management and break handling

- Flying pause setup and permission configuration

- Role-based access and workstation-linked front-end

- Multiple roles per user and role switching

- Guest application publishing and white-labeling approach

- Finance & ledger architecture overview

- VAT / tax calculation logic

- Deferred revenue and ledger flow

- Refund ledger sequencing and refund policy

- Customer support / chat integration approach

- Settlement and reconciliation process

- Billing, fees, reporting and ERP integration roadmap

- Chart of accounts and account mapping

- Finance module walkthrough (dashboards, transactions ledger, revenue recognition, payments, refunds, shift/till management, financial reporting)

- AI financial assistant and vector database compliance

- Infrastructure components for compliance review

- POS hardware specification requirements

- Progress update on workflows and schemas

- Next steps and meeting planning

### 1. POS Session Management and Break Handling

Chinmay opened by referencing the requirement matrix's "one user per session" rule for the POS and asked how breaks — where a live cashier needs to step away — should be handled. Allam confirmed the model: the logged-in user must either log out or suspend their shift before a second user can log into the same workstation; the workstation and user session are tied together, so no second user can log in over an active session. Qossai confirmed this matches the intended meaning of "one user, one session" — a user can take a break and a different user can log in afterward, but never concurrently on the same workstation.

### 2. Flying POS Setup and Permission Configuration

Chinmay asked for clarity on how the "flying pause" (a mobile/roaming POS instance not tied to a fixed terminal) is set up and permissioned, referencing the earlier point-of-sale/FP module split (e.g., a park entrance terminal configured only for ticketing vs. a theatre terminal configured for both ticketing and FP). Allam explained that every device running the application is assigned a unique workstation ID, which determines what modules and permissions are available at login, based on the roles and permissions configured for that user. Qossai added that ultimately the device itself is secondary to the user's configured role: whatever role a user is logged in under determines what they see, regardless of which physical workstation, tablet, or laptop they log in from — illustrated with a cashier who sees the full park ticket range at a main-gate POS but only the food & beverage menu when logged in from a restaurant POS, because access is scoped to their assigned role, not the device.

### 3. Role-Based Access and Workstation-Linked Front-End

Allam added that, in addition to role-based access, each workstation can be linked to a specific front-end "sales board" — for example, of ten workstations, five could be assigned to ticketing, three to food & beverage, and two to retail — so that when a cashier logs in on a given workstation, the system automatically opens the matching front end (ticketing, F&B, or retail) for that workstation. Qossai reiterated that a finance user logging in from any workstation, laptop, or from home would only see finance reports and related information, since access is entirely role-driven.

### 4. Multiple Roles per User and Role Switching

Chinmay confirmed that, like the pause application, the web/admin version would also be configured to load a user's access automatically at login rather than requiring self-configuration. Allam noted a further capability typically reserved for admin/IT staff: a single user can be assigned multiple roles (e.g., admin, cashier, supervisor, manager simultaneously) and choose or swap between them at login to see the corresponding privileges. Chinmay proposed the resulting rule: if a user has only one assigned role they log in directly into it; if they have more than one, they are prompted to select which role/account to use. Allam confirmed this was correct, noting that in the standard case a user is assigned only a single role.

### 5. Guest Application Publishing and White-Labelling

Chinmay raised the question of how client-branded guest applications (e.g., for a venue such as Ferrari World) should be published, once the client has re-themed or configured the interface to their own branding. He outlined two options: the client publishes their own independently listed app on the App/Play Store, or all venues are accessed through a single universal TICVAI app where the user selects their venue. Qossai's view was that regardless of the branding approach, the TICVAI name must always remain visible to the end user in some form (e.g., a "Made by TICVAI" credit in the app listing) and cannot be removed by the client. Chinmay asked whether there should be a dedicated client-facing module with customization screens and a publish action tied to CI/CD, versus simply providing the client a canvas to export and publish the build themselves. Qossai and Allam asked Softlabs to prepare and present both options with their pros and cons so the two teams can jointly decide the best approach; Chinmay agreed to bring this analysis to a future session rather than over email, given the volume of related design questions still emerging.

### 6. Finance & Ledger Architecture Overview

Moving into the finance-specific portion of the session, Chinmay presented the backend data model for the platform's ledger system. The platform will maintain full account-level records — not just process payments — with transactions classified down to the individual user and tenant level. Two ledgers underpin the model: a primary ledger tracking transaction-level entries (used for reconciliation) and a second ledger recording journal entries reflecting each financial event, enabling trial balance, P&L, and balance sheet generation at any point in time without additional transformation. The database is planned to scale horizontally to absorb peak-season load (e.g., during high-volume ticketing periods); the specific approach for redeploying multiple database instances/clusters is still being worked out. The stack will be built on .NET and PostgreSQL for strong typing and ACID guarantees, structured as an append-only ledger — transactions are never deleted; refunds and corrections are appended as new entries — enabling automatic reconciliation to produce the balance sheet. An AI-assisted reporting layer for accountants/finance managers is planned but parked for phase two; the underlying data model is being kept "AI-ready" so it can be integrated later without rework. Example financial events include online ticket sales, gateway sales, and gift card purchases, with debits covering receivables/bank statements and credits covering ticket revenue across venues.

### 7. VAT / Tax Calculation Logic

VAT will be calculated per line item rather than on the overall basket total, since different items (e.g., tickets vs. bottled water) can carry different VAT rates — each line will carry its own VAT calculation to ensure accuracy for taxation purposes. Qossai reminded the group of a prior requirement to support tax-on-tax (VAT charged on VAT), which has come from multiple existing clients. Allam emphasized that the tax component must be configurable to support multiple countries' tax structures — not only the UAE's relatively simple flat 5% rate but more complex structures such as Egypt's — including whether discounts are applied inclusive or exclusive of tax. Chinmay confirmed a dedicated, isolated taxation model is planned to support this configurability, including country-specific additions, and that this will be explored in more detail in a dedicated tax workshop.

### 8. Deferred Revenue and Ledger Flow

Chinmay walked through the deferred revenue and ledger posting flow: placing an order has no ledger impact; capturing payment triggers VAT calculation and receivables recognition, with the liability carried in the second ledger and reported by visit date. Ticket revenue is only recognized (moved into the primary ledger) once the visit/redemption occurs — refunds are deliberately excluded from the primary ledger until fully resolved, since including them earlier would complicate later corrections; revenue is instead held in a separate ledger until the visit date to allow refunds or transfers to be cleanly managed. Allam noted the revenue recognition rules should follow the document Qossai had previously shared and should all be configurable. Chinmay confirmed the current design is based purely on the requirement matrix's recognition points — e.g., immediate recognition for POS sales, recognition on redemption for gift cards, straight-line or per-visit recognition for annual passes, and breakage revenue recognized on expiry for unused tickets. Allam asked Chinmay to also cross-check the ticketing system's user manual, which contains additional recognition rules beyond the requirement matrix; Chinmay confirmed he is working through the (lengthy, legacy-format) manuals already.

### 9. Refund Ledger Sequencing and Refund Policy

Chinmay outlined a six-step refund flow: a refund initiated from the POS/ticketing software calls the refund service, which connects to the ledger; since committed funds are held in the ledger before being moved to the second ledger at the event, refunds can be initiated directly from the ledger without routing through the second ledger, calling an external worker which connects to the payment gateway to initiate the refund. The refund engine must support time-banded rules (refunds disallowed after a cut-off), chargeback handling, and full audit trail entries (credit memos, adjustments to an issued invoice without moving cash). Allam added further refund requirements: configurable refund percentage by time band (e.g., full refund a set number of days before the event, reduced percentage closer to or after that threshold); support for both online and on-site refund initiation (a POS-initiated refund routed for approval before hitting the bank, and a customer-initiated refund request raised directly from their account/profile, triggering a notification to operations for approval, rejection, or a request for more information); and support for partial refunds. Chinmay confirmed this maps to a preset, time-gated refund percentage structure with the ability for an authorized approver (e.g., venue or finance manager) to apply a custom override percentage, and asked at what organizational layer this approval authority should sit. Allam confirmed access should be fully role-driven and configurable — no role or permission is predefined; any privilege (including refund approval) can be assigned to any custom-built role.

### 10. Customer Support / Chat Integration Approach

Chinmay asked whether the platform needs to account for client-side chat/call support — since TICVAI will not maintain client support staff directly — via integration adapters into each client's own support systems. Allam clarified this would typically mean the client's own contact center accessing the platform to look up reservation/ticket issues. Qossai and Reshma discussed two approaches: connecting external client chat systems via an adapter, versus keeping all support interactions within the TICVAI platform (with client staff logging in to view and respond to their own tickets/chats). Reshma favored keeping everything within TICVAI's own application to retain a full audit trail and avoid inconsistent inputs across different client systems, particularly since TICVAI is responsible for its own reconciliation and settlement. Qossai agreed this suits larger clients but suggested smaller clients without their own support infrastructure could use a native, white-labelled TICVAI chat feature offered as a subscription add-on, with a built-in AI chat assistant as the first line of response before escalation to a human/CR representative role within the platform. The group agreed on this phased approach: build native chat/AI-assisted support into the platform first (creating a dedicated CR-representative role for incoming chats), while keeping the door open to build client-specific integration adapters in phase two for larger clients who need a peer-to-peer connection to their own support systems.

### 11. Settlement and Reconciliation Process

Chinmay described the planned settlement/reconciliation flow, run at the end of each week or month, in five steps: ingest data, parse, match, classify, and auto-resolve. The goal is to automate what is traditionally a manual reconciliation process performed by an accountant, so that only genuinely mismatched amounts are escalated for human review — reducing manual effort and improving speed, accuracy, and auditability compared to reviewing thousands of entries by hand.

### 12. Billing, Fees, Reporting and ERP Integration Roadmap

Chinmay outlined the broader billing/fees/reporting/ERP scope: subscription and membership billing, fee management, financial reporting, payment gateway management, payment device management, and ERP integration (the latter planned for phase two, consistent with the currently limited/agreed integration scope). The taxation model discussed in item 7 will also sit within this area and will be covered in a separate, dedicated workshop. Allam added that payment gateway integrations (Stripe, Network International) must be full end-to-end integrations that consume all relevant APIs — not just the "happy path." He gave two examples: (a) a payment inquiry API to check whether a payment actually succeeded when the success response failed to reach TICVAI's system (so the order can still be closed and tickets issued), and (b) recovering from a customer completing an OTP/payment step but closing the browser before the session finalizes — in both cases a backend service should periodically check incomplete sessions against the gateway's payment-status API and complete the order if payment succeeded. Chinmay related a personal example of this exact failure mode with an unrelated ticketing app and confirmed his understanding of the required flow; Allam confirmed on-site payment failures (e.g., a card machine charging the customer but the confirmation message not reaching the POS due to a network/communication gap) require the same kind of reconciling background service.

### 13. Chart of Accounts and Account Mapping

Chinmay asked for clarity on how chart-of-accounts data would be structured, expecting the platform to ingest CSV files from clients into the ledger, and requested more detail on the resulting account table structure. Allam confirmed the platform should support both scenarios: creating a chart of accounts natively on the TICVAI platform, and mapping to an externally maintained chart of accounts where a client already has one. Chinmay acknowledged some due diligence remains on his side for this item and will follow up with any questions in a future workshop.

### 14. Finance Module Walkthrough — Dashboards, Chart of Accounts & Entities

Allam then walked through a set of reference finance-module screens built from the shared finance requirement/metric sheet, explicitly framed as a base for TICVAI's own UI/UX design rather than a template to copy exactly. The first screen set covered: a finance dashboard showing gross revenue, net revenue, recognized revenue, deferred revenue, and refunds (with graphical charts, selectable by period); a legal entities view listing all tenant sites with country, currency, and active/inactive status for multi-tenant setups; the chart of accounts (with external-system codes for ERP/third-party mapping, and classification into assets, liability, income, or expense); a chart-of-accounts hierarchy and edit view showing parent-account relationships and financial dimensions (e.g., profit-center classification, cost centers); transaction-to-account and payment/offset account mapping; financial year/period setup (which varies by country, e.g., UAE's January–December year vs. India's April–March) with the ability to close a period to lock further postings; and an ERP integration center for external system connections. Qossai confirmed with Chinmay that sharing this reference material (including sub-page detail beyond the summary shown) would help the front-end and API design process, given the scale of the requirement matrix; Chinmay agreed this visual/backend reference materially helps translate the written requirement matrix into a concrete system design.

### 15. Financial Transactions Ledger and Journal Entries

The second screen set covered the financial transactions ledger: a list of all system transactions with daily counts and totals, a pending/failed sync status for transactions awaiting an external system integration, and a transaction detail view showing chart-of-account mapping, payment method, product-level detail, and whether a given line sits in sale, deferred, or redemption status. A journal entry list showed all posted debit/credit entries, alongside a manual journal entry capability (for cases such as manually booking revenue) and an approval workflow — a finance user posts a voucher, a finance manager/director reviews and approves it, and only then does it hit the ledger.

### 16. Revenue Recognition Rules and Allocation Splits

The revenue allocation screen showed recognized vs. unrecognized (wallet) revenue graphically, alongside the revenue recognition rule configuration itself — for example, F&B revenue is recognized immediately on sale, while annual memberships use monthly straight-line allocation (e.g., a 1,500 AED annual membership recognizing 150 AED per month over its term, with the balance recognized at membership expiry). A "revenue allocation split builder" allows a combo/package ticket's price to be split across products (e.g., a portion to tickets, a portion to F&B) or across legal entities (e.g., a two-day pass covering two venues, split by fixed amount or percentage per venue) — Chinmay confirmed the typical model is a percentage-of-total-price split, and Allam confirmed both fixed-amount and percentage-based splits are supported.

### 17. Payments Reconciliation

The payments screen consolidates all payments collected across gateways (Stripe, NI) and on-site methods (cash, card), with an automated reconciliation and matching capability comparing platform-recorded payments against the payment gateway's records (e.g., flagging a variance between 10,000 AED shown by the gateway vs. 9,500 AED recorded internally). Allam suggested this depends on available payment-gateway reconciliation APIs and should be investigated further. Chinmay sought clarification on the intended mechanism — a periodic reconciliation file from the bank/payment partner compared in bulk, rather than a per-transaction API call (which he flagged as impractical at scale) — and Allam confirmed the intended approach is a monthly file-based reconciliation against which discrepancies/variances are flagged for review, rather than a per-transaction check.

### 18. Bulk Refund Processing and Refund Requests

Allam flagged an additional refund requirement raised for the first time in this session: bulk refund processing — for example, refunding roughly 5,000 transactions in one action if an entire event is cancelled, rather than requiring transactions to be refunded one at a time. This should support bulk selection/refund at the event or date level (for both online and on-site bookings), subject to an approval step before all selected refunds are processed together. A related refund-requests screen shows customer-initiated online refund requests awaiting a decision from finance/operations (accept, request more information, or auto-deny).

### 19. Cash/Shift and Till Management

Allam then walked through cash/shift ("till") management: a shift/session view showing open and closed sessions per workstation, expected cash and card totals, and a "blind" cash-out process where a cashier does not see their expected total when closing out (only their float plus sales should reconcile against what they physically deposit) — with the system flagging any shortage or overage for supervisor review, and optionally blocking shift closure entirely until the discrepancy is resolved or explained. Shift closure requires supervisor authorization, generates a denomination-itemized closing receipt, and triggers automatic email of the closing report to finance/leadership. A live till monitor dashboard shows real-time cash status per workstation and open/close codes; a configurable cash-drawer limit allows a cashier to "unload" excess cash mid-shift on a busy day, with the system tracking the unloaded amount separately so it reconciles correctly at final shift close. Chinmay confirmed the need for a mid-shift "partial hold" state that preserves the removed cash for end-of-shift reconciliation.

### 20. End-of-Day Reports and Overage/Shortage Handling

A defined set of end-of-day reports was reviewed, including a cashier shift report, till report, sales-by-location report, payment type summary, cash management report, variance report, refund report, and end-of-day consolidated report — illustrated with an example showing an expected cash total of 8,480 AED against an actual deposit of 8,460 AED, a 20 AED variance/shortage. Any such variance posts automatically to a dedicated overage/shortage ledger account, visible at month-end for review.

### 21. Financial Reporting (P&L, Balance Sheet, Trial Balance)

The financial reporting module automatically generates a profit & loss statement (revenue realized per category, cost of sales — e.g., F&B ingredient procurement costs offset against F&B revenue to derive profit), a balance sheet (assets and liabilities), a trial balance and ledger view, revenue and deferred-revenue analytics, and site-wise revenue performance. A financial approval center/financial controls screen surfaces transactions with exceptions or variances requiring review. A set of automatable daily, weekly, and monthly finance summary reports rounds out the reporting suite; Allam summarized the core reporting pillars as profit & loss, balance sheet, cash flow, trial balance, and operational/review-related reports.

### 22. AI Financial Assistant and Vector Database Compliance

Chinmay raised the AI financial-assistant component and the plan to use a vector database, expressing concern that Postgres's native vector capability may not be sufficient at the expected data volume, and proposing Qdrant as an alternative — subject to confirming it satisfies UAE compliance requirements, to avoid discovering a limitation only after reaching production. Allam confirmed this was timely, as he has a meeting scheduled with the Dubai Compliance Authority on Friday and needs a list of the specific components/services planned for the AWS/Azure infrastructure (e.g., PostgreSQL as the database) in order to raise and validate them with the authority.

### 23. Infrastructure Components for Compliance Review

Allam asked Chinmay to provide a list of the planned infrastructure components (database, database structure, and other AWS/Azure services in scope) by end of day, so he can review internally before Friday's Compliance Authority meeting and report back afterward on any concerns raised (e.g., prior findings around certain database services' compliance status). Chinmay agreed to send this by end of day. Given the Friday call's compressed schedule, Qossai proposed starting the joint Friday session 15 minutes earlier (10:45 AM Chinmay's time) to cover the infrastructure/compliance discussion first, before the main workshop continues at 11:00 AM; Allam requested that TICVAI's infrastructure team (Dinesh Jadhav and Siddhesh) join this portion so they have full context and can respond to any recommendations directly. Reshma confirmed Dinesh and Siddhesh would be looped in, and Allam agreed to forward the calendar invite, covering both AWS and Azure infrastructure options.

### 24. POS Hardware Specification Requirements

Chinmay noted that for the pause/terminal hardware specifications, TICVAI can independently source publicly available documentation or manuals as references, but needs at minimum a list of the exact hardware models and reference numbers currently in use, to inform device/driver configuration. Qossai confirmed he and Allam would compile this list next week.

### 25. Progress Update on Workflows and Schemas

Chinmay gave a status update on TICVAI's internal workstream: workflow and schema design is underway but currently covers only around 20% of the full scope, following a deliberately process-centric (rather than user-centric) approach, informed in part by discussion points raised in this and prior sessions. Front-end page isolation is proceeding in parallel, to be followed by full API definition once complete — consistent with the API-first approach discussed previously, intended to accelerate downstream development. Once further along, Chinmay expects to be able to share both low-level and high-level design diagrams.

### 26. Next Steps and Meeting Planning

Qossai proposed sharing the full design set (screens) with explanations for each page so TICVAI's team can review and raise queries — noting the shared material would represent a summary level (main pages), with sub-pages to follow. Qossai will forward his existing page-level explanations (in PDF) to Allam, who will compile everything into a single Word document for TICVAI. The team agreed the next joint workshop — tentatively Friday, following the shorter infrastructure/compliance discussion — will cover food & beverage, retail, the licensing module, and shift management, with both sides presenting their respective materials. Reshma reiterated the standing request for TICVAI's team to receive the full set of screens with explanations to review and raise any queries.

### Decisions Made

- POS Sessions, Roles & Access

One user per session is confirmed at the workstation level: a user must log out or suspend their shift before another user can log into the same workstation; access and front-end module selection are entirely role-driven and tied to the individual, not the physical device.

Each workstation can be pre-linked to a specific front-end (ticketing, F&B, retail) via a "sales board" configuration, auto-loading the correct interface based on which workstation the cashier logs into.

A single user can be assigned multiple roles and select/switch between them at login; a user with only one assigned role logs in directly, while a user with multiple roles is prompted to choose.

- Guest Application

- The TICVAI name/branding must remain visible to end users in any client-branded (white-labeled) guest application, regardless of publishing method.

Softlabs will prepare and present both guest-app publishing options (client-branded independent App Store listing vs. a single universal TICVAI app) with pros and cons before a final decision is made.

- Finance & Ledger Architecture

The platform will use a dual-ledger, append-only data model (no deletions; refunds/corrections are appended) built on .NET and PostgreSQL, designed to scale horizontally for peak-season load.

VAT will be calculated per line item (not on the total basket), with configurable support for tax-on-tax (compound tax) and multi-country tax structures, inclusive or exclusive of discounts.

Revenue is only recognized into the primary ledger at the point defined by the requirement matrix (e.g., on redemption, per-visit, or on expiry for breakage); refunds are deliberately excluded from the primary ledger until fully resolved.

- An AI-assisted financial reporting layer is confirmed for phase two; the underlying data model will be kept "AI-ready" now to avoid future rework.

- The chart of accounts must support both a natively created TICVAI chart of accounts and mapping to an externally maintained (client/ERP) chart of accounts.

- Refunds & Reconciliation

Refunds will follow a six-step ledger-to-gateway sequencing flow, with configurable time-banded refund percentages, an authorized-approver override capability, partial refunds, and support for both operations-initiated and customer-initiated (self-service) refund requests.

Bulk refund processing (e.g., refunding all transactions for a cancelled event in one approved action) is confirmed as a required capability, in addition to single-transaction refunds.

- Settlement/reconciliation will follow a five-step automated flow (ingest, parse, match, classify, auto-resolve), escalating only genuinely mismatched amounts for human review.

- Payment gateway reconciliation will use a periodic (monthly) file-based comparison against internal records rather than a per-transaction API call.

- Support, Payments & Reporting

Customer support/chat will be built natively into the TICVAI platform first (with a built-in AI assistant and a dedicated CR-representative role), while keeping client-specific integration adapters as a phase-two option for larger clients.

Full end-to-end payment gateway integration is required (not just the happy path), including payment-status inquiry APIs to recover incomplete or unconfirmed transactions, for both online and on-site payments.

Cash/shift (till) management will use a blind cash-out reconciliation model with supervisor authorization for shift closure, a configurable cash-drawer limit with mid-shift cash unloading, and automatic overage/shortage posting to a dedicated ledger account.

- Core financial reporting will include P&L, balance sheet, trial balance, cash flow, deferred revenue/site-wise analytics, and an exception-based financial approval/controls view.

- AI & Infrastructure

Qdrant is proposed as the vector database for the AI financial assistant (in place of native Postgres vector support), pending confirmation of UAE compliance requirements.

- TICVAI will provide a list of planned AWS/Azure infrastructure components to support Softlabs' discussion with the Dubai Compliance Authority on Friday.

- Process

Friday's session will begin 15 minutes early (10:45 AM) for a short infrastructure/compliance discussion, joined by TICVAI's infrastructure team (Dinesh Jadhav and Siddhesh), before the main workshop resumes at 11:00 AM covering F&B, retail, the licensing module, and shift management.

- Softlabs will compile the page-by-page design set with explanations into a single Word document for TICVAI's review.

This session covered a broad mix of operational and financial ground: POS session/role handling and the roaming "flying pause" model, the guest application's white-labeling and publishing approach, and an in-depth walkthrough of the finance and ledger architecture — including the dual-ledger data model, per-line VAT and tax-on-tax handling, revenue recognition, a six-step refund flow (extended to include bulk refunds), settlement/reconciliation, and end-to-end financial reporting. ## 2026-08-14

`sources/mom/TICVAI_MoM_2026-08-14.docx` · 2,385 words

### Minutes of Meeting

- TICVAI Kick-off Meeting — FnB, Wireframe Q&A & POS/Workstation Management

### Date

- 14 August 2026

### Project

- TICVAI

### Meeting Type

- Workshop — FnB Flow, Product Q&A, Design/Wireframe Walkthrough

### Prepared by

- Chitrangi Mestry

### Primary Objective

To resolve open functional and design questions raised by the Softlabs team across AI, finance, front-end (guest website/app), Food & Beverage, retail, POS/kiosk branding, queue management, and parking, and to walk through Allam's wireframes for workstation, till, and POS/device management dashboards, ahead of finalizing the discovery-phase deliverables.

### Participants

- TICVAI Team

- Softlabs Team

### Agenda

- AI configuration assistant — phase-one scope

- Finance — currency locking rules for refunds

- Guest website vs. guest mobile app — architecture and feature parity

- White-labeling and tenant branding/customization boundaries

- Movie ticketing as a supported product category

- Food & Beverage — ordering, delivery, and redemption flows

- Retail — cart, inventory, and cross-venue stock rules

- POS/Kiosk branding and UI ownership

- Queue management — live wait-time integration

- Parking — integration models with third-party systems

- Wireframe walkthrough — workstation/POS/till management dashboards

- Multi-tenant / multi-region database architecture and data residency

- Outstanding deliverables and next steps

### 1. AI Configuration Assistant — Phase-One Scope

Chinmay clarified that forecasting-type AI use cases (e.g., demand/revenue forecasting) require substantial historical data to train models and cannot be delivered in phase one, though the supporting front-end, back-end, and database components can be built. Qossai and Allam confirmed the priority AI use case for phase one is a configuration assistant that helps a system admin set up products, promotions, and similar configurations conversationally (e.g., prompting the admin on product type — admission, time slot, etc.) rather than data-dependent forecasting. Chinmay also flagged a feasible near-term AI use case: auto-generating a map/seating layout and associated ticket configuration once a venue uploads its map schema and layout image.

### 2. Finance — Currency Locking for Refunds

Chinmay raised the question of at which point (purchase, redemption, or expiry) a currency value should be locked for refund purposes. Allam clarified the platform's model: all transactions are stored and reconciled in the base/local currency configured for the system's region (e.g., UAE). Foreign-currency payments are converted and recorded at the local-currency equivalent at the time of transaction; change and refunds are always issued in the local currency, never in the foreign currency originally tendered. A separate foreign-currency transactions report will show cashier-level foreign-currency activity for reconciliation, but the underlying value is locked at purchase in the base currency regardless of subsequent exchange-rate movement.

### 3. Guest Website vs. Guest Mobile App

Pradnya asked whether each tenant needs its own guest website or shares a common one. Allam described two models: (a) a shared instance where small tenants operate under a subdomain/subpath of the TICVAI domain, and (b) a dedicated tenant model where larger clients get a fully dedicated URL on their own domain. On feature parity, both agreed the guest website and guest mobile app should share the same CMS/back-end publishing and the same branding, look, and feel, but functionality can differ: the mobile app carries full tenant/product/venue information end-to-end (since it's downloaded per tenant), while a client's own website typically only links out to a TICVAI-hosted checkout ('Buy Tickets') rather than being managed by TICVAI directly.

### 4. White-Labeling and Customization Boundaries

Qossai and Allam agreed the base structure (header, footer, layout) stays consistent across tenants, but branding elements — logo, color, font — and module-level visibility (e.g., hiding Dining or Retail if a client doesn't offer them) must be configurable per tenant, independently for web and mobile if needed.

### 5. Movie Ticketing

Pradnya asked whether movie tickets are in scope. Allam confirmed yes — a dedicated seat management module will support this, citing an existing client (a museum/science center in Kuwait with an in-house educational cinema) as a reference use case.

### 6. Food & Beverage — Ordering, Delivery, and Redemption

Ticket + combo meal: a single QR code encodes both the admission ticket and the meal entitlement; the guest scans once at entry and again at the F&B counter to redeem the meal, after which it cannot be redeemed again.

On-seat delivery: for seated events, a guest can choose pickup or delivery to their seat; for open/outdoor venues (e.g., a beach or water park), physical QR codes placed at each seat/location let the guest scan to specify exactly where food should be delivered.

Group bookings: the system supports either one shared QR code for the whole group (redeemed together at the counter) or individual QR codes per person (each guest can link their ticket to their own profile via the mobile app). For small groups (2–4 people), the cashier can assign specific meals per ticket at time of sale; for large groups this is impractical and it was agreed the group would instead redeem centrally at the counter.

Order-only-inside-the-park: guests already inside the venue should be able to order F&B directly from the mobile app without visiting the counter, choosing pickup or in-park delivery to a specified location.

Standalone F&B purchase without a ticket (i.e., entering just to buy food) was discussed as a rare edge case; the team agreed to exclude it from scope, as it falls under general food-delivery apps rather than TICVAI's use case.

### 7. Retail — Cart and Inventory

Ticketing, F&B, and retail will share a single cart/checkout and a single unified receipt and QR code per customer — no separate receipts or wristbands per product line.

Inventory will be centralized at the venue level across all sales channels (web, mobile, kiosk, POS). Stock is not shared across venues by default; an inter-venue stock transfer capability will allow moving stock between venues when needed, with the destination venue's system-recorded stock (not physical stock) gating what can be sold.

Add-on entitlements (e.g., adding a locker) can be linked to an existing ticket's QR code by scanning it, rather than issuing a new QR code.

### 8. POS / Kiosk Branding

Allam and Qossai confirmed that POS and tablet interfaces used by staff (cashiers) should always carry TICVAI branding, not client branding, with 'Powered by TICVAI' shown consistently across staff and guest-facing surfaces. Kiosks, however, are guest-facing (used directly by park visitors) and should therefore be white-labeled to the client's branding, similar to the guest website, while still following a kiosk-specific layout.

### 9. Queue Management

Chinmay asked how ride/attraction wait times would be sourced. Qossai explained that venues typically calculate wait time from entry-counting sensors or cameras (e.g., people entering × average time per person) and expose this via a live API; TICVAI would consume that wait-time API/data feed and surface it in the guest mobile app, potentially feeding an AI recommendation ('which ride to visit next') in future phases.

### 10. Parking Integrations

Chinmay and Qossai reviewed three parking integration models: (1) no integration — TICVAI issues its own QR code and on-site security manually verifies it; (2) ANPR/plate-number integration — the guest enters their plate number at checkout, and TICVAI's API pushes the plate number to the parking system's whitelist so the barrier opens automatically; (3) QR-code handoff — TICVAI sends a QR code to the parking system's barrier for entry validation. A separate, pay-per-hour parking model (unrelated to ticketing) can be handled independently via the parking system's own POS. Qossai noted the team has integrated with such parking APIs before (consuming and pushing data) and that the architecture should be built to make future parking-vendor integrations quick (targeted at a few days, not weeks).

### 11. Wireframe Walkthrough — Workstation, Till & POS Management

Workstation Overview Dashboard: shows all configured workstations for a venue (or across venues in a multi-venue setup), grouped by department/sub-department, with online/offline/health status and workstation type (mobile POS, kiosk, on-site POS).

New Workstation setup: captures workstation name, auto-generated ID, department, and mode; workstation detail view shows ID, department, IP address, configuration, linked devices, operator/shift activity, and sales totals.

- Hardware & Peripheral Management: configures devices per workstation (receipt printer, cash drawer, payment terminal, barcode/ticket scanner/printer) and shows device-level status.

Live Workstation Monitor: department-level health overview, with a proposed graphical park-map view showing workstation locations and live status — feasibility depends on clean input metadata (zones/regions) from the venue, or manual drag-and-drop placement as a fallback.

- Software Configuration: tracks software version and pending/completed updates per workstation.

Till / Cash Management: total cash and card transactions, variance tracking, till configuration, denomination setup (configurable per currency/region — e.g., UAE 2 decimals vs. Bahrain/Kuwait 3 decimals, with no rounding of the third decimal), opening float (by amount or by denomination), and cash-in/cash-out for mid-shift cash pickups.

Shift Management: shift assignment and scheduling by cashier/department, shift templates and policies, shift opening/closing, and exception/alert handling; Allam suggested exploring a merge of the shift-closing and till-closing screens to reduce dashboard count.

POS Profile & Layout Management: links each department to its workstation types and counts, and defines a distinct front-end product layout per workstation type (ticketing, F&B, retail, kiosk) via drag-and-drop product/category configuration, plus sales rules restricting which products a given workstation can sell (e.g., admission-only vs. membership-only).

- Offline Policies and a venue-level Operations Summary Dashboard were also shown, aggregating the department-level views into a single venue overview.

Allam and Qossai stressed the wireframes are reference-only (partly generated via ChatGPT prompting on functional requirements) and not to be replicated as-is; Chinmay's team has full discretion to consolidate dashboards and should cross-check the shared functionality matrix, since some matrix items are not yet reflected in the wireframes.

### 12. Multi-Tenant / Multi-Region Database Architecture

Chinmay raised a scenario around cross-region validity (e.g., a membership pass purchased in one region needing to work across other regions/countries, drawing an analogy to a globally valid F1 season pass). Allam explained that for a single client operating within one jurisdiction (e.g., Miral Experiences in the UAE), all venues/tenants share a single centralized database, distinguished by venue/site ID, even as new venues are added within that region. If a client's new venue falls under a different jurisdiction with data-residency requirements (e.g., a Qatar venue with local data-hosting law), a separate, isolated database would be created for that region, and cross-region-valid entitlements (e.g., a multi-region membership) would then need to be synced between the databases. For TICVAI's own shared multi-tenant infrastructure (used by smaller clients who don't want to bear dedicated infrastructure cost), all tenants can reside in one physical database for cost efficiency, but must be logically and securely isolated by venue/tenant ID so no tenant can see another's data or configuration. Clients wanting full isolation can pay for a dedicated database as a premium option. Dinesh confirmed the shared database must be built to scale to high-volume, short-duration events (e.g., 20,000–30,000 attendees/day) even for otherwise small tenants, and the team agreed cost/efficiency should guide the isolation boundary rather than segregating for its own sake.

### 13. Outstanding Deliverables and Next Steps

Aishwarya flagged that the POS/ticketing UI reference PDF (as distinct from the F&B POS PDF already shared) was missing from an earlier session. Allam and Qossai clarified no separate PDF was created for this — the team had instead pointed to a previously shared demo software link as the UI reference for ticketing POS design, since the earlier PDF referenced was based on an outdated UI. Chinmay confirmed he is building a hosted, interactive reference tool listing all pages, functionalities, contracts, and back-end schema/tables for Qossai's team to validate against, to be shared once hosted (targeted for next week).

### Decisions Made

- The phase-one AI scope will focus on a configuration assistant for admins (product/promotion setup guidance), not data-dependent forecasting models.

Refund and change amounts are always issued in the local/base currency, locked at the value recorded at time of purchase; foreign-currency activity is tracked via a separate reporting layer only.

Guest website and guest mobile app will share the same branding, look, and feel and be driven by a common CMS, but can differ in functionality — the mobile app carries full tenant detail, while client-owned websites link out to a TICVAI-hosted checkout.

Base UI structure (header, footer, layout) is fixed across tenants; branding (logo/color/font) and module visibility (e.g., hide Dining/Retail) are configurable per tenant, independently for web and mobile.

- Movie/cinema ticketing is in scope via the seat management module.

Ticketing, F&B, and retail share one cart, one receipt, and one unified QR code/wristband per customer; add-ons are linked to the existing entitlement rather than issued separately.

- Retail inventory is centralized per venue across all channels; cross-venue stock is not shared automatically and requires an inter-venue stock transfer.

- Staff-facing POS and tablet UIs are TICVAI-branded; guest-facing kiosks are white-labeled to client branding.

- Standalone F&B purchase without an admission ticket is excluded from scope as an edge case better served by third-party food-delivery apps.

Multi-tenant data isolation will be logical (shared database, isolated by venue/tenant ID) by default for cost efficiency, with dedicated, fully isolated databases offered as a paid option; jurisdiction-driven data-residency requirements will force a separate regional database with sync for cross-region entitlements.

### Action Items

- Action Item

- Status

- Update the shared functionality matrix (metrics) to add a column capturing the AI configuration-assistant requirement discussed today

- Chinmay Parab

- Pending

- Cross-check the workstation/POS wireframes against the functionality matrix and consolidate/redesign dashboards as needed

- Chinmay Parab / Softlabs Team

- In Progress

- Chinmay Parab

- In Progress

- Chinmay Parab

- Pending

- Schedule a short (10–15 min) dedicated session to review and close out the task tracker early next week

- Chinmay Parab / Allam

- Pending

- Confirm scheduling for Monday/Tuesday's workshop (Food & Beverage, Retail, and Procurement/Inventory topics)

- Chinmay Parab

- Pending

- Next Meeting

- Date: Monday or Tuesday (17–18 August 2026) — to be confirmed

- Time: To be confirmed

- Planned Topics

- Food & Beverage, Retail, and Procurement/Inventory workshop (topics to be finalized based on interdependencies)

- Tracker review and close-out session (10–15 minutes)

- Closing Remarks

This session resolved a broad set of open functional questions spanning AI scope, finance/currency handling, front-end architecture, white-labeling, Food & Beverage flows, retail/inventory, POS and kiosk branding, queue management, and parking integrations, and included a detailed walkthrough of Allam's workstation/POS/till management wireframes. Both teams also aligned on the multi-tenant, multi-region database strategy, balancing data isolation, compliance, and infrastructure cost. Next steps include updating the functionality matrix and task tracker, finalizing the Food & Beverage/Retail/Procurement workshop schedule, and a short tracker close-out session early next week.
