`sources/mom/MoM_FnB_Retail_Procurement_Inventory_18Aug2026.docx` · 1,934 words

### Minutes of Meeting

- Workshop – Food & Beverage, Retail, Procurement & Inventory — POS Backend Configuration, Table Management & Procurement Deep-Dive

### Date

- 18-August-2026

### Project

- TICVAI

### Meeting Type

- Technical Workshop — POS Backend, Inventory & Procurement

### Prepared by

- Chitrangi Mestry

### Primary Objective

Solution/Product team to walk the client through the proposed POS backend configuration for Food & Beverage outlets, table management, and the Inventory & Procurement module, for review, validation and alignment on outlet-level vs. venue-level configuration approach.

### Participants

- TICVAI Team

- Softlabs Team

### Agenda

- Walkthrough of the F&B POS backend configuration – outlets, menus, recipes, kitchen and table management

- Discussion on outlet-level vs. venue-level configuration and role-based access control

- Walkthrough of the F&B stock, inventory item master, warehouse structure and costing methods

- Walkthrough of supplier management and purchase order workflows

- Review of the project tracking platform and alignment on next steps

### 4. Detailed Discussion

- 4.1 F&B Command Center — Overview & Outlet Setup

Allam walked through the F&B Command Center, giving a real-time, consolidated view across all outlets – total sales, orders, average order value, average preparation time, kitchen load, top-selling items and operational alerts.

Outlets can be categorised into types (fine dining, quick service, coffee, etc.), each with configurable features – e.g., quick-service outlets do not require table booking, while fine-dining outlets need a table layout.

- Every outlet is linked to a main department (Food & Beverage) and sub-department (outlet name), along with cost centres and status.

- 4.2 Recipes, Operating Hours & Service Channels

- Recipe-based stock depletion can be configured at the outlet level, either in real time or at end-of-day, depending on outlet type.

- Operating hours and service periods (breakfast, lunch, dinner, late night) can be defined per outlet to analyse revenue by time slot.

- POS & device management allows configuration of receipt printers, kitchen printers and KDS devices per outlet/terminal.

- Service channel configuration allows enabling/disabling specific items per sales channel (POS, kiosk, QR ordering, online) per outlet.

- 4.3 Kitchen & Preparation Stations

- Kitchens can be divided into stations (grill, fryer, beverage, dessert, etc.), each mapped to specific printers or KDS devices.

Order routing and KDS printer rules determine where an item is printed/displayed, based on category or item, with a fallback station/device if the primary one is offline or faulty.

- F&B Controls allow global configuration of approval workflows (e.g., void approval, refund approval) based on amount thresholds and user privileges.

- 4.4 Menu, Product & Recipe Management

- The Menu & Product Command Center tracks menus, active recipes and products, and flags products without mapped recipes or with unavailable ingredients.

Menu Builder defines the front-end POS layout per outlet – categories, item tiles (image, name, price) and configurable button sizes for fast-selling items; agreed the current layout is a reference only and UI/UX can be improved.

- Product creation captures product name, auto-generated PLU code, category/sub-category, pricing type, inventory-tracking toggle, recipe linkage, unit of measurement and preparation time.

- Modifiers can be free or chargeable with minimum/maximum selection rules; combo meals support component selection with upgrade options and additional cost.

- Recipe & BOM management captures ingredient quantity, unit, cost (from purchase data), preparation time, yield, selling price and margin.

Ingredient substitution allows an alternate ingredient to be used automatically when the primary ingredient is out of stock, subject to availability. Production planning aggregates recipe requirements to forecast prepared-item quantities.

- 4.5 Outlet-Level vs. Venue-Level Configuration — Key Discussion

A detailed discussion took place on whether F&B configuration (menus, recipes, costing, inventory) should be managed at the venue level or the outlet level, particularly for outlets leased out to third-party operators.

Qossai noted that when a venue leases a restaurant to a third party, the operator typically manages its own costing, inventory and procurement, with the venue only taking a revenue share (~10%) – favouring outlet-level configuration for leased outlets.

- Chinmay Parab flagged that supporting both venue-level and outlet-level configuration would effectively require two variations of the application/data model, adding development complexity.

Decision: The team agreed to proceed with outlet-level configuration for F&B, applying the same segregation logic to Retail for consistency. Venue-owned, homogeneous outlets (e.g., popcorn/ice-cream booths) may still be set up centrally once and applied across outlets, but the underlying configuration model remains outlet-level.

- 4.6 Role-Based & Outlet-Level Access Control — Open Item

Allam raised the need to restrict a user's visibility/access to specific outlets (e.g., an F&B manager for one outlet should not see other outlets' items).

Chinmay Parab identified two possible approaches: (a) adding dedicated segregation tables, or (b) introducing a venue/outlet ID key into the existing schema. The first offers granularity but increases long-term maintenance; the second is simpler but needs validation.

- Action: Chinmay Parab to evaluate both approaches and confirm the most feasible and efficient option before the next workshop (also relevant for ticketing/event-specific access).

- 4.7 Kitchen Operations & Course-Wise Ordering

- The Kitchen Operations Command Center shows live order counts, items pending/firing and kitchen station status.

Course-wise ordering (mainly for fine dining) groups orders by course (starters, main course, dessert) so the kitchen fires each course at the right time, ensuring freshness.

A live “fired” timer on each kitchen ticket tracks elapsed time since the order was sent (not a countdown) and resets when a course within that ticket is completed/dished out. Not applicable to quick-service outlets, which print and prepare orders immediately.

- 4.8 Table Management (Fine Dining)

A visual floor/table map (main hall, terrace, VIP lounge, etc.) shows table status and allows tables to be tagged with a customer category (e.g., VIP) to help staff prioritise service.

Decision on table status flow: Available → Ordered → Table Closed (post payment) → Reserved (when booked in advance). A separate “Cleaning” status was discussed and deliberately excluded – agreed this is an operational task managed manually by staff and does not need a system status, avoiding unnecessary complexity.

Reservation module includes table selection (with system recommendations), customer details, guest count, location/outlet, and an optional deposit adjusted against the final bill; walk-in and waitlist management are also supported.

A per-table activity log (seated, drinks ordered, food ordered, sent to kitchen, course served, etc.) is available, along with actions like Add Guest, Change Server and Transfer Table.

- 4.9 Unified Customer Profile

Decision: A single, unified customer profile will be used across ticketing, F&B and retail to give a 360° view of guest activity and avoid duplicate records (a known issue in other systems where the same name is created multiple times with spelling variations). Example: a guest who buys tickets online and later dines at a restaurant will be matched by name/mobile number and associated with the same profile.

- 4.10 F&B Stock, Wastage & Requisitions

- The F&B Stock Command Center shows stock value, low-stock/critical/out-of-stock items and recipe-based ingredient consumption.

Production execution & batch management tracks planned vs. actual vs. yield quantity and batch losses; wastage/spoilage must be recorded per item to keep costing accurate.

- Requisitions allow an outlet to request replenishment stock from the central warehouse when running low.

The consolidated F&B Command Center rolls up sales, orders, food cost and gross margin across outlets, with breakdowns by sales channel and hour; dashboards will be role-based (e.g., F&B Director sees all outlets; outlet manager sees only their own).

- 4.11 Inventory & Procurement — Item Master, UOM & Costing

- The Inventory & Procurement module covers both F&B and Retail – total inventory value, item counts and out-of-stock items, broken down by department/sub-department.

Item Master captures category, item type, status and unit of measurement (UOM), which is essential for accurate recipe costing and handles pack-size conversions (e.g., 1 carton = 24 pieces; 1 case = 2 litres = 2000 ml).

Costing methods discussed: Weighted Average (costing averaged across received batches at different prices – most commonly used) and FIFO (earliest received batch consumed/costed first). The system should support both options.

Warehouse & location structure supports a customisable hierarchy (e.g., main warehouse → food warehouse → beverage warehouse), with flexibility to receive stock centrally or directly at an outlet/kitchen for fast-moving perishables.

- Expiry tracking must be maintained at batch/date level, and reorder & alert configuration will notify staff when stock reaches a minimum threshold.

- 4.12 Simplification Principle — Guiding Decision

Decision: While the reference material includes many granular statuses (put-away, picking, packing, dispatching, etc.), the team agreed NOT to implement every status. The goal is to keep day-to-day workflows simple and fast for end users, and this principle should guide UI/UX and workflow design across inventory and warehouse operations.

- 4.13 Supplier & Purchase Order Management

- Suppliers can be categorised (F&B, retail, engineering, etc.), with a Supplier Master capturing details, linked item categories, compliance documents and performance scorecards.

Purchase Request → Approval → Purchase Order is the standard flow when stock needs replenishment; Request for Quotation (RFQ) allows comparing prices from multiple suppliers before finalising an order.

Three purchase order types identified: Regular PO (standard item/quantity/price entry), Contract PO (pre-agreed fixed pricing for a defined period, auto-picked on subsequent orders), and Service PO (for non-inventory items/services such as equipment maintenance).

- Spend analysis provides visibility into category-wise, supplier-wise and contract-wise spend.

- 4.14 Project Tracking Platform (Development Readiness)

Chinmay Parab shared an overview of the internal tracking platform being built to manage development scope – organising work into “spines”, “satellites” and contracts, and mapping screens, user journeys, API calls and the database tables each API reads from/writes to.

The tool is intended to help both client and development team validate functionality screen-by-screen and journey-by-journey, and to make AI-assisted development more accurate by having the schema and API structure pre-defined.

Currently populated in depth for the POS/ticketing module; other modules (Retail, CRM, resource management, seat assignment, etc.) are pending and will be added progressively. The team acknowledged that full 1:1 alignment with the original plan is unrealistic (typically ~80–85% coverage), which is an acceptable working assumption.

### 5. Key Decisions & Agreements

- F&B (and, by extension, Retail) configuration will be managed at the outlet level rather than the venue level.

- Table status flow simplified to: Available → Ordered → Table Closed → Reserved (no separate “Cleaning” status).

- A single, unified customer profile will be maintained across ticketing, F&B and retail to avoid duplicate records.

- Inventory/warehouse workflows will be kept simple – not every granular status (put-away, pick, pack, dispatch, etc.) will be implemented in the system.

- System must support both Weighted Average and FIFO costing methods for inventory valuation.

- Three purchase order types – Regular, Contract, and Service – will be supported.

### 6. Open Items / Questions for Follow-Up

- Outlet-level user access restriction: which approach (segregation tables vs. venue/outlet ID key) is most feasible – Chinmay Parab to evaluate and confirm.

- Final confirmation on whether retail will fully mirror the outlet-level configuration decision made for F&B.

- Detailed design of role-based dashboards (F&B Director vs. outlet-level roles) to be finalised.

- Document explaining each F&B screen (today's and last Friday's session) – pending from Allam.

## 2026-08-19

`sources/mom/TICVAI_MoM_2026-08-19_FnB_Retail_Procurement_Inventory.docx` · 1,800 words

### Minutes of Meeting

- Workshop — Retail Operations, Database Architecture & Inventory Deep-Dive

### Date

- 19-August-2026

### Project

- TICVAI

### Meeting Type

- Technical Workshop — Retail POS, Database Architecture & Inventory

### Prepared by

- Chitrangi Mestry

### Primary Objective

Solution/Product team to walk the client through the proposed retail front-end and back-end configuration (dashboard, store setup, POS and device management, product catalog, pricing and promotions), the inventory and procurement processes shared with F&B, and to align on the database isolation strategy for the platform, for review, validation and alignment on the outlet-level configuration approach.

### Participants

- TICVAI Team

- Softlabs Team

### Agenda

- Walkthrough of the retail dashboard, store setup and POS/device configuration

- Walkthrough of the retail product catalog, pricing, bundles and promotions

- Discussion on database architecture and isolation strategy

- Walkthrough of inventory management — requisitions, transfers, stock counts and RFID-based counting

- Discussion on returns, refunds and online order fulfillment

- Review of retail intelligence and planning for remaining workshop topics

### 4. Detailed Discussion

- 4.1 Retail Command Center — Dashboard & Store Setup

Allam walked through the retail dashboard, giving a consolidated real-time view across all outlets — total retail sales, total and average transactions, store performance snapshot, system alerts and out-of-stock indicators, viewable by day, week or month.

Store setup follows the same department/venue/zone structure used in F&B, with department type set to "Retail" and the specific retail shop configured as a sub-department; unlike F&B, retail does not require sub-classifications (e.g., fine dining vs. QSR), since core operations are simplified to scan-and-sell.

- Confirmed: inventory continues to be managed at the outlet level (Chinmay).

- In addition to scan-and-sell, a retail item purchased with a ticket (e.g., a souvenir bundle) can be redeemed on-site via QR code scan.

Operating hours, sales periods, and POS/device assignment (workstation name/code, receipt printer, barcode scanner, cash drawer) were reviewed, along with sales channel configuration, primary/replenishment store settings, and global retail settings including offline sales support.

- 4.2 Product Catalog, Variant & Pricing Management

- The Retail Product & Catalog Command Center tracks total products per store, product classification into catalogs, top products sold, and product-by-category breakdowns.

The product master captures price, stock and variant attributes (e.g., size/color) with a distinct barcode per variant; stock is tracked at the individual variant/size level.

- Decision: size/variant attributes (e.g., small/medium/large) will be configurable in the admin panel per product type, and reflected dynamically when products are added.

- Category, Brand & Hierarchy supports multi-level categorization (e.g., Apparel > Retail > Apparel > T-Shirt) with subcategories.

Catalog Builder & Store Assortment allows mapping which products are sold on which channel (on-site, online, or restricted), managed at the catalog level rather than per individual product.

Price Book supports date-based pricing (e.g., regular pricing this month, promotional pricing next month) and dynamic discount types such as "buy 2 get 1 free" or "lowest-priced item discounted" — full functional detail is captured in the requirements matrix.

- 4.3 Pricing, Bundles & Promotions

Bundling: multiple retail items (e.g., a t-shirt plus a cap) can be combined into a combo package with bundle-level pricing, configurable for both on-site and online presentation with product images and descriptions.

Promotion Builder supports rules such as "buy X get Y" and "buy 3, lowest-priced item discounted" (fully or partially), fully driven by configurable promotion rules.

- Omni-channel fulfillment: buy-online-pickup-in-store and buy-online-ship-to-address were reviewed. Shipping fees can be configured by region/city (e.g., Dubai, Abu Dhabi, international).

Decision: shipping/courier rates and margins will be captured and configured manually by the operations team (who negotiate their own courier agreements), rather than through a live courier-API integration at this stage.

- 4.4 Database Architecture & Isolation Strategy — Key Discussion

Chinmay raised the question of how the database should be structured to prevent a failure in one module (e.g., POS or F&B) from affecting others (e.g., retail or the guest-facing website).

Allam's proposed approach, based on prior TICVAI discussions: a single centralized database shared across all sales channels and modules, so that if one point-of-sale terminal goes down, only that terminal is affected, not the entire database. During a full outage, only capacity-based (dated/timed) products would be blocked from sale; non-capacity products could still sell and sync later.

Chinmay clarified he is not proposing multiple physical servers, but isolating multiple databases (e.g., one per module: ticketing, F&B, retail) within a single MySQL instance, primarily for read/write performance segregation.

Allam, drawing on prior project experience, suggested a simpler two-database model instead: one primary database for all transactional/configuration/log data, and one read-only replica used exclusively for reporting/BI, so heavy reporting queries do not impact live transactional performance.

Offline behavior per module/device was also flagged — each edge device may need its own local database (e.g., SQLite) for offline mode. Chinmay noted Siddhesh's input would be valuable and suggested this could warrant its own dedicated workshop.

- Action: Chinmay/Softlabs to prepare a pros-and-cons comparison of the single-DB vs. multiple-DB approaches (performance, reporting, offline sync) for further discussion.

- 4.5 Inventory Management — Requisitions, Transfers & Stock Counts

- Store Stock & Availability: search by product to view stock-on-hand vs. available stock, factoring in pending online purchases awaiting pickup/shipment.

- Inter-store Requisition: outlets can raise a requisition to replenish stock, subject to an approval workflow before transfer.

- Store-to-Store Transfer: stock can be transferred between any two stores (outlet-to-outlet, warehouse-to-outlet, or outlet-to-warehouse).

- Receiving, stock count (monthly/weekly/as needed) and damage/loss adjustments are supported, with a fully configurable, user-defined reason list extendable in the backend without additional development.

Decision: stock can be reserved/held (e.g., for a VIP customer) and allocated per sales channel (e.g., 50 units online, 50 on-site), sold independently against each channel's allocation.

- 4.6 RFID/Barcode-Based Bulk Stock Counting — Open Item

Allam raised a client requirement to support bulk stock-taking using handheld RFID scanners, where scanning a batch of RFID-tagged items (rather than counting one by one) automatically updates system quantities once verified and saved.

Qossai referenced a similar prior installation at the Dubai Mall Art Museum (bulk reader/curtain-style capture) and noted more advanced dual-antenna gate readers exist for high-volume counting (e.g., trolley-based bulk scans).

Chinmay clarified his primary interest is in the data the RFID system produces (for reconciliation between the existing database state and newly scanned data), rather than the underlying scanning mechanism.

- Action: Allam/Qossai to share RFID reader/device specifications and reference data.

- 4.7 Returns, Refunds & Exchanges — In-Store and Online

In-park returns are managed operationally: return policy (e.g., allowed within 1 or 7 business days) is communicated on the receipt; customers typically contact the call center first, and the park directs them to a service counter. Returns outside stated policy are generally accepted only for damaged items or valid exceptions.

Online/app purchases follow a standard e-commerce return flow: the customer submits a return request with a reason (and photo, if applicable); the request goes to an approval team; once approved, a courier is arranged for pickup; upon verified receipt, the refund is processed.

- Confirmed: an item purchased via POS can also be returned through the web portal, subject to approval.

Automated courier integration (auto-generating pickup requests, shipping labels and instructions without manual operations involvement) was flagged as a future integration item, dependent on the specific client–courier agreement; the front end can be built to support this, with courier-specific API integration handled separately per partner.

- 4.8 Online Order Fulfilment & Shipping Configuration

Shipping fee configuration by destination region/city (including international shipping), with the operations team manually setting and maintaining courier rates and margins in the system rather than through a live courier-API integration.

- Once a delivery address is entered, the applicable fee is shown automatically for the customer to accept before payment.

- 4.9 Retail Intelligence & Reporting

Sales and outlet performance, top-performing stores, demand forecasting (based on both retail sales history and online ticket booking trends), and target-vs-actual performance tracking (e.g., monthly sales target vs. achieved sales, with variance reporting) at the outlet level.

- 4.10 Workshop Planning & Remaining Scope

- The CRM module (~12 screens) will require a dedicated session, tentatively the next day, pending final timing confirmation.

- Remaining uncovered topics identified by Qossai: resource management, access control, promotions & bundles, wallets, membership, virtual queue and dynamic pricing.

Qossai explained dynamic pricing has two components: (1) rule-based pricing tied to time and venue capacity (e.g., +20% once capacity reaches 70%, with early-booking discounts), and (2) factor-based dynamic pricing driven by external conditions such as weather, which would rely on AI/data inputs.

- Decision: proceed with the rules-based dynamic pricing component near-term; the AI/factor-based component depends on forecasting mechanisms to be scoped separately.

Qossai estimated more than 50% of overall requirement items are now covered and proposed 1–2 hours per day to complete the remainder within the next two weeks.

### 5. Key Decisions & Agreements

- Inventory is managed at the outlet level for retail, consistent with the F&B approach.

- Size/variant attributes (e.g., small/medium/large) will be configurable per product type in the admin panel.

- Stock can be reserved/held and allocated independently per sales channel (e.g., online vs. on-site).

- Shipping/courier rates will be manually configured by operations by region/city, rather than via live courier-API integration at this stage.

- An item purchased via POS can be returned through the web portal, subject to approval.

- Dynamic pricing will proceed in two phases: rules-based (time/capacity) first, factor-based (weather/AI-driven) later.

### 6. Open Items / Questions for Follow-Up

- Database isolation strategy — single shared DB vs. multiple DBs per module within one server instance — pending Chinmay's pros-and-cons analysis.

- Offline database behavior per module/edge device — to be scoped, potentially in a dedicated workshop with Siddhesh.

`sources/mom/TICVAI_MoM_2026-08-20_CRM_Marketing_CMS.docx` · 1,863 words

### Minutes of Meeting

- Workshop — CRM, Marketing Automation, Loyalty & CMS / White-Label Configuration

### Date

- 20-August-2026

### Project

- TICVAI

### Meeting Type

- Functional Workshop — CRM, Marketing Automation & CMS

### Prepared by

- Chitrangi Mestry

Note: This recording is filed under “F&B, Retail, Procurement & Inventory,” but the session actually covered CRM, marketing automation, loyalty/wallet, RBAC and CMS/white-label configuration — no F&B, retail, procurement or inventory content was discussed. This MoM reflects the content actually covered; the F&B/Retail/Procurement/Inventory workshop remains outstanding (see Open Items).

### Primary Objective

Solution/Product team to continue the functional walkthrough of the TICVAI reference platform — covering CRM and customer profile management, identity resolution and duplicate handling, consent and data privacy, audience segmentation, loyalty/membership/wallet mechanics, marketing automation, role-based access control, AI chat/case management, and CMS/white-label website and mobile app configuration — for review, validation and alignment on functional scope and simplification opportunities.

### Participants

- TICVAI Team

- Softlabs Team

### Agenda

- Walkthrough of CRM — customer profiles, unique/mandatory fields, family & guardian linking

- Duplicate profile detection, identity resolution and merge rules

- Consent policy, data privacy and retention/archival

- Audience segmentation, behavioural analytics and data migration

- Loyalty, membership tiers and wallet functionality

- Marketing automation — campaigns, offers and the Visual Journey Builder

- Role-based access control (RBAC) for CRM and configuration modules

- AI chat box, routing/queue management and case management

- Surveys and gamification

- CMS and white-label website / mobile app configuration, with reference-site walkthroughs

### 4. Detailed Discussion

- 4.1 CRM — Customer Profiles, Unique Fields & Family/Guardian Linking

Allam walked through the reference CRM's guest dashboard (active/inactive/duplicate profile counts, lifetime value), guest directory/search, and customer segmentation by source (individual, corporate, group, travel agent, OTA).

Profile fields must be fully configurable/user-defined (e.g., nationality vs. country of residence), with per-field unique and required flags; group profiles (group name, description, contact person) mirror individual fields but are independently configurable.

Decision: at least one of e-mail address or mobile number will be enforced as mandatory (not both), since some customers decline to share e-mail; the system supports conditional “either/or” mandatory-field rules.

Family/guardian linking confirmed as a core requirement (e.g., father, spouse, daughter linked as one family unit), consistent with family-ticket and family-membership configurations; Chinmay confirmed the same linking model should extend to operations-team entitlement relationships.

Wallet balances are shared across a linked family — a parent's top-up can be drawn down by a linked child's wristband without a separate top-up.

- Corporate/B2B profiles support a self-service onboarding flow: company profile creation (name, address, trade licence, VAT certificate), admin approval/rejection, rate/product setup, and credential issuance.

- 4.2 Duplicate Detection, Identity Resolution & Merge Rules

Guest checkout creates a new profile on every purchase unless matched to an existing one. Matching rules (fuzzy name similarity, exact mobile match, exact e-mail match) flag likely duplicates for merge, as demonstrated on the sample “duplicate review and merge” screen (500 profiles, ~100 matched by mobile number).

Extended discussion (Qossai, Chinmay) covered edge cases: two accounts with different e-mails but matching name/mobile; a customer intentionally maintaining separate accounts (e.g., personal vs. corporate); and which e-mail becomes the login of record after a merge.

Decision: profiles cannot be merged automatically without customer consent. The system will identify likely-duplicate profiles algorithmically and notify the customer (push notification or e-mail); the merge proceeds only on customer confirmation. An admin-side review queue will also track flagged duplicates independent of customer response.

- 4.3 Consent, Data Privacy & Retention

- Consent policy configuration governs marketing/newsletter/survey communications; customers who do not opt in must not receive promotional communications.

- A data-subject-request module manages privacy inquiries (access, correction, deletion) with status tracking (submitted → in progress → completed).

Decision: data retention/archival periods (e.g., 3–5 years of “live” data before archival) will be configurable per tenant/venue at setup time, with a system default that administrators can override.

- 4.4 Audience Segmentation, Behavioural Analytics & Data Migration

- A dynamic segment builder supports rule-based segments (e.g., purchase value bands, product-specific purchases, recency of purchase) for sales/marketing reporting.

- Static list import (CSV/Excel) supports migrating historical customer/segment data during onboarding.

- Action: hold a dedicated data-migration workshop to define import formats and validation rules.

Google Analytics will be integrated to capture full on-site behavioural tracking (browsing, cart abandonment, checkout drop-off) natively into the platform's own reporting, feeding behavioural segments (cart-abandon, app session, campaign-open, survey-completed, etc.) directly into marketing automation.

- 4.5 Loyalty, Membership & Wallet

Loyalty rules support point accrual by product/spend tier (e.g., bronze/silver/gold thresholds with corresponding point values) and tier-based benefit unlocks (e.g., platinum-tier discounts on F&B and ticketing).

- Loyalty and wallet are both modelled as customer-linked entities, consistent with the family-wallet-sharing behaviour in 4.1.

- Action: hold a dedicated follow-up session to define the full loyalty programme configuration (tiers, point rules, redemption, expiry) — today's material was high-level only.

- 4.6 Marketing Automation — Campaigns, Offers & Visual Journey Builder

- Campaign tracking covers click-through, conversion and revenue attribution per campaign, with configurable success criteria (e.g., 80% conversion target).

The Visual Journey Builder triggers automated, rule-based touchpoints (e.g., abandoned-cart recovery) based on configurable wait periods (same-day, one week, one month), audience segment, and optional incentive (e.g., coupon code).

Chinmay raised implementation questions on how journey “offer” blocks would be parameterised in the builder UI; Allam clarified offers/discounts are pre-configured in a separate Offers module (coupon code, dynamic discount, or auto-discount URL) and only referenced — not freely defined — within the journey builder.

Decision: offer blocks in the Visual Journey Builder will pull only from pre-configured, system-validated offers (product/ticket-type scoped); ad-hoc discount values cannot be entered directly in the builder.

Cart-abandonment triggers support minimum cart-value and product-type filters (e.g., trigger only for membership-ticket abandonment, not general admission). Additional journeys reviewed: birthday rewards, anniversary reminders, cross-sell/upsell, and reservation/survey requests — all gated by customer consent.

- 4.7 Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)

Chinmay proposed a three-tier permission model per module: edit & view, view-only, and hidden (no access) — e.g., a marketing officer should not see the Finance module at all, while a “CRM Officer” vs. “CRM Admin” distinction determines visibility of configuration screens within an accessible module.

Decision: RBAC will be configured per role, per module, with three access levels (edit/view, view-only, hidden), and further sub-permissions within a module (e.g., a CRM role could access Campaigns and Communications but not Journeys). Default role templates will be provided, customisable by admins.

- 4.8 AI Chat Box, Routing/Queue & Case Management

The AI chat box responds to guided/predefined queries (booking status, rescheduling) and logs guest-conversation history across channels (WhatsApp, web, Instagram, Facebook) with per-channel conversion attribution.

Chinmay confirmed the routing/queue configuration (reservation, general, membership & billing, technical support queues with priority and SLA policy) applies specifically to AI-agent conversation routing based on detected query intent.

- Decision: conversation retention for chat/case history will be configurable (e.g., default of one month, extendable), consistent with the broader data-retention approach.

- Case management supports logging from both the customer-facing app/website and the call-centre/admin side, with category, priority, channel, and SLA-based escalation rules.

- 4.9 Surveys & Gamification

- Surveys can be triggered at multiple points (post-purchase, post-visit, post-ticket-scan, membership renewal, case closure), fully configurable by business rule.

- Gamification includes badges/status tiers (e.g., Explorer, Adventurer, Legend) driven by spend or engagement thresholds, feeding into the loyalty tier structure in 4.5.

- 4.10 CMS & White-Label Website / Mobile App Configuration

The CMS supports multi-site/multi-venue management (branding, colour palette incl. custom hex codes, fonts, Google Analytics site IDs, production/staging environments) and a drag-and-drop page builder; page layout is standardised (header, footer, hero/card components) but adapts contextually to product type (seat map for seated products, standard flow for general admission).

Chinmay requested documentation of reusable page components per venue type (e.g., seat-map component for stadiums/amphitheatres, park-map component for attraction-style venues) so the same layout can be reused across venues with only imagery/data swapped.

Action: finalise the component-count logic for the experiences/dining section on the guest-app landing page (fixed 2–3-card layout vs. a scalable N-count layout) and confirm with Allam's team.

Allam distinguished the main venue website (fully managed by the venue/client) from the white-labelled B2C purchase flow that TICVAI powers once a guest clicks “Book Now” — the white-label flow retains the venue's header/footer branding but product-selection, cart and checkout screens are TICVAI-managed; header/footer links to non-checkout pages redirect back to the main venue site.

Two reference sites were walked through end-to-end to illustrate target checkout simplicity: a Six Flags–style attraction site (product selection → quantity/name capture → cart summary → login/guest checkout with dual OTP validation) and Platinum List (event → date → interactive seat map with colour-coded pricing → seat selection → one-page checkout via Quick Order/Apple/Google, completing in as few as four clicks, with an optional post-purchase profile-completion prompt).

Decision: the TICVAI B2C checkout journey should target a minimal, low-friction flow (in the range of 3–4 steps) modelled on the PlatinumList example, deferring full profile capture to an optional post-purchase step rather than gating checkout on it.

### 5. Key Decisions & Agreements

- At least one of e-mail or mobile number is mandatory at profile creation; both cannot be optional simultaneously.

- Profile merges require customer confirmation; algorithmic matches are notified to the customer, with an admin review queue in parallel.

- Data and conversation retention periods will be configurable per tenant/venue, with system defaults.

- Visual Journey Builder offer blocks reference pre-configured, system-validated offers only — no freeform discount entry.

- RBAC follows a three-tier model (edit/view, view-only, hidden) configured per role and per module, with default role templates.

- The B2C checkout journey targets a minimal 3–4 step flow, modelled on the Platinum List reference, with profile completion deferred to post-purchase.

### 6. Open Items / Questions for Follow-Up

- Data migration formats and validation rules for customer/segment import — pending dedicated workshop.

`sources/mom/TICVAI_MoM_2026-08-21_Seat_Management_CMS.docx` · 1,848 words

### Minutes of Meeting

- Workshop — Seat Management & B2C Checkout / CMS Configuration

### Date

- 21-August-2026

### Project

- TICVAI

### Meeting Type

- Functional Workshop — Seat Management, CMS & B2C Checkout

### Prepared by

- Chitrangi Mestry

### Primary Objective

Solution/Product team to walk through the reference seat management and venue map configuration capabilities (manual seat map builder, AI-assisted import, layouts/templates, inventory status, seating rules) and the CMS/B2C checkout journey, using the Platinum List, Coca-Cola Arena and Six Flags Kidiya reference sites, so that Chinmay's team can assess functionality and align on a simplified, low-friction configuration and checkout design for TICVAI.

### Participants

- TICVAI Team

- Softlabs Team

### Agenda

- Reference walkthrough — Platinum List seat selection & checkout journey

- Seat map builder — section types (seated, non-seated/zone, standing, suite)

- Best-seat logic, seating rules and social distancing configuration

- AI-assisted seat map import and layout/template management

- Multi-performance assignment, temporary blocking and tiered/early-bird release

- Seat inventory status, holds and automatic release

- Deferred seat assignment model and ticket delivery / turnstile integration

- B2C checkout journey review — Six Flags Kidiya reference walkthrough

- Website builder flexibility — standalone vs. B2C-only configuration

### 4. Detailed Discussion

- 4.1 Reference Walkthrough — Platinum List Seat Selection & Checkout Journey

Allam walked through the Platinum List reference site end-to-end using a sample event (Luma Show Circus, Dubai): event page (short video + image + description) → select tickets → calendar (collapsed to a week view, expandable to full month) → time-slot selection → interactive, colour-coded seat map (price tiers shown by colour) → seat selection with live cart hold and countdown timer → checkout via Quick Order / Apple ID / Google ID.

A second reference (Coca-Cola Arena / Richard Maxart event) showed a capacity-based “best available” flow: the customer selects a section and quantity only — no seat-level selection — and exact seats are assigned internally, with the seat-level ticket/QR code released closer to the event date.

Decision: the reference model confirms three seat-selection scenarios the platform must support: (1) unnumbered/zone-based capacity selling with no seat numbers, (2) system-assigned “best available” seat allocation with deferred disclosure, and (3) full customer seat selection — selectable per section, per event.

- 4.2 Seat Map Builder — Section Types (Seated, Non-Seated/Zone, Standing, Suite)

Qossai added that non-seated/zone configurations (e.g., the Bahrain Dana Theatre and Dubai Racing Club projects) are priced and sold by zone/capacity rather than individual seat number — customers are told their zone but not an exact seat.

Allam confirmed a single seat map can mix section types — e.g., 8 of 10 sections seated and 2 standing/non-seated (common for concert “fan pit” areas close to the stage) — and that suites can be sold either as a private bulk-priced suite or as individual seats within the suite.

Decision: section type (seated / non-seated-zone / standing / suite) will be a configurable attribute set at the section level within a single seat map builder screen, rather than requiring separate configuration screens per type as shown in the reference tool.

Action: Chinmay's team to confirm how the seat map builder will consolidate the reference tool's multiple configuration screens (canvas, standing zone, suite, best-seats, entrance/exits) into one unified screen.

- 4.3 Best-Seat Logic, Seating Rules & Social Distancing Configuration

Best-seat ranking (e.g., last-row-is-best vs. first-row-is-best, depending on venue sightlines) must be configurable per seat map/event so the system can recommend or auto-assign the best available seat correctly for that venue.

Chinmay confirmed reservation/holds should be section-wise (choose section → choose/hold seats within it) rather than a freeform polygon selection as shown in the AI-generated reference mockup.

Seating rules were discussed in depth: consecutive-seat enforcement (preventing a customer from leaving a single empty seat between bookings) and an optional social-distancing rule (auto-blocking adjacent seats after a booking) were both cited as configurations the platform previously supported and should retain.

Decision: seating rules (consecutive-seat enforcement, social-distancing buffer, seat-kill rule, company/held-seat rule) will be configurable per venue/event, defaulting to the venue's operational policy rather than a single fixed platform-wide rule.

- 4.4 AI-Assisted Seat Map Import & Layout/Template Management

In addition to manual drag-and-drop seat map building, an AI-assisted import path was reviewed: uploading a PDF or image of a venue layout lets the AI recognise sections, and a companion Excel/CSV file supplies row/seat naming conventions — together the AI generates a draft seat map for validation before publishing.

Saved seat maps can be reused, copied, or partially copied (a single section's layout and seating can be copied into another seat map) to avoid rebuilding from scratch for similar venues/events. A template library and a layout comparison tool (to diff seat counts/configuration between two saved layouts) were also reviewed.

Decision: the platform will support both manual seat map building and AI-assisted import (PDF/image + Excel/CSV), plus full and partial (section-level) copy-paste between seat maps, and a layout version-comparison view showing seat-count/configuration differences.

- 4.5 Multi-Performance Assignment, Temporary Blocking & Tiered/Early-Bird Release

A seat map is configured independently and then associated with one or more events/performances on a separate event-configuration screen, linking seat map, pricing, and event/performance date-time.

Temporary seat blocking (holding seats off public sale, e.g., for VIP or maintenance reasons) and scheduled seat release (releasing held sections at a later time, e.g., once early sales pick up) were reviewed, along with a tiered/early-bird release pattern (e.g., releasing only 30–40 of 100 seats in a section at a discounted early-bird price, then releasing further tranches progressively).

Decision: the platform must support partial/tranche-based inventory release per section (temporary blocking, scheduled release, and tiered/early-bird sale volumes) rather than exposing full section inventory at go-live.

- 4.6 Seat Inventory Status, Holds & Automatic Release

A real-time seat inventory view was reviewed, showing per-event seat status (available, on hold, reserved, sold) along with availability/holder trackers, sales & allocation tracking, and audit/reconciliation reporting.

Decision: seats placed on hold (added to cart) must auto-release after a configurable timeout if checkout is abandoned, and must also auto-release immediately if a payment attempt fails, so inventory is not held indefinitely against an incomplete transaction.

- 4.7 Deferred Seat Assignment Model & Ticket Delivery / Turnstile Integration

Chinmay raised how ticket/QR generation would integrate with TICVAI's own turnstile system when a venue uses the deferred (“best available”) assignment model — i.e., how seats get finalised and QR codes issued if the customer isn't shown a seat number at purchase time.

Allam clarified the operational pattern: the sale is confirmed immediately (section + quantity), but exact seats are assigned internally; closer to the event, the operations/admin team triggers a bulk e-mail to all confirmed bookings for that event, at which point customers receive their QR-coded tickets with final seat assignments — giving the venue flexibility to rearrange seating right up to that point.

Decision: the platform will support a deferred seat-assignment workflow: confirmed section/quantity sale at purchase, internal seat allocation held until an admin-triggered bulk release (e-mail + QR ticket issuance) ahead of the event, in addition to immediate seat assignment for venues that require it.

- 4.8 B2C Checkout Journey Review — Six Flags Kidiya Reference Walkthrough

The team (Qossai screen-sharing) walked through the Six Flags Kidiya B2C site: fixed header with configurable navigation (logo, Explore/Tickets/Passes, sub-menus — all toggleable via CMS), a clear four-step journey indicator (Ticket Selection → Add-ons → My Cart → Checkout), in-page ticket browsing (no multi-page navigation to view ticket types), short descriptions with an expandable “view more details” control, and configurable hero image/video per product.

For season-pass/family-type products, the flow requires first and last name capture per individual pass holder (not just the purchaser), reviewed via the “add guest name” step. “View all ticket types” expands additional categories in place, and a family-pass example showed a dynamic-pricing calendar applied at the ticket-type level.

Decision: the TICVAI B2C checkout should mirror this pattern: a visible step indicator, in-page (not multi-page) ticket-type browsing and expansion, an optional/removable add-ons step (skippable in configuration for products with no add-ons, collapsing the flow to Ticket Selection → Cart → Checkout), and per-person name capture for family/season-pass products.

Action: Chinmay's team to refine the guest-app/B2C flow already in progress based on today's Kidiya walkthrough feedback and share the updated flow back with Allam's team.

- 4.9 Website Builder Flexibility — Standalone vs. B2C-Only Configuration

Qossai raised that the website builder needs to support two distinct client scenarios: (1) clients with no existing website, who need a full landing page plus integrated ticket-sale flow built by TICVAI, and (2) clients with an existing main website, who only need the B2C purchase flow (header, product cards, footer, checkout) embedded or linked from their existing site.

- Decision: the CMS/website builder will support both a full landing-page-plus-checkout mode and a B2C-only embedded mode, configurable per client, using the same underlying builder.

### 5. Key Decisions & Agreements

The seat map builder must support three seat-selection models (zone/capacity-only, system-assigned best-available, full customer selection) and mixed section types (seated, non-seated, standing, suite) within a single unified configuration screen.

- Best-seat ranking logic and seating rules (consecutive-seat, social distancing) are configurable per venue/event, not fixed platform-wide.

- AI-assisted seat map import (PDF/image + Excel/CSV) will be supported alongside manual building, with full and section-level copy-paste and layout version comparison.

- Inventory release will support temporary blocking, scheduled release, and tiered/early-bird tranches rather than exposing full section capacity immediately.

- Held/cart seats auto-release on checkout timeout or payment failure.

- A deferred seat-assignment workflow (confirm sale → admin-triggered bulk QR release closer to the event) will be supported alongside immediate seat assignment.

- The B2C checkout will use a visible step indicator, in-page ticket browsing, an optional/removable add-ons step, and per-person name capture for family/season-pass products.

- The website/CMS builder will support both a full landing-page-plus-checkout mode and a B2C-only embedded mode, per client.

### 6. Open Items / Questions for Follow-Up

- Technical approach for seat map copy/paste (map-to-map and section-to-section) and layout version comparison — pending confirmation from Chinmay's team.

- Guest-app/B2C flow refinement based on today's Kidiya walkthrough feedback — in progress.

- Dinesh's service specification & deployment discussion — write-up of questions pending; to be shared ahead of Monday's call.

`sources/mom/TICVAI_MoM_2026-08-24_Infra_Cost_Ticketing.docx` · 1,573 words

### Minutes of Meeting

- Workshop — Infrastructure Costing, Cloud Architecture & Database Strategy Discussion; Ticketing Configuration Walkthrough

### Date

- 24-August-2026

### Project

- TICVAI

### Meeting Type

- Technical Workshop — Infrastructure Costing, Cloud Architecture & Database Strategy; Ticketing Configuration Walkthrough

### Prepared by

- Chitrangi Mestry

### Primary Objective

To resolve the client's open questions on cloud infrastructure sizing, costing and scaling strategy, and to align on the database architecture approach (centralized vs. tenant-owned, and per-module segregation) ahead of Softlabs finalizing the platform's technical architecture; and, following that discussion, to walk the client through the proposed ticket type configuration (open-dated, group/family, membership, event, gift voucher and money card tickets) and the event/ticketing setup flow for review.

### Participants

- TICVAI Team

- Softlabs Team

### Agenda

- Client Q&A on cloud infrastructure sizing, costing models and scaling strategy (AWS/Azure)

- Discussion on database architecture — centralized/shared platform vs. independent tenant-owned deployments

- High availability, disaster recovery and environment strategy (dev/QA/pre-prod/prod)

- Security, penetration testing and multi-tenancy isolation considerations

- Walkthrough of ticket type configuration (open-dated, group/family, membership, event, gift voucher, money card)

- Walkthrough of event setup, seating, resource management and ticket variants

- Planning for remaining workshop sessions

### 4. Detailed Discussion

- 4.1 Infrastructure Costing & Cloud Architecture Approach

Qossai and Allam requested clarity on infrastructure costing, since the team is finalizing decisions on architecture and components, and asked for a transparent cost model at different scale levels, covering both AWS and Azure.

Dinesh explained the architecture is being planned on a microservices basis, with each service (ticketing, order, F&B, etc.) potentially isolated at the database level, and outlined the cost/scale trade-off between a fully centralized database versus per-service databases.

Requested: the client asked Softlabs to document three illustrative deployment scenarios — (a) independent tenant deployment, (b) centralized/shared platform for small-to-medium tenants, and (c) dedicated infrastructure for large/mega events and flash sales — each with an architecture diagram, auto-scaling behavior and failure-handling response.

- 4.2 Database Architecture — Centralized vs. Tenant-Owned

Two hosting models were distinguished: (1) a TICVAI-hosted/managed database for small-to-medium tenants and short-duration event clients, and (2) tenant/client-owned infrastructure for large enterprise clients — Qossai estimated ~90% of large clients will host their own database/infrastructure, for whom Softlabs will only need to provide minimum specification requirements.

Near-term expectation: roughly 100–200 tenants on the centralized platform, alongside independently-deployed large-tenant environments and short-duration, high-concurrency dedicated event environments (e.g., a single high-demand ticket sale reaching tens of thousands of concurrent users within a few hours).

- Chinmay raised whether database segregation per microservice should be done from day one or retrofitted later.

Decision: Dinesh recommended segregating databases from the start, since splitting a centralized database after 2–3 years in production is significantly more difficult than starting isolated and reconciling/merging later if needed.

Confirmed: multiple databases can run on a single database server instance (e.g., separate DB instances within one SQL Server/Postgres/AWS RDS instance) — this does not require separate physical servers.

- Confirmed: analytical/reporting queries will run against a separate replica database rather than the main transactional database, to avoid impacting live transaction performance.

- 4.3 Scaling, High Availability & Multi-Tenancy Isolation

Decision: high availability does not require multi-region setup — same-region/same-zone HA is sufficient. Multi-region is reserved for disaster recovery (DR), which will be offered as an optional, client-dependent add-on rather than a default.

Decision: HA will be applied selectively to revenue-critical, customer-facing components (ticketing, POS, B2C front end) rather than uniformly across all modules — e.g., the finance module does not require HA.

Key requirement (Allam): on the centralized/shared platform, one tenant's traffic spike (e.g., an unexpected event surge) must not degrade or crash the platform for other tenants sharing the same infrastructure.

Infrastructure is expected to start minimal (sized for the first ~5 clients) and auto-scale progressively as tenant count grows — not pre-provisioned for a large future scale from day one. Continuous monitoring with scale-up triggers (e.g., around 70% utilization) was agreed as the operating approach, with a possible “reserve instance” strategy floated by Dinesh for isolating a spiking tenant temporarily.

Qossai noted that once the platform matures, the client (TICVAI) will bring on a dedicated infrastructure engineer to manage servers and scaling on an ongoing basis, working alongside Softlabs.

- 4.4 Security & Environment Strategy

- Standard security best practices and a web application firewall will be implemented on the infrastructure from Softlabs' side.

Action: a third-party security audit / penetration test covering the ticketing/client application, B2C and B2B applications, and mobile apps is required before go-live, with any identified severities to be resolved.

Decision: for the centralized platform, 4 environments (dev, QA, pre-prod, prod) will be maintained during the current active development phase, reducing to 3 (dev, pre-prod, prod) post-rollout; QA and dev may run as separate instances within a shared environment rather than fully separate environments. Client-owned infrastructure will continue to follow Softlabs' standard 2-environment model (pre-prod, prod).

- 4.5 Ticketing Configuration Walkthrough (presented by Allam)

- Walked through the end-to-end ticket configuration flow: basic information → ticket type configuration → validation → publish.

Reviewed the ticket types supported: Open-Dated ticket (no fixed visit date; used for general admission and B2B/travel-agent QR-code resale, e.g., bulk-issued tickets sold onward by travel agents), Group & Family ticket (configurable group size, with single-scan or multi-scan QR-code options), Membership/Subscription ticket (captures full guest details per member; supports renewal, upgrade and cancellation), Event ticket (requires date/time selection; supports resource management and capacity/reservation-based admission), Gift Voucher, and Money Card (e-wallet, to be discussed in a separate session).

Guest information capture (name, mobile number, nationality, visit survey, etc.) is configurable per ticket type — even an open-dated admission ticket can optionally be set up to collect this data.

Packages: multiple components (e.g., admission + F&B item + retail item, or admission + show) can be bundled with package-level pricing; a package is not required to include F&B or retail — any combination of ticket-type components can be bundled.

Reviewed event ticket setup in detail: event validity window; performances (recurring date/time slots); admission models (general admission, capacity control, reserved seating, resource control, or no admission control); seat map, section and quota-per-sales-channel configuration (shared pool or split inventory); and resource management (e.g., allocating vehicle and driver resources for an activity such as a desert safari, checked against availability before a ticket can be sold).

Reviewed supporting configuration areas: ticket variants (adult/child/senior/VIP, fully configurable), waitlist management, pre-sales/sales rules (on-sale/off-sale timing and cut-offs), entitlement and access rules (single/multi-venue, number of entries, zones, early-entry windows), fulfilment channels (email, WhatsApp, SMS), after-sales rules (upgrade, reschedule, cancellation windows), and dynamic/fixed pricing and promotions.

- 4.6 Workshop Planning

- Remaining product modules (continuation of ticket type/event configuration detail, resource management, wallets) will be covered in daily ~30–60 minute sessions going forward.

Qossai is finalizing the access control / facial recognition vendor selection this week, evaluating HID and Suprema (South Korea); vendor details will be shared once confirmed, expected this week or next.

### 5. Key Decisions & Agreements

- High availability will be applied selectively to critical, revenue-generating components (ticketing, POS, B2C); disaster recovery will be an optional, client-dependent add-on.

- Database segregation per microservice/module will be implemented from the start rather than retrofitted later.

- Reporting/analytics queries will run against a separate replica database, not the main transactional database.

- Infrastructure will start minimal and auto-scale progressively as tenant/client count grows, based on continuous monitoring and utilization-based scale-up triggers.

- 4 environments (dev, QA, pre-prod, prod) will be maintained during the current active development phase, reducing to 3 post-rollout.

- A third-party security audit / penetration test (ticketing, B2C, B2B, mobile apps) is required before go-live.

Ticket configuration will support six core ticket types — Open-Dated, Group/Family, Membership/Subscription, Event, Gift Voucher, and Money Card — each with independently configurable guest-data capture.

### 6. Open Items / Questions for Follow-Up

- Recommended infrastructure architecture proposal (AWS and Azure component options, three deployment scenarios, auto-scaling/failure-handling diagrams, and cost model at each scale) — pending from Dinesh/Softlabs.

- Pros-and-cons comparison of centralized vs. per-module database architecture — pending from Softlabs' internal session.

- Rough cost-tier expectations for small/medium vs. large tenants — to be discussed once Softlabs shares its architecture/cost proposal.

- Access control / facial recognition vendor selection (HID vs. Suprema) — pending from Qossai, expected this week or next.

`sources/mom/TICVAI_MoM_2026-08-25_Ticketing_ProductConfig.docx` · 2,561 words

### Minutes of Meeting

- Workshop — Ticketing & Product Configuration (Ticket Catalog, Ticket Types, Validity, Capacity, Entitlements & Policies)

### Date

- 25-August-2026

### Project

- TICVAI

### Meeting Type

- Product Workshop — Ticketing & Product Configuration Deep-Dive

### Prepared by

- Chitrangi Mestry

### Primary Objective

To walk through the back-end product/ticketing configuration module in detail — how products and tickets are created, the full range of ticket types and their rules, validity and expiry management, capacity and performance management, entitlements and access control, eligibility rules, special product types, and the policies and approval workflow governing publication — so the team can align on configuration strategy ahead of build.

### Participants

- TICVAI Team

- Softlabs Team

### Agenda

- Product/ticket catalog creation workflow — from scratch, templates, cloning, import from file, and AI-assisted draft creation

- Ticket configuration reference — identity & classification, category hierarchy, localization, attributes/metadata, preview and publish flow

- Ticket type deep-dive — open-dated, dated/special-day, time-slot (performance-based), multi-day, membership/pass, and camping/lesson-based tickets

- Product combination matrix (guest category, admission tier, residency) and ownership/anonymity rules

- Validity management and expiry rules

- Performances, capacity management and AI-driven demand suggestions

- Entitlements, access control and consumption tracking

- Eligibility rules, special product types, membership lifecycle and stored value

- Product relationships/bundles, add-ons, upsell/cross-sell, donation campaigns and policies

- AI governance — approval workflow, versioning and rollback

- Planning for the next session

### 4. Detailed Discussion

- 4.1 Product / Ticket Catalog Creation

Allam introduced the product lifecycle dashboard, showing overall counts of products in draft, in approval, and published status, with filters by venue/department — every product goes through an authorization step before it can be published online or on-site.

Reviewed the product creation wizard, offering four paths: create from scratch (step-by-step, field-by-field); create and save as a reusable template (e.g., an events template that can be replicated for each new event); clone an existing product (e.g., duplicating a general admission ticket to create a child ticket); and import from file, using a standard template shared with tenants/clients to collect their product and pricing information ahead of configuration.

Action: Allam to share the existing ticket configuration template (“technical data sheet,” with multiple sheets covering different information types) so the team can adapt it to TICVAI's own product strategy and database architecture.

AI-assisted draft: an AI wizard can ask the user what type of ticket they want to create and the relevant fields to capture, then auto-configure a draft ticket for review before approval and publish. Chinmay proposed extending this so the AI can also parse unstructured input (including OCR on images) and prompt the user for any missing details needed to complete the ticket — confirmed as a valid extension by Allam.

Chinmay noted the team already has a copy of the database schema showing which fields are captured for tickets, and will share it for cross-reference against the configuration template.

- 4.2 Ticket Configuration Reference

- Identity & classification: product name, product ID, main/sub-category, venue association (for multi-venue setups), and ticket type (single-day, multi-day, open-dated, performance-based).

Category hierarchy manager: packages and ticket types can be grouped and sorted under categories (e.g., admission > general admission > single-day, multi-day, annual pass, packages, vouchers).

- Content localization: separate content (images, descriptions) can be configured per sales channel (POS vs. B2C/B2B) and per language (e.g., English/Arabic).

Attributes & metadata: configurable ticket-level attributes such as minimum age, ID-proof requirements (e.g., Emirates ID for UAE-resident tickets, with format validation or photo upload), or embedded ID-reader integration for on-site verification — confirmed these are configurable per region/ticket rather than fixed.

Preview & publish: a product-review/preview step shows how the ticket will appear on the B2C front end before publishing. Chinmay requested this preview also cover the PDF ticket layout and Apple Wallet / Google Wallet formats so the reviewer can see all output formats, not only the web preview — Allam confirmed this is feasible as a separate design association.

- 4.3 Ticket Type Deep-Dive

Open-dated ticket: the simplest ticket type — name, description, price, and validity period (e.g., 1 day, 1 month, 6 months), with a configurable reservation rule controlling whether customer details (name, email, phone) are captured at point of sale.

Dated ticket with special-day setup: used for fixed-date tickets (e.g., a New Year ticket valid only on 1 January), with its own sales window and a configurable “allow date change” flag — typically disabled for special-day tickets given dedicated pricing, versus enabled for standard general-admission tickets.

Decision: date-change/reschedule policy will be a configurable, product-level on/off setting with its own policy rules (e.g., reschedule allowed up to 24 hours before visit, denied within 24 hours) rather than a separate dedicated screen — raised by Chinmay to reduce configuration complexity, agreed by Allam.

Time-slot (performance-based) ticket: requires configuration of early/late entry and an entry time window (e.g., entry allowed from 30 minutes before the event start until a defined cut-off).

Multi-day ticket: valid across multiple days/parks (e.g., a 3-day ticket), configurable as consecutive-day use or flexible use within a longer date range (e.g., any 3 days within a month).

Membership/pass ticket: seasonal, monthly, or annual membership classes with configurable renewal/auto-renewal, including tokenized card-on-file for auto-renewal billing ahead of expiry, subject to consent on terms and conditions.

Camping/lesson-based ticket: a performance-based ticket for recurring classes (e.g., ski or snowboard lessons held on a regular schedule), where the guest selects specific class dates/performances when purchasing a multi-lesson package.

- 4.4 Product Combination Matrix & Ownership

Products are classified using fully configurable components (e.g., guest category, admission tier, residency) rather than a fixed/predefined structure — e.g., resident/non-resident, then standard/VIP tier, then adult/child/youth within each tier. New components can be added as needed; not every venue will use every component (e.g., a venue with a simple product strategy may only need guest category).

- Ownership/anonymity: tickets can be configured as anonymous (no guest details required to purchase) or requiring captured details, depending on business need.

- 4.5 Validity Management & Expiry Rules

Validity types include fixed date-range validity, variable/rolling validity (e.g., 90 days from date of issue), and first-use activation (validity period starts when the ticket is first scanned rather than at date of sale) — the latter commonly used for memberships that start on first use rather than date of purchase.

- Weekday/calendar rules allow different validity and pricing for weekday-only vs. all-days products (e.g., Global Village's weekday vs. weekend-inclusive tickets).

Confirmed: a fallback/dynamic expiry rule is required for first-use-activation tickets — if a ticket is never scanned, it must still expire after a defined period (e.g., date of issue + 30 days) so revenue can be recognized rather than leaving tickets open indefinitely.

Blockout dates: certain ticket types (e.g., some memberships) can be excluded from use on public holidays or special event days, requiring the guest to purchase a separate ticket for those dates.

- 4.6 Performances & Capacity Management

Performances (time slots) can be created individually or via a reusable time-slot template (e.g., every 30 minutes from a start to end time) that auto-generates the full schedule for an event.

Capacity is set by default at the event level and inherited by all performances created for that event, with the ability to override capacity for specific performances (e.g., higher capacity for evening slots).

AI-driven suggestions: based on sales forecasts, the system can recommend adding/removing time slots, merging under-sold adjacent slots (with guest notification of the time change), and applying dynamic pricing (e.g., increase price when a slot is more than ~80% sold, decrease when under ~20–30%).

Two distinct capacity types were distinguished: sales capacity (how many tickets can be sold per performance) and admission capacity (a real-time, scan-based count of guests currently inside the venue via entry/exit turnstiles), used to cap total on-site attendance independent of how many tickets were sold for the day.

Decision: venue-level admission capacity should supersede event-level capacity, with a system prompt/validation preventing an event from being configured or sold beyond the remaining venue capacity; overriding this will be an authorization-gated (role-based access control) action for authorized users only.

Inventory pool association allows capacity to be split by ticket type (e.g., 50% general admission, 30% child, 20% senior) and/or by sales channel (e.g., 50% of an event's capacity reserved for online sale, 50% for on-site), with a capacity hierarchy of global → attraction → product → variant → time slot.

Cancellation/reschedule handling: when a booking is cancelled, refunded, or rescheduled, the business can configure whether that slot's capacity is released back into inventory for resale or held.

- 4.7 Entitlements & Access Control

Entitlements define what a ticket can redeem beyond admission — e.g., a combo ticket bundling park admission with an F&B item and a retail item, redeemed via QR-code scan at each respective counter.

Admission entitlements control number of entries permitted per ticket (e.g., maximum 2 entries); product entitlements define time-bound access to a specific experience (e.g., a 60-minute activity window starting from first scan).

F&B/retail entitlement via stored value: a combo product can bundle admission with a stored-value credit that the guest draws down against F&B or retail purchases (wallet mechanics to be covered in a dedicated session).

Discussion (referral-to-wallet): Chinmay raised whether referral rewards could be credited as currency/points directly into a guest's wallet (similar to consumer apps such as Swiggy), rather than only as a discount voucher. Qossai and Allam agreed this is a reasonable, business-configurable extension of the referral/loyalty entitlement model.

Check-in/check-out enforcement: if a guest exits without a matching checkout scan (e.g., a manually opened door), the system should flag and block a subsequent re-entry scan until check-in/check-out is properly reconciled.

A ticket look-up screen will show full consumption history for a ticket — transaction date/time, number of scans, expiry, and (if applicable) wallet balance and F&B/retail spend against that ticket.

- 4.8 Eligibility Rules, Special Products & Memberships

Eligibility rules are fully configurable and can include residency/nationality/geography restrictions (e.g., UAE-resident-only tickets requiring Emirates ID capture), minimum age (e.g., date-of-birth check for a minimum age activity), guest-profile category (e.g., VIP-only products), and minimum loyalty points or spend to qualify for a membership tier.

- Quantity and purchase limits can be set per order, per guest, per account category, and per sales channel (e.g., maximum 6 tickets per transaction).

Special product types — group tickets (configurable minimum/maximum group size, single or multiple QR codes), family tickets (configurable minimum/maximum composition), and corporate/allocation-based tickets — are managed within the same product configuration screen rather than requiring separate screens.

Membership lifecycle rules cover upgrade, downgrade, suspend (freezes validity until re-enabled), deactivate, and cancel, with configurable timing windows (e.g., upgrade allowed only in the final two months before expiry).

Stored value configuration covers minimum stored value, top-up maximum balance, expiry of stored balance, and refund destination (original payment method or credited back to wallet balance).

- 4.9 Bundles, Add-Ons, Donations & Policies

- Product relationships/bundles: multi-park and multi-attraction/multi-venue tickets can be visually mapped, showing which venues, meal vouchers, VIP parking, or upgrade options a bundle includes.

Add-ons, upsell and cross-sell: mandatory or optional add-ons can be attached to a main product; cross-sell offers related add-on products, while upsell proposes a higher-tier product (e.g., upselling an adult admission ticket to a membership).

Donation campaigns can be configured with fixed or variable amounts, enabled per sales channel, and triggered at a specific product level or across all products, with proceeds tracked to a separate account code.

Open question (raised by Chinmay): whether donation contributions should be taxable and require a taxation-module configuration — Allam's understanding is that donations are typically not taxable, but agreed the system should still support enabling/disabling a tax or service fee on donations if required. Chinmay to confirm the correct treatment.

Policy management covers reschedule, exchange, refund, cancellation, upgrade and downgrade rules, ownership transfer, and membership-to-pass conversion — all managed centrally rather than through separate screens.

- Each product is also mapped to pricing, chart-of-accounts/GL account code, promotion/discount linkages, and sales-channel availability.

- 4.10 AI Governance & Publish Workflow

The AI governance/dashboard view shows product counts by status (draft, pending approval, approved, published) and supports versioned publishing — each price, terms, or policy revision is tracked as a new version.

- Role-based approval: publish rights are restricted to the user/department authorized to approve a given product change.

- Version history and rollback: if a published change causes an issue, the system should support rolling back to a prior published version.

- 4.11 UX Simplification & Distributed Inventory

Requested: Chinmay flagged that the number of configuration screens/pages should be reduced and related settings/toggles consolidated, to avoid an overly long, click-heavy configuration flow for admins; Allam agreed and referred the team to the previous system's demo as a starting reference for simplification.

- Confirmed (Chinmay Patkar): inventory can be distributed across sales channels and will be configurable at the venue/event level.

### 5. Key Decisions & Agreements

- Date-change/reschedule behavior will be a configurable on/off setting with associated policy rules, not a dedicated separate screen.

- Venue-level admission capacity will supersede event-level capacity, with a system-enforced validation and a role-based override for authorized users only.

- Guest/ID-proof attributes (e.g., Emirates ID, passport, handicap/PoD documentation) are configurable per ticket and per region rather than fixed system behavior.

Special product types (group, family, corporate) and all policy types (reschedule, exchange, refund, cancellation, upgrade, downgrade) will be managed within the unified product configuration screen rather than separate dedicated screens.

- Referral rewards may be extended to credit currency/points directly into a guest's wallet, in addition to discount vouchers, as a business-configurable option.

- The preview/publish step will be extended to show PDF ticket and Apple Wallet / Google Wallet formats, not only the B2C web preview.

### 6. Open Items / Questions for Follow-Up

- VAT/tax treatment for donation contributions, and whether a taxation-module configuration is required — pending confirmation from Chinmay.

- Simplified, reduced-click configuration flow proposal, referencing the previous system's demo — pending from Softlabs.

- Ticket configuration template (“technical data sheet”) and database schema/field list cross-reference — pending exchange between Allam and Chinmay.

- Hardware specification document — to be aligned internally by Allam/Qossai and presented to the team shortly after this session.

- Events configuration document (sent separately) — to be reviewed given its overlap with today's ticketing discussion.
